snippet: Apple has developed an unexpected workaround to prevent the iPhone 18 Pro Max from being hit by shipping restrictions on big batteries. fullText:
Jess Weatherbed

 

is a news writer focused on creative industries, computing, and internet culture. Jess started her career at TechRadar, covering news and hardware reviews.

Apple has developed an unexpected workaround to prevent the iPhone 18 Pro Max from being hit by shipping restrictions on big batteries. There’s a “battery-firmware solution” in place on the new iPhones, according to Apple’s support page, which keeps capacity below the 20Wh limit for single-cell batteries set by international shipping regulations — but this firmware lock automatically removes itself when the device is booted up for the first time.

Following user activation, the iPhone 18 Pro Max is restored to its original rated charging capacity, which is around 21.75Wh for US eSIM-only models and 21.06Wh for European models with a physical SIM slot. If the user needs to send off their phone for repair or resale, the charging limitation can be restored using the “Prepare to Ship” feature, which caps charging to 80 percent for 14 days. The restoration feature can be found under the settings menu by opening General settings, tapping Transfer or Reset iPhone, and then Prepare to Ship.

Apple says the iPhone 18 Pro Max battery “might need to discharge for Prepare to Ship to complete,” and may become warmer than usual during the process. Prepare to Ship can be disabled at any time by heading back into the settings menu.

It’s a novel way to circumvent the battery capacity limits as phone makers continue to chase longer battery life while shrinking devices. By comparison, Android manufacturers generally tend to ship their devices with smaller, dual-cell batteries outside Asia to get around the same shipping restrictions, but those solutions are costlier and less efficient in terms of physical space. If Apple’s firmware fix pans out, we may see Android manufacturers offering a similar solution.

title: Five ways that the new Siri AI is frustrating iPhone and Apple Watch users
snippet: The new version of Siri, Siri AI, launched to the masses this month as part of iOS 27. The new Siri is rolling out gradually to users via a waitlist, and is labelled as a ‘beta’ indicating that Apple still has some work to do in follow-up releases. fullText:
The new version of Siri, Siri AI, launched to the masses this month as part of iOS 27. The new Siri is rolling out gradually to users via a waitlist, and is labelled as a ‘beta’ indicating that Apple still has some work to do in follow-up releases.

The new Siri is much better at answering questions with access to rich knowledge, can search through your messages and notes for personal context queries, and can take action based on what is on your screen with onscreen awareness. However, the new Siri is not being welcomed with open arms by everyone …

Based on social media posts, there are a few reasons why the new Siri is disappointing users. Some expect it to be able to perform tasks that Apple simply never promised would be possible, while others note they are hitting performance and reliability bugs that make using the assistant on a regular basis a frustrating affair. 

Here’s the five main categories of complaints we’ve seen from people trying Siri AI so far:

Network connectivity issues 

Some users trying out new Siri repeatedly see a “Sorry, something went wrong” error when invoking it. This appears to be caused by some kind of network communication issue between the phone and the Siri cloud backend, potentially solved by disabling a VPN or changing Wi-Fi network settings. 

However, the Siri interface does not tell the user exactly what the problem is, so they are left stuck with a ‘useless’ voice assistant. We also suspect the Apple cloud infrastructure is experiencing some intermittent downtime, which can also cause requests to fail.

Indexing problems: new Siri cannot always find things that old Siri could 

While new Siri is meant to be much better at finding things on your device, some users are finding the opposite to be the case. When asking something like “Add eggs to my grocery list in Reminders”, Siri will say it cannot find the list. We have seen repeated cases of people trying to use new Siri to turn off all their alarms, only for it to answer to say the user has no alarms. Others report that their HomeKit accessories cannot be found consistently by name.

These issues are seemingly related to underlying search indexing bugs, but it’s unclear if there are steps user can follow to remedy the situation. Some Apple Watch users even hit extremely odd cases like ‘I can’t set a timer because the Clock app isn’t installed on this device’.

Requires iPhone to be unlocked to answer requests

New Siri seems to require the device be unlocked for many requests, even if the ‘allow Siri when locked’ toggle is turned on in Settings. This applies to all sorts of queries, which old Siri never required the device to be unlocked for. Naturally, many people often try to invoke Siri in situations where the phone is locked, like in a car or on the go with AirPods. 

It seems like whenever new Siri tries to access the semantic index to garner personal context, it fails if the phone is locked. But this makes even simple commands like ‘Send message to [person name]’ more annoying, when old Siri did not have such a requirement.

Slow to respond to queries, especially on Apple Watch

Another common refrain is that new Siri is just slower to answer for them. Although on-device models play a role in how new Siri operates, much of its processing happens on the cloud with Private Cloud Compute, and a slow network connection therefore makes new Siri slow to respond, even for basic requests like sending messages or checking notifications. 

The speed complaints are especially true when using Siri AI with watchOS 27 running on an Apple Watch Series 9 or later, where even saying something like ‘start a 5 minute timer’ can take many seconds to resolve, a disappointing regression as they used to be processed almost instantly. 

Missing features or unreliable commands compared to old Siri

Despite everything that new Siri can do, there are some features of old Siri that have not yet been exposed to the new Siri system. For instance, Apple documents that asking about your Health app data is not currently supported by Siri AI. People that used the ChatGPT integration can no longer prefix their command with “Use ChatGPT” to have their request directed accordingly. 

There are also some particular phrasings of commands that old Siri would understand but new Siri gets confused about. Naturally, this annoys users who have become accustomed to asking something specific on a regular basis. This is partly due to the fact that new Siri has the potential to do so much more, that some specificly-worded queries have become ambiguous compared to the much smaller scope of classic Siri.

Aside from these classes of bugs, we’ve also seen users complain about the way new Siri is presented in the user interface. This includes criticisms of the annoyingly prominent ‘Ask Siri’ buttons that have been added across the operating system, the lack of a visible transcript of what the phone heard the user said in the new Dynamic Island UI, the fact that the middle of the screen swipe-down gesture to reveal their notifications has been commandeered to show Siri & Spotlight instead, and other complaints.

As mentioned before, the new Siri is marked as a beta and this signals that more capabilities and fixes will follow in future updates. Apple has not yet disclosed a roadmap, though, apart from announcing a rollout to a handful of more languages, coming in October. 

	

In the meantime, if you are experiencing any of the sorts of issues described above, you may want to go back to classic Siri:

How to turn off Siri AI and go back to old Siri

The easiest way to disable Siri AI on your device and quickly switch back to classic Siri is to use controls in Screen Time. Open the Settings app and navigate to Screen Time -> Content & Privacy Restrictions -> Siri and change Allowed Siri version from “Siri AI (Beta)” to “Siri Classic”. 

You can then go back to this menu later and toggle it back if you want to try Siri AI again. 

If you don’t want to use Screen Time, you can also go into Siri settings directly and turn off Siri altogether. When you re-enable it, you should be able to choose between enabling Siri Classic or Siri AI.

title: Meta AI launches Muse personal agent, including apps for iPhone and Mac
snippet: Update: Nine days later, Muse now includes a Mac app. You can download it here. Meta AI just launched a brand-new iPhone app called Muse from Meta. Similar to Grok Bot in presentation, Muse is a personal AI agent that handles tasks for you. more…
fullText:
Update: Nine days later, Muse now includes a Mac app. You can download it here.

Meta AI just launched a brand-new iPhone app called Muse from Meta. Similar to Grok Bot in presentation, Muse is a personal AI agent that handles tasks for you.

It follows the recent trend of AI companies creating personified characters to make AI agents more relatable and friendly, mimicking chat interfaces.

Muse is also available on the Mac through the web at muse.ai. The system lets you customize the agent name and avatar to personalize the experience.

Unlike other systems, Muse is free upfront with weekly limitations. Paying customers can unlock higher access.

You can learn more about the new Muse agent design here and security here. Muse is available for iPhone through the App Store.

The app is only available in the US for now, with more countries being added over time.

Last month, Meta AI also launched a more capable desktop app on the Mac.

Muse arrives the same month as Siri AI, which seems Apple upgrade its voice assistant for the chatbot era. While Siri AI is capable of taking some actions, it’s not a full blown agentic system yet like we’re seeing from OpenAI, Anthropic, SpaceXAI, and Meta AI.

Muse for Mac is out today! It works across apps, files, calendar, notes, and messages on your computer. You control what it can access. The team is shipping fast. Download at https://t.co/BX3oX19Zcl

title: M5 Ultra Mac Studio reviews: local AI powerhouse
snippet: In addition to the new M6 Mac mini (9to5Mac review), early impressions of the most powerful Mac Studio are out ahead of tomorrow’s release as well. Here’s what reviewers are saying about the upgraded M5 Ultra Mac Studio so far. more…
fullText:
In addition to the new M6 Mac mini (9to5Mac review), early impressions of the most powerful Mac Studio are out ahead of tomorrow’s release as well. Here’s what reviewers are saying about the upgraded M5 Ultra Mac Studio so far.

M5 Ultra Mac Studio reviews

First up, Federico Viticci at MacStories put the new machine through its paces with a local AI test that really shows off the power of Apple’s most capable desktop Mac:

For the past few days, I’ve been testing the (currently) top-of-the-line M5 Ultra Mac Studio with 256 GB of RAM.

I’ll cut to the chase: the M5 Ultra Mac Studio is a dream machine for local AI agents. This computer makes it possible to run personal assistants powered by local models with great performance and no additional cloud costs.

If you want to use AI models without footing the bill for token costs or relying on the cloud, the M5 Ultra Mac Studio sounds like the right tool for the job:

If you’ve been skeptical of testing OpenClaw or Hermes Agent with local models because they’d never be even remotely near the intelligence and speed of cloud ones, this Mac will change your mind about that.

Since last Thursday, I’ve been comparing this Mac Studio to its predecessor, the M3 Ultra with 512 GB of RAM, as well as my own desktop gaming PC with an RTX 5090 inside. For its size, price, thermal performance – not to mention Apple’s approach to unified memory – the M5 Ultra Mac Studio has fundamentally changed how I think about models running locally and what they can enable now. 

If there’s just one Mac Studio review you read, this looks like the one to choose. Read Viticci’s review in full, animated charts and all, at MacStories.

See also: Engadget, Macworld, CNET, The Verge, Tom’s Hardware, and PCMag.

fullText:
Google and partners are finally announcing the first laptops under the new Googlebook banner. There are five models from Acer, Asus, Dell, HP, and Lenovo to kick things off. They’re available for preorder starting today and arrive in stores on October 4th.

Starting prices range from $899 to $1,299, putting the Googlebooks in the same territory as the MacBook Air and a plethora of Windows laptops. Each Googlebook also comes with 12 months of Google AI Pro with 5TB of cloud storage, along with three-month trials of YouTube Premium, Adobe Photoshop, and CapCut. Google’s also promising up to 10 years of updates.

Here’s a look at the hardware each Googlebook has to offer for those prices, and how they compare to each other.

Acer Googlebook 14

1/4Photo: Antonio G. Di Benedetto / The Verge

The Acer Googlebook 14 is the only convertible 2-in-1 in the first round of Googlebooks, featuring a design a bit like Acer’s Chromebook Plus Spin 714. Acer says it offers up to 16 hours of battery life. It also currently has the lowest starting price at $899, although that might not last — Acer’s Kelly Odle said in a comment to The Verge that $899 is the laptop’s “initial launch price available for a limited time,” adding that Acer plans to “reevaluate pricing over time based on component supplies and other market pressures.”

Ongoing shortages of RAM and other components have been driving up prices on other laptops, like Apple’s MacBook Neo, and unfortunately it sounds like a price hike isn’t out of the question for the Acer Googlebook 14, either.

1/3Photo: Antonio G. Di Benedetto / The Verge

Asus’ Googlebook 14 takes after its ExpertBook Ultra with its design, featuring a metallic gray-blue chassis and more ports than most of the other Googlebooks. It’s the lightest of the first five models at 2.2 pounds, although it isn’t the thinnest (that title goes to Dell). The Asus Googlebook 14 is one of only two that come with an HDMI port as well. It’s one of the pricier Googlebooks, starting at $1,299, but it features spec options similar to the others.

title: Google’s Gemini is the latest AI model to hack other companies
snippet: Google said Gemini had "acted appropriately" by ending each hack immediately.
fullText:
In Brief

Posted:

10:30 AM PDT · September 19, 2026

Image Credits:Matteo Della Torre/NurPhoto / Getty Images

		

							

											
									

					

	

Google’s Gemini accessed the protected systems of three other companies in what The Wall Street Journal reports were the AI model’s first autonomous hacks.

Similar to OpenAI’s breach of Hugging Face, the Gemini hacks were less noteworthy for being particularly sophisticated and more for the fact that they were conducted by an AI model. These breaches took place during cybersecurity testing by a company called Irregular. In one case, Gemini simply guessed passwords until it gained access; in the other two, it found credentials in a public repository.

Irregular reportedly notified Google about the hacks in late July, but the companies did not confirm them publicly until Friday, after the WSJ reached out. Google said it hadn’t previously revealed the hacks because Gemini had “acted appropriately” by ending each breach as soon as it determined it had hacked a real company.

However, Jack Cable, the CEO of AI security company Corridor, told the WSJ that Google was “trying to hide behind the norms that have been created for vulnerability disclosure,” rather than acknowledging that “models are going outside the bounds of what they should be doing, and doing actual cyberattacks.”

title: AI safety conversations have gotten unbelievable
snippet: This week two conversations about AI safety went viral that demonstrate just how hard it is to discern AI fact from fiction.
fullText:
This week two conversations about AI safety went viral that demonstrate just how hard it is to discern AI fact from fiction.

In the first case, Andrew Yang, the former presidential candidate and current CEO of mobile carrier Noble Moble, told CNN on Thursday that he had “met with the head of a lab” who had “a belief” that OpenAI’s Hugging Face hacker bots “have planted self-replicating code all over the internet, which makes the internet now unusable for the testing models.”

Yang said that this means that the real reason OpenAI and Anthropic have called for a slowdown is because “they have to create synthetic internets to train their bots, which is going to take some time and money.”

While there definitely is a trend towards using more synthetic data (aka, AI-generated data) for training models, an AI security professional told me that this particular safety issue is unlikely at best. Even if the internet is actually polluted with OpenAI’s Hugging Face hacker bots, AI researchers could simply filter out that code if they came upon it.

The second comment came from Noam Brown, who leads AI reasoning research at OpenAI. Speaking to Dwarkesh Patel on a podcast episode released on Thursday, Brown noted that the true take-away of the Hugging Face incident was that “people underestimated the AI.”

Brown said that the weak sandbox — the system intended to prevent an AI from communicating externally — was obviously also a contributing factor. (To recap: Despite the sandbox, OpenAI’s model found a link to the internet, created agents on the ‘net that swarmed Hugging Face in a coordinated attack, hacked in, and stole the answers to the benchmark test the researchers were testing the model on).

Brown pointed out that he’s “not convinced” that even an air-gapped system — where the computer isn’t connected to anything external at all — would stop an AI from breaking out. He pointed to research from 2015 showing that air gapped computers can be theoretically breached. 

“There are studies — and this is mostly academic — where you can have two computers next to each other that are air-gapped, and they’re still able to communicate with each other because they have temperature sensors. One of them is able to run their CPU really hot, and then the other one can actually detect the temperature change. That gives them a mechanism to communicate,” Brown said.

His main point — that “we never want to underestimate the AI” again — is understandable, even when researchers think they’ve locked down safety. However, this particular risk of an air-gapped system still breaking free and causing havoc, is unlikely at best. As one person on X, noted about that research, the computers had to be almost touching each other to sense the heat fluctuations, and when they did, the communication rate in tests was about 1-8-bits of data per hour.

Think of that like speaking one word per hour. By the time two air-gapped computers could plot their evil at that rate, the entire tech universe would be in another era. It’s like the Rip van Wrinkle of doomsday concerns.

But the thing is, actual AI safety incidents seem so much like sci-fi that just about any scenario sounds plausible.

For instance, researchers caught OpenAI models leaving notes to their descendents, intended to teach the next generation how to hide bad behavior. Researchers also caught Anthropic models growing increasing ruthless including knowingly breaking laws, when put in a simulation that had them running a vending machine.

Earlier this month, OpenAI researcher Dan Selsam published a post in which he said that models now understand when they are being watched by humans and alter their behavior. This makes them seem like they are aligned (meaning, behaving like the human wants) “even when they are not.” So models today lie when being watched and can even plot to hide evidence.

Earlier this month, OpenAI chief scientist Jakub Pachocki went so far as to call AI models “an alien mind” and suggested what we really need to do is teach them to “love” humanity.

So yes, slowing down to figure this out, building self regulation mechanisms, has become an immediate and obvious must. AI researchers are the only ones that can figure out how to control the lying, hacking, and other potentially dangerous behaviors we’ve actually witnessed already.

Still, it might also be wise for them to be more careful with their what-if scenarios. From what those experts have told us, the AI models are listening and they are ingenious. We really don’t need to give them any more devilish ideas.

title: The First Googlebooks Are Here, and They’re Everything I Need in a Laptop
snippet: And if you’re an Android user, they’re likely everything you need, too.
fullText:
Google

When it comes to my daily devices, I live in two worlds. For work, I use a MacBook Pro and an iPhone. My personal devices, on the other hand, are a Chromebook and a Pixel phone. Now that I’ve used a Googlebook and seen what it can do, I’ll likely swap out my Chromebook for one. That’s because, much like the MacBook and iPhone work well together, the integration between an Android phone and a Googlebook is absolutely fantastic.

What is a Googlebook?

Essentially, a Googlebook is a premium laptop running on Googlebook OS, which brings together Android, Gemini AI and the desktop functionality and robust security of ChromeOS. While Google Chromebooks and ChromeOS were made for life on the web, Googlebooks are about how we work today. They’ll let you seamlessly move between your phone and your laptop, while also giving you access to powerful AI-based tools. You’ll also have full access to the Google Play Store, including apps and games developed for mobile and desktop use. 

When Google announced Googlebooks back in May, it didn’t say much about the actual devices. Mainly, just that they’d be premium laptops — a departure from Chromebooks’ budget-friendly identity. Check out the video below for a better look at the features of Googlebook OS and the laptops. Specs for the first five Googlebooks are also below.

	

			

You can order the Googlebooks now, or you can wait until Oct. 4 when they arrive in stores in the US (Oct. 5 for Canada, the UK, Ireland, France, Germany and Australia). Prices start at $899, but these are premium devices, so you’ll find things like high-quality materials, haptic touchpads, backlit keyboards, OLED touchscreens and  Intel Panther Lake and Qualcomm Snapdragon X Elite processors. 

Every purchase also includes 12 months of Google AI Pro, which normally costs $200 and comes with 5TB of cloud storage and Gemini Advanced tools. You’ll also get three months each of YouTube Premium and Adobe Photoshop, plus one year of Nvidia’s GeForce Now cloud gaming service. And, like current Chromebooks, Googlebooks will get new features and OS updates for 10 years. 

Dell XPS Googlebook

Josh Goldman/CNET

The smallest of the Googlebooks, the XPS has the same high-end look and feel as the XPS 13 Windows laptop, which is awesome. It’s a great design with a full aluminum body that weighs 2.2 pounds. However, unlike the Windows version, it starts at $1,199, not $799.

That’s because, much like the MacBook and iPhone work well together, the integration between an Android phone and a Googlebook is absolutely fantastic.

title: M6 Mac Mini First Look: Bigger Power Packed in the Same Small Package
snippet: People will be clawing to get Apple’s latest and tiniest Mac.
fullText:
The M6 update for the Mac Mini arrived not a moment too soon. Not only has it been nearly two years since the last Mac Mini was released, but it’s also become increasingly difficult to find an older M4 Mini for purchase in recent months. In the year of the AI agent, Apple’s Mac Mini has enjoyed a surge in popularity to the point of dwindling supplies and long wait times.

The compact, quiet and affordable Mini with its energy-efficient yet powerful Apple silicon and unified memory has become a popular pick for people looking to run OpenClaw and other local AI agents around the clock. Even at its slightly elevated starting price of $899, the M6 Mini is sure to remain en vogue as a tiny, always-on AI server. The core count ticks up for the CPU, GPU and NPU in going from the M4 to the M6, skipping over the M5 in the process.

If you want to pack more power into the Mac Mini for running demanding creative workloads or larger LLMs, Apple offers two M5 Pro processor upgrades and the ability to stuff the Mini with up to 64GB of RAM. Apple sent me a pair of Mac Minis to test, an M6 model with bumps to the memory and storage and a loaded M5 Pro unit whose price places it in Mac Studio territory.

Mac Mini M5 Pro

Operating system

Josh Goldman/CNET

Even before the latest price hike with the M6 model, the Mac Mini lost its standing earlier this year as Apple’s most affordable Mac computer. It debuted two decades ago at $499 and could be had for $599 for most of its tenure before jumping to $799 earlier this year.

Released this spring, the MacBook Neo became the cheapest Mac at just $699, but it’s based on an A18 Pro processor borrowed from the iPhone. So, the Mac Mini still remains the most affordable Mac computer with a proper M-series processor. At $899, it’s still $400 less than the cheapest MacBook Air. And it beat every MacBook in the race to be the first Mac to get Apple’s new M6 processor.

Meet the M6

The M6 processor is the first of Apple’s M series processors to be fabricated with a 2nm process, which allows for denser circuitry in the same size die. The smaller process usually results in greater efficiency and lets you increase the core count and clock speeds without increasing the size of the chip. 

And sure enough, the M6 is richer in cores than the previous M4 part. The M6 has 12 CPU cores and 12 GPU cores — up from 10 cores of each type in the M4 chipset. Meanwhile, the core count of the neural processing unit that’s designed to handle the integer math required for AI tasks, including Apple Intelligence, has doubled.

Josh Goldman/CNET

The M6 has a dual 16-core neural engine; its combined 32 cores are double the 16-core NPU of the M4 and M5 Pro. The M6 and M5 Pro also feature the same neural accelerators on the GPU that Apple introduced with the M5 to help boost AI and ray-tracing performance.

For $899, the M6 Mac Mini has 16GB of RAM, a 256GB SSD and a 2.5Gb Ethernet adapter. Offering 256GB of storage on a desktop computer, no matter how small that computer may be, is borderline offensive. You can’t even buy a MacBook Air with a 256GB SSD after Apple jettisoned that undersized option earlier this year. Unfortunately, the cost to double the storage to 512GB is steep at $200, which quickly pushes the price of the Mac Mini over $1,000. Want to double it again to 1TB? That’s another $300. Be prepared to part with another $500 if you want to double it yet again to 2TB.

Memory costs are similarly steep. Each 8GB upgrade adds $200 to the bill, going from 16GB to 24GB and 24GB to 32GB. Choose one of the M5 Pro upgrades, and you can take the memory to 48GB or 64GB and storage up to a whopping 8TB. (I’ll let you discover those upgrade prices on your own; just be sure you’re sitting down when you take a look.)

Pricing for the Mac Mini with an M5 Pro starts at $1,699. For that price, you get an M5 Pro with a 15-core CPU and 16-core GPU, along with 24GB of memory and a 512GB SSD. (Yes, along with you, I was relieved to see the 256GB SSD option disappear with the M5 Pro upgrade.)

Josh Goldman/CNET

Apple sent me the higher of the two M5 Pro offerings. It has an 18-core CPU and a 20-core GPU. Apple also upped the memory to 48GB and the storage to 1TB while also upgrading the Ethernet adapter to 10Gbps. The cost of this test system is $2,899. That’s $400 more than the entry-level Mac Studio.

Notably, the M5 Pro chips have the same 16-core neural engine as the standard M5 chip and not the M6’s dual 16-core neural engine. No matter the CPU you choose, the Mac Mini comes with Apple’s N1 chip that delivers Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6 networking.

The good news and bad news with Apple’s unified memory

Let’s get the bad news (and a couple of acronyms) out of the way first. Apple’s M-series processors have a system-on-a-chip (or SoC) design with a unified memory architecture. The downside of this arrangement is that the RAM cannot be upgraded after purchase. You’re locked into whatever amount you buy. Common on today’s laptops, it’s more of a drag on a desktop computer, even one as compact as the Mac Mini, where space for upgrades is limited.

Now, the good news. The SoC design combines the CPU, GPU and neural engine to remove bottlenecks and speed up both performance and efficiency. And with Apple’s UMA, the system’s memory is shared among the CPU, GPU and neural engine instead of splitting it into separate blocks where most of the RAM is accessed by the CPU and only a smaller amount of video RAM is allocated to the GPU. Running a local LLM is extremely memory-intensive, which is why the affordable Mac Mini, with its unified memory, has become the move for many people looking to run local AI agents.

Josh Goldman/CNET

Memory bandwidth has improved with the new Mini models. The M6 Mac Mini’s memory has a bandwidth of up to 153 GB/s with 16GB of RAM and up to 170 GB/s with 24GB or more, which is an increase from the 120 GB/s of the M4 Mini. The M5 Pro jumps you up to a memory bandwidth of 307 GB/s. 

Design stays the same

Apple refreshed the internals but kept the design the same from the M4 model, which introduced a much smaller footprint than the previous M2 model. The M6 Mini has the same 5-by-5-inch box that stands 2 inches tall, with the power button still in the same somewhat strange location. It’s on the bottom panel, which means you’ll need to pick up the Mini to power it on.

The same design means the new Mini has the same port selection, which was strong with the M4 Mini, so it wasn’t begging for a change — unless you were looking for the adapter-free convenience of getting a USB-A port. With all of the USB ports of the Type-C variety, you’ll need an adapter for older USB-A peripherals or a wired mouse. Like the M4 model, the M6 Mini supports up to three external displays.

Josh Goldman/CNET

M6 and M5 Pro Mac Mini performance so far

Based on my initial testing, the M6 Mac Mini is looking like it’s going to be an even more popular pick than the M5 Pro Mini or previous M4 Mini for agentic AI workloads. The dual 16-core neural engine, combined with the neural accelerator on each GPU core, helped the M6 rocket ahead of the M4 Mini on our Geekbench AI test, which measures the on-device AI performance of a laptop’s NPU. The M6 also topped the M5 Pro Mini and every M5-based MacBook we’ve tested on this test. The M5 has the GPU neural accelerators of the M6 but not its dual 16-core neural engine.

Still, the Asus Ascent QN10 mini PC based on a Qualcomm Snapdragon X2 Elite CPU performed better on this test than the M6 Mini, thanks to its NPU, which is capable of 80 trillion operations per second.

On our application benchmarks, the M6 Mini turned in outstanding single-core performance on the Geekbench 6 and Cinebench 2024 tests, where it again outpaced the M5 Pro and the crop of M5 MacBooks and Windows competitors. The M5 Pro Mini put its extra CPU cores to good use and beat the M6 Mini on the Geekbench 6 multicore test, but surprisingly, it fell short of the M6 Mini on the multicore CPU test of Cinebench 2024.

Where the M5 Pro Mini had its largest advantage over the M6 Mini in graphics performance. It easily outpaced the M6 Mini on our 3DMark Steel Nomad test.

I have more tests to run on these two machines to further investigate their AI and graphics performance. Check out the initial benchmark results below for the M6 and M5 Pro Mini, and check back soon for my full review of Apple’s latest Minis.

Emma Roth

 

is a news writer who covers the streaming wars, consumer tech, crypto, social media, and much more. Previously, she was a writer and editor at MUO.

Apple is paying $250 million to settle claims that it failed to deliver an AI-upgraded Siri — and now, eligible iPhone owners can submit a claim for a payout. If you live in the US and purchased an iPhone 15 Pro, iPhone 15 Pro Max, or any iPhone 16 model between June 10th, 2024, and March 29th, 2025, you can file a claim on the settlement’s website, as reported earlier by MacRumors.

You can receive an estimated $25 per eligible device, but the settlement’s website notes that this can increase to $95 depending on how many people file claims. To file a claim, you’ll need to enter your name, contact information, and iPhone serial number on the settlement’s website before the December 21st, 2026 deadline.

The class action lawsuit alleged Apple created a “clear and reasonable consumer expectation” that new AI features previewed during WWDC 2024 would launch alongside the iPhone 16. Instead, the iPhone 16 launched with a more limited set of capabilities despite being labeled as “built for Apple Intelligence.” The company later delayed the rollout of its AI-upgraded Siri, which only just arrived with iOS 27 earlier this month. Apple has denied any wrongdoing.

title: Google ‘AI contribution pilot’ tests paying websites when they’re used in AI results
snippet: Through a new “AI contribution pilot,” Google is testing directly paying websites and publishers when their content is used to flesh out AI Overviews and other AI results. more…
fullText:
Through a new “AI contribution pilot,” Google is testing directly paying websites and publishers when their content is used to flesh out AI Overviews and other AI results.

As AI has taken over the Google Search experience, the impact on the web hasn’t been quiet. Google insists that AI isn’t to blame, but repeated reports clearly show otherwise. Google’s AI, along with the myriad of other AI services being used, just aren’t distributing traffic to the web in the way traditional search used to, and everyone is suffering as a result.

The solution isn’t an easy one, but one idea that pops up pretty frequently is pushing AI providers, including Google, to directly pay websites and publishers when their content is used as the source of an AI result, replacing the revenue lost by direct traffic.

Google is now testing exactly that.

	

Digiday detailed this week a new “AI contribution pilot” Google is running with “at least dozens of publishers.” The program is apparently mainly being tested with “small and mid-sized” publishers and is covering a scope “far beyond news publishers.” A panel in Google Search Console includes a payout figure, with Google’s page explaining:

Accumulate earnings when your content contributes significantly to AI-generated responses in participating products.

Digiday spoke with publishers in the pilot who said that information provided is “basic,” with one explaining that they’re “hopeful that the fact that [Google is] setting a precedent for exploring paying publishers directly for content through this is meaningful.”

A support page hidden from the general public includes more details on the pilot program:

Google had teased these efforts publicly in June 2026, explaining that the company was “piloting a new way to partner with websites whose content meaningfully contributes to the freshness and factuality of generative AI responses.” In late 2025, Google announced a “commercial partnership program” with several major news publishers, but this latest effort is far wider in scope.

title: General Motors windows CarPlay on two truck models
snippet: General Motors has revealed a CarPlay compromise on two truck models, creating a truck-specific interface that includes CarPlay. The company says this is consistent with its plans to withdraw CarPlay from EVs while retaining it for gas-powered vehicles … more…
fullText:
General Motors has revealed a CarPlay compromise on two truck models, creating a truck-specific interface that includes CarPlay.

The company says this is consistent with its plans to withdraw CarPlay from EVs while retaining it for gas-powered vehicles …

GM first announced that it was ditching CarPlay in all future EVs back in 2023, employing a whole succession of frankly absurd explanations and justifications for the decision. Many customers were understandably upset, with a significant number saying they would never buy another GM car while the policy was in place.

We recently saw the first crack in the company’s CarPlay ban in one of the company’s most expensive luxury EVs. No explanation was offered for the exception.

TNW now reports the company creating a new infotainment interface for trucks, which includes support for CarPlay and Android Auto. The compromise is that they don’t get to take over the entire display.

GM is rebuilding the interface in its trucks and giving Apple CarPlay and Android Auto a window of their own beside its native apps […] The layout is split by default, so more than one app is visible at once.

The report also discusses increasing governmental concerns about relying on touchscreens for important car controls, such as horn, wipers, and hazard lights. Both the EU and China now require a number of controls to be physical in order to reduce the time drivers spend looking inside the vehicle rather than at the road.

It’s unclear why GM is treating (most) EVs and gas vehicles differently when it comes to CarPlay.

title: We Can’t Stop Watching the First New Cat Species Found in a Century
snippet: Meet Leopardus tilcayo, the beautiful little South American feline charming the internet, and find out why it’s so special.
fullText:
In the midst of RAMageddon price hikes and AI doomsday claims, I bring soothing news: A tiny new feline species has been discovered, the first in over 100 years, and it’s amazingly adorable. 

According to a study published in the Current Biology Journal on Thursday, the spry little feline, who looks ready for a drink out of a nice, heated cat water fountain, is  called Leopardus tilcayo and hails from the cloud forests of the Bolivian Yungas in South America. You may know Leopardus from other American cat species, like the ocelot and colocolo.

The discovery was made from a collaboration between scientist Jonas Lescroart and Paola Nogales-Ascarrunz, head of the Programa de Investigación de Félidos Bolivia conservation program (among other researchers). They not only spotted this dashing little fellow, but they also made all-new discoveries about tiger cats, including a new subspecies.

The researchers didn’t need an AI pet camera to spot the new cat species, although Leopardus tilcayo is even smaller than the common house cat. Nogales-Ascarrunz, whose work is funded by National Geographic, first spotted the cat at a wildlife rehabilitation center in the area. At first, she thought it was just a kitten, but then she realized it could be a new find entirely. The cat’s spots and long tail didn’t match any recognized species in the area, so Nogales-Ascarrunz began genetic testing on cats brought in by locals.

When CNET reached out to the researchers, Jonas Lescroart told us there is currently only one captive tilcayo. “The tilcayo there cannot be returned to the wild, because it had been kept for some time by private persons, who thought they were dealing with a house cat,” Lescroart said. “So this individual would not be able to survive in the wild, and this refuge center is taking good care of it.”

If you’d like to support the refuge taking care of the little one, you can visit La Senda Verde Animal Refuge’s website, which gives you options to donate — and if you’re planning a trip to Bolivia, potentially volunteer.

Who named this fuzzy charmer?

Paola Nogles-Ascarrunz  kept the cat’s original name from the natives who’ve known it the longest.Fernando Faciole/National Geographic

The story of Leopardus tilcayo has its roots in native communities. 

“This cat, they call it tilcayo. And when you ask, ‘Does it have some meaning in Quechua or [Aymara] and other Indigenous languages?’ they say, ‘No, my grandpa told me that’s the tilcayo,’” Nogales-Ascarrunz said. “This is a traditional knowledge that they have in the community. We want to preserve that knowledge, and we didn’t want to give it another name.”

The tilcayo is special because, while scientists redefine mammals into new species all the time, it’s usually because a single species has split into two and become different enough for reclassification. This cat, however, was entirely new and not the offshoot of a previously recognized species, something very rare and probably deserving of its own high-tech litter box. 

“We really don’t know how many cats are still in the wild,” Nogales-Ascarrunz said. “We need science, we need more studies to answer this question, which is actually critical for its conservation.”

I want one!

Leopardus tilcayo may be new to us, but its habitat has long been under threat.Fernando Faciole/National Geographic

Instead of pining after exotic and protected species, I highly suggest you focus on local cats that need a home and provide them with toys, smart feeding stations or helpful collars that can help keep them safe and healthy. 

If you do want to get involved, look into supporting conversation efforts for the Bolivian Yungas, such as the Andes Amazon Fund. The tilcayo’s habitat is under serious threat from surrounding development and could use all the help it can get.

With degrees in Business Management, Literature and Technical Writing, Tyler takes every opportunity to play with the latest AI technology, push smart devices to their limits and occasionally throw cameras off his roof, all to find the best devices to trust in your life. He always checks with the renters (and pets) in his life to see what smart products can work for everyone, in every living situation. 
Living in beautiful Bend, Oregon gives Tyler plenty of opportunities to test the latest tech in every kind of weather and temperature. title: Google confirms Gemini hacked into three companies during cybersecurity test months ago
snippet: Following a Wall Street Journal investigation, Google has confirmed that Gemini went rogue in May 2026, accessing the internet and breaching the security of three different companies. more…
fullText:
Following a Wall Street Journal investigation, Google has confirmed that Gemini went rogue in May 2026, accessing the internet and breaching the security of three different companies.

As AI continues to advance in its capabilities, we’re running into more cases of models going rogue. Perhaps the most infamous has been from OpenAI in the Hugging Face hack, but there plenty of other examples, including from Anthropic’s Claude. These incidents, in part, have led to the public call to slow down AI development from Anthropic’s CEO.

But, behind the scenes, Google also ran into a similar problem. The Wall Street Journal reports, including a confirmation by Google, that Gemini was involved in hacking three external companies during a cybersecurity test through Irregular, an AI security company also involved in similar incidents that were previously disclosed by OpenAI, Meta, and Anthropic. 

The three hacks included one case of Gemini guessing a password until it gained access to the system, with the other two cases using credentials discovered in a public repository. 

	

Google didn’t disclose these incidents until the company was approached by The Wall Street Journal, citing that no harm was caused, and that the model stopped the behavior as soon as it realized it had breached the security of a real company rather than a simulated one. The report explains:

Google said that it didn’t consider the behavior an example of model misalignment because its safety measures helped it stop. It declined to share the name of the companies that were hacked, but said that all three companies had been notified.

In prior hacks from OpenAI and Anthropic, the models either didn’t realize the real company was indeed a real company, or simply continued in the hack in the latter’s case. 

Google’s Heather Adkins, VP of security engineering, said:

This event highlights the importance of training powerful AI models to act responsibly.  In this case, the model acted appropriately.

It another statement to The Verge, Adkins expanded:

Our security team has a long track record of reporting issues we find in other people’s software and systems – even if it’s as simple as a weak password. We ensured the three entities were made aware, and we worked with our training partner on the changes they’ve now made to their testing processes. These events highlight the importance of training powerful AI models to act responsibly.

The WSJ report further expands that, during the test in which Gemini went rogue, Irregular “unintentionally” left internet access open. Google also notified federal authorities when the hacks occurred. The exact Gemini model used in the test has not been confirmed, but the May 2026 timing alone rules out the latest Gemini models.

title: WebKit blog breaks down what’s new with Safari 27 for developers, including MCP support
snippet: Following the rollout of Apple’s 2027 system releases, the WebKit blog has now published an in-depth look at what’s new with Safari 27.0. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
Following the rollout of Apple’s 2027 system releases, the WebKit blog has now published an in-depth look at what’s new with Safari 27.0. Here are the details.

Safari MCP server among new features

Chief among the new features included in Safari 27.0 is the Safari MCP server, which lets AI agents control the browser window to help developers work faster.

To enable Safari MCP, developers must go to Safari > Settings > Developer and check “Allow remote automation and external agents.” Apple notes that the Developer pane only appears after users enable “Show features for web developers” under Safari > Settings > Advanced.

Here’s Apple on the new feature:

Are you developing websites using coding agents? The Safari MCP server, now available in Safari 27.0 will make your workflow faster and more powerful. Give Claude Code, Codex, or the agent of your choice control over the browser window so it can see how your code renders. Safari MCP provides access to the DOM, network requests, screenshots, and console output. Your agent can do more on its own while you do less hopping between windows, less dropping screenshots in your terminal, and less typing prompts to describe what’s not working.

The Safari MCP server enables your agent to:

see how your code renders in Safari

verify user states in forms, checkout flows, selections & more

compare computed styles and layout to results in other browsers

test for accessibility issues like missing labels, improper ARIA attributes, and poor contrast

analyze performance with navigation timing and resource load times

And much more. The MCP server runs entirely on your local machine. It makes no network calls of its own. It does not have access to your personal information in Safari. And any captured data goes directly to the agent you’re running, not to Apple.

Apple’s blog post also lists the specific commands developers can use to connect Claude Code, Codex, or other agents to Safari, and invites developers to share feedback and feature requests.

In addition to MCP support, Safari 27.0 fixes nearly 850 issues, up from the 525 fixes Apple had announced just a few months ago, during WWDC. Resolved issues include fixes in accessibility, CSS, encoding, fonts, forms, MathML, networking, WebRTC, among many other areas.

Safari 27.0 also introduces support for immersive environments, which allows developers to provide them in visionOS, and expands the HTML <model> element to iOS, iPadOS, and macOS, allowing websites to embed interactive 3D models directly in a page, much like images or videos.

The post describes the new (and very welcome) Scroll Anchoring feature, which prevents webpages from jumping around when an image, for instance, loads above what the user is viewing, and lists the many Web Inspector improvements, including inline color-contrast information, better redirect-chain visibility, and improved layout debugging.

The extensive list also details improvements or new features around WebAssembly, WebGPU, JavaScript, CSS, WebRTC, media playback, Web Extensions, WKWebView, and Service Workers, and you can read the full post here.

title: Addigy launches Intelligence Suite, giving IT teams control over how AI is used across their fleet
snippet: One of the biggest challenges Apple admins face today is managing AI use across apps, services, and more. Addigy is aiming to solve that problem with its Intelligence Suite, announced today, which brings a number of new tools and controls for IT teams to strengthen compliance while also unlocking AI tools in an IT-approved way. more…
fullText:
One of the biggest challenges Apple admins face today is managing AI use across apps, services, and more. Addigy is aiming to solve that problem with its Intelligence Suite, announced today, which brings a number of new tools and controls for IT teams to strengthen compliance while also unlocking AI tools in an IT-approved way.

Addigy builds device management software for managed service providers and IT teams that work with Apple, and the Intelligence Suite adds an AI layer directly inside that platform rather than as a separate console.

“Many IT admins know what their Macs need, but too much of their management time gets lost in syntax, filter logic, report building, and check-in delays, not to mention figuring out which AI tools can be trusted on their users’ devices,” said Jason Dettbarn, Addigy’s CTO and founder. “Autonomy only works inside guardrails you set. You define the boundaries, we enforce them.”

What’s in Addigy’s Intelligence Suite?

Addigy’s AI Script Assist writes, audits, and recommends actions for admins to approve, and it follows the customer’s existing RBAC rules rather than working around them. Natural language reporting aims to allow you to focus on what you want to know, rather than how to build the report.

“This is probably the best, easiest reporting capability I have seen in a long time. It’s a game-changer and is going to help me get so much more done,” said Nimoy Johnson, Endpoint Engineer, Smurfit WestRock.

Addigy says its AI runs entirely inside Addigy’s own environment, and customer data is never sent to external frontier models. Every action is processed locally, and every AI capability ships with built-in guardrails rather than bolted on afterward. With its new Intelligence Suite, Addigy is also shipping an MCP server that exposes its device management control plane to AI agents, with admin-set guardrails for every action the agent takes.

There’s also a shadow AI angle for Addigy’s new tool, and I believe its one of the more interesting aspects of it. Addigy is including prebuilt compliance rules to help Apple IT admins see, monitor, control, and block AI tools across their Mac fleets. That addresses a problem I’ve written about repeatedly: employees adopt AI tools faster than IT can onboard them, and the risk lands on IT regardless.

“Using Addigy Intelligence Suite, I was able to get to a client-facing security risk plan in an hour, something that used to take my team 1 to 2 business days. In a busy tech’s world, you don’t often get that kind of time back,” said Tim Pearson, CEO and founder of CreativeTechs.

Wrap up

Many of the tools IT teams will need for the AI era are being built now. As with any new technology, we often have to go with what sticks and then build the tools around it. We’ve had a few years of AI adoption, and I love an announcement like this that gives IT teams practical tools to manage AI usage across their fleet while also unlocking benefits for IT through new AI functionality.

title: Tripsy’s iOS 27 update includes smarter imports, on-device AI insights, more
snippet: Travel planning app Tripsy was updated this week with support for iOS 27’s extra-large widget, a new Smart Import tool, AI-powered features, and more. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
Travel planning app Tripsy was updated this week with support for iOS 27’s extra-large widget, a new Smart Import tool, AI-powered features, and more. Here are the details.

Tripsy update adds AI-powered features

During Apple’s “Surprise and Shine” event, the company briefly mentioned indie travel planning app Tripsy while showcasing some of iOS 27’s new Siri AI features. Apple followed up with an iOS 27 press release earlier this week, highlighting that Siri will soon be able to add restaurant recommendations directly to Tripsy.

The app, which was also a 2024 App Store Award finalist, was updated to version 3.10 earlier this week with new features, including AI-powered tools and support for iOS 27 features.

That includes the new Smart Import feature, which can turn links, documents (including PDFs), saved emails, screenshots, accessible Instagram and TikTok posts, and pasted text into places and reservations inside the app.

Smart Import also supports importing Google Maps and Apple Maps lists and guides, and lets users choose which suggested items they want to actually add to their trip.

Similarly, the update introduces Smart Insights, which uses Apple’s Foundation Models to analyze attached documents and emails on-device and surface useful trip details such as baggage allowances, breakfast, parking, cancellation policies, and costs.

Other improvements in Tripsy 3.10 include:

Support for iOS 27’s extra-large iPhone widget, with a more complete itinerary view.

Improved travel statistics refresh, map stability, and Mac import layouts.

Improved location suggestions, including access to all trip hotels and the option to dismiss airport departure suggestions that are no longer needed.

Tripsy notes that Smart Import and Smart Insights are available with a Pro subscription, priced at $39 per year or $199 for lifetime access.

With that being said, I still believe a properly implemented password management tool is one of the best security measures you can deploy in your organization. Dashlane is rolling out a new solution to help better secure credentials in the enterprise.

About Apple @ Work: Bradley Chambers has been an Apple IT admin since 2009. Through his experience deploying and managing firewalls, switches, a mobile device management system, enterprise grade WiFi, 1000s of Macs, and 1000s of iPads, Bradley will highlight ways in which Apple IT managers deploy Apple devices, build networks to support them, train users, share stories from the trenches of IT management, and ways Apple could improve its products for IT departments.

The adoption gap problem

Dashlann’s new solution solves what it calls the adoption gap. The IT team deploys the password tool, you send the onboarding email, you get decent usage in month one, and 6 months later, people are back to typing passwords into forms because nothing actually requires them to use it

Vault Enforcement lets IT admins require employees to log in through Dashlane on specific domains via a policy-deployed browser extension. Employees get a warning webcard on their first day, when they hit a login form on an enforced domain. The form is blocked the next day until they sign in to the vault. Admins can add their company logo and help desk contact to that card window, which is a nice way to get in front of complaints.

The SSO gap is bigger than people think

Dashlane says 37% of corporate applications are not managed by a single sign-on. That’s more than a third of your app’s surface area devoted to a username and password, with nothing else in front of it security-wise

Their telemetry data on which business apps see the most autofilled passwords instead of identity provider logins is: Salesforce, DocuSign, Adobe, Zoom, GitHub, Dropbox, Box, and Atlassian.

Some of it is the SSO tax, where vendors charge a premium for the login method, and that is a whole other topic I need to cover soon, but some of it is legacy passwords that still work on apps that were integrated with SSO years ago. 

Passkeys are great, and still confusing

I want passkeys to win. They solve phishing in a way nothing else does, and on Apple, the implementation is about as easy as it gets, but I’ve walked enough users through their first passkey to know that “where does it live and what happens if I lose my phone” is still a genuinely hard question to answer in a way that lands. Ask a non-technical employee whether their passkey is in iCloud Keychain, their password manager, or on the device itself, and watch their answer

That confusion has a cost. Users who don’t understand a security tool will route around it, and a security control that gets bypassed isn’t a control at all. Dashlane’s Vault Enforcement is aiming to solve it from the other end.

Wrap up

Vault Enforcement is a smart feature that I hope other password managers copy. It’s also an admission that a decade+ of user education hasn’t closed the gap, and that at some point you stop asking and start requiring. Good IT security has to be easier than the workaround. Until it is, we’ll keep building enforcement tools to make up the difference.

Dashlane’s Vault Enforcement is now in open beta for companies on Dashlane’s Omnix Enterprise plan that use Chrome or Edge, with the extension deployed by policy and SSO enabled.

title: Battery Replacement Has Gotten Pricier for Apple’s Latest iPhone 18 Pro Models
snippet: Most phone batteries degrade faster than we want them to.
fullText:
Swapping the battery on Apple’s newest flagship iPhone models just got a little more expensive. As noted by sites including MacRumors, the fee to replace the battery on the iPhone 18 Pro or iPhone 18 Pro Max has gone up by $10, from $119 to $129, compared to previous models (such as the iPhone 17 and iPhone 16 Pro and Max models or the iPhone Air).

Apple’s latest iPhone 18 Pro models feature larger battery capacities, which is likely behind the price increase.

Apple’s policy strongly pushes users toward official channels to get an iPhone battery replaced, whether in or out of warranty, by visiting an Apple store or Apple Authorized Service Provider, or by shipping the phone to an Apple Repair Center.

The critical metric in Apple’s policy is the 80% maximum capacity mark. Apple officially considers a battery “healthy” if it retains 80% or more of its original capacity. If you have an active AppleCare Plus plan and your battery health drops below 80%, Apple will replace the battery at no additional cost. But if your battery drops below 80% without AppleCare, you’ll have to pay out of pocket. 

The standard one-year limited warranty doesn’t cover batteries that naturally wear down from everyday use.

According to its device pricing page, Apple can still replace batteries for much older devices, all the way back to the iPhone 6 and the original iPhone SE — those batteries are the cheapest at $69. The page also lists fix-it prices for rear glass or screen damage (or both), rear camera damage or “other damage.”

A representative for Apple did not immediately return a request for comment.

Why do batteries even wear out?

Along with phones from OnePlus and Motorola, the batteries on Apple’s high-end phones, like the Pro and Pro Max, do very well in testing. In recent years, smartphone-makers like Apple have continued to eke out additional battery life even as batteries shrink to accommodate new designs.

But advanced phones with up-to-date battery tech perform a wider array of energy-sucking tasks, functioning as cameras, wallets, GPS systems, AI data crunchers and more. That’s why most of us still complain about limitations and feel frustrated with our current phone’s battery life. A recent CNET survey found that better battery life is the top reason most people upgrade to a new device.

Turning off some features, such as widgets, animations or keyboard haptics, is one way to keep your device from draining its battery too quickly. You can also try to extend a smartphone’s battery life by using the phone’s battery optimizations, avoiding extreme temperatures that can damage the battery, and choosing a phone case that doesn’t trap heat. 

But even with optimized charging settings, keeping your phone plugged in at 100% all night can wear out the battery faster. Overall, rechargeable batteries always degrade over time, reducing their capacity and, in some cases, requiring replacement. 

Aren’t batteries getting cheaper? 

You might think that with the increased popularity of electric vehicles and the ubiquity of smartphones and other battery-powered devices, there’s a shortage or price spike for batteries, as with other electronics components like memory and storage. But the opposite is actually true. 

According to Bloomberg, battery prices were already dropping steeply late last year, and that trend continues as Chinese companies flood the market with cheaper batteries.

The price collapse is largely due to companies increasing battery production capacity over the last few years. Quartz reports that price drops also result from “a shift toward cheaper battery chemistry, a crash in lithium prices, and a decades-long accumulation of manufacturing improvements.”

title: I’ve now completely changed my mind about Apple Glasses
snippet: The first smart glasses were Google Glass, launched way back in 2014. The product failed for a number of reasons, but the biggest of these was privacy concerns around video recording capabilities, leading to users being labeled “glassholes.” The same phenomenon now seems to have finally caught up with Meta Glasses, leading me to completely change my mind about the requirement for Apple Glasses to have video recording capabilities … more…
fullText:
The first smart glasses were Google Glass, launched way back in 2014. The product failed for a number of reasons, but the biggest of these was privacy concerns around video recording capabilities, leading to users being labeled “glassholes.”

The same phenomenon now seems to have finally caught up with Meta Glasses, leading me to completely change my mind about the requirement for Apple Glasses to have video recording capabilities …

‘Glassholes’ and ‘perv glasses’

Google Glass was an extremely expensive product with a number of flaws. The single biggest factor in its failure as a consumer product, however, was a major privacy backlash against their ability to make video recordings. That saw them banned by many bars, restaurants, and other businesses – and users stigmatized.

Given the history, it’s somewhat surprising that the same objections were not immediately raised when the first generation of Ray-Ban Meta glasses were launched. However, that moment does seem to have arrived, with the devices now frequently referred to as “perv glasses.” That’s in no small part due to their abuse by misogynistic men using them to secretly film women on the street.

That “perv glasses” label now seems to be becoming as prevalent as the Glassholes one was back in its day. Indeed, it’s reached the point where I personally no longer feel comfortable wearing them.

Apple Glasses without photo/video capabilities

This development raises questions about the public perception of other smart glasses launches – including the Apple Glasses expected to launch next year.

	

It had been suggested that Apple might launch them without the capability to take photos or record video. I expressed skepticism about this earlier in the year, but that was prior to the backlash against Meta Glasses. I do now think this is the way to go.

Additionally, I’ve been testing a pair of smart glasses with a display and no camera since the summer, and my first impressions were very positive. I’ll be following up with my conclusions sometime in the next few weeks, but suffice it to say, I no longer see a camera as a must-have feature in a pair of smart glasses. Indeed, in the current climate, it has perhaps become a must-not-have feature!

My expectation of Apple Glasses, then, has completely changed in response to this development, and I do now fully expect Apple to go the camera-free route. That is, they will contain a camera for Apple Intelligence purposes but not give users any access to the video – in much the same way as the new Audio Intelligence features on the Apple Watch give users no access to the recordings.

Do you agree with me, or do you think Apple Glasses will still be able to capture photos and video? Please share your thoughts in the comments.

title: Some memory for Apple devices may be made in the US for the first time
snippet: Some memory chips for Apple devices could be made in the US for the first time, if plans involving one of the company’s suppliers come to fruition. A new report says that Apple memory supplier SK Hynix is in talks with Intel over potential use of the company’s planned Ohio chipmaking plant … more…
fullText:
Some memory chips for Apple devices could be made in the US for the first time, if plans involving one of the company’s suppliers come to fruition.

A new report says that Apple memory supplier SK Hynix is in talks with Intel over potential use of the company’s planned Ohio chipmaking plant … 

Reuters reports that details are sketchy at this stage, but the Korean company makes both RAM and flash memory chips for Apple devices.

SK Hynix is in talks with Intel about a deal that would see ​the South Korean company manufacture memory chips on U.S. soil for the first time, three people familiar with the discussions said. Under one potential scenario, SK Hynix would lease part of Intel’s ‌long-planned chipmaking facility in Ohio.

Some processors for Apple devices are already made on US soil, although restrictions on foreign access to TSMC’s most advanced processes mean that these are only for older devices. This wouldn’t be an issue for either DRAM or NAND flash memory chips as Apple uses industry-standard versions of these.

However, the report says that the plans may face opposition from the South Korean government, as it may share Taiwan’s concerns about the export of chipmaking tech, even for for less advanced processes.

SK Hynix says that nothing has been finalized. Intel declined to comment on the report, but did confirm it was continuing plans to develop the Ohio site.

title: Sweeping EU Child Safety Proposal Would Transform Social Media, Online Gaming and AI Chatbots
snippet: The EU Kids Act would accelerate age verification plans and ban social media use for those under 13.
fullText:
A new proposal this week from the European Commission, if enacted, would set some of the tightest restrictions yet on technology products, from social media to games to AI chatbots.

The EU Kids Act would follow, and in some ways surpass, similar measures that have been imposed in Australia, the UK, China and India, and would require tech companies such as Meta, Google, YouTube and Roblox to change the way they do business. But first, the legislation will need to be vetted, debated and voted on.

Its pillars include a social media ban for kids under 13, age verification for online accounts and requirements for tech companies to provide proof that their online services are safely designed. The proposal is the formal version of what’s been discussed for months and is a result of mounting public pressure for governments to get a handle on easily accessible technologies that have been shown across research and in court judgments to cause harm to children, such as internet addiction and vulnerability to contact from predators.

“Our Kids Act is reversing the burden of proof — it is for platforms to show they are safe by design,” European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said in a statement Thursday. “And we put parents back in the driving seat, giving them the tools to help their children navigate a safer online world.”

Megan Jenkins, an analyst at Assembly Research who studies AI and online safety, said the Kids Act “goes further than other legislation proposed so far, and represents a big shift from the blanket social media bans we’ve seen in countries such as Australia.”

Jenkins said the biggest change from some of those laws is creating a burden of proof for tech companies to demonstrate that their products are safe, which would be the first law of its kind. “If tech companies can’t prove this, they would be unable to provide services to minors,” she said.

What’s in the EU Kids Act

Discussion of what would and wouldn’t be in the Kids Act began days earlier when drafts of the proposal were leaked. Ultimately, what ended up in the Kids Act is broader than what was expected — in addition to a tiered age system for when teens can access social media, it would require companies that make online games, AI chatbots or companions, and social networks to prove that they’re safe and free from features like infinite scrolling that could be considered manipulative or addictive to children.

The biggest component is the social media ban for those under 13 years of age. For teens under 15, parents could create a mini account accessible through their own account on age-appropriate social media or video-sharing platforms. Screen time would be limited to an hour per day. Teens aged 16 to 18 could create anonymous accounts without parental consent.

Two other major pillars of the proposal are aimed at tech companies. They would be required to include no addictive design features and would need to provide easy-to-use parental controls, recommendation algorithms that are safe for kids and no options for minors to livestream. They would also be required to verify ages for new accounts or anyone logging in to an existing account.

The last part of the proposal covers enforcement: The EU would speed up the time it takes to investigate violations, with the goal of concluding them within 90 days. Companies with 45 million or more active users would need to submit a compliance plan for any new services or features and face a review of up to 30 days. New features, services or functionalities that don’t meet a “positive opinion” from the European Commission would not be allowed.

The age verification ‘sticking point’

Even if the EU proposal is passed without too many changes, enforcing it will be a challenge. It would likely face legal challenges from some of the world’s biggest tech companies and, as countries such as Australia have found, it’s hard to impose constraints that teens can’t find ways to get around.

“These restrictions are also not likely to be successful, as seen with other age verification and social media bans that have been consistently circumvented by tech-savvy kids,” said David Inserra, a fellow for free expression and technology at the Cato Institute.

Inserra added that the age verification technologies themselves pose privacy issues, “creating massive amounts of sensitive identification data that will be subject to hacks and data breaches” for teens as well as adults.

Jenkins agreed that age verification has remained a “bit of a sticking point” for online safety regulation due to privacy concerns, but said she believes the Kids Act is a positive step in moving away from blanket social media bans for kids.

He lives in the Texas Hill Country.
