title: Googlebooks feel like the first laptops built for Android owners
snippet: Googlebook OS is a little bit like ChromeOS and a whole lot like Android. There's a good chance that my next laptop will be a Googlebook. If you're an Android user like me, then yours might be too, because Google is making a compelling pitch: The Googlebook does for the Android phone what the MacBook does for the iPhone (and then some). John Maletis, Google's head of laptops and tablets, said at my press briefing that the Googlebooks were designed to "work seamlessly with your Android phone." You can start using an app on your phone then pick it up on the laptop, navigate your phone's files from the laptop, run any phone app from the computer, and manage all your notifications in one place. It's a good pitch. A … Read the full story at The Verge.
fullText:
There’s a good chance that my next laptop will be a Googlebook. If you’re an Android user like me, then yours might be too, because Google is making a compelling pitch: The Googlebook does for the Android phone what the MacBook does for the iPhone (and then some).

John Maletis, Google’s head of laptops and tablets, said at my press briefing that the Googlebooks were designed to “work seamlessly with your Android phone.” You can start using an app on your phone then pick it up on the laptop, navigate your phone’s files from the laptop, run any phone app from the computer, and manage all your notifications in one place.

It’s a good pitch. And after spending a couple of hours playing with the first five Googlebooks — from Lenovo, Dell, HP, Acer, and Asus — I really hope Google delivers on it.

The enhanced integration begins at setup, which lets you link your Google account and Android device so that the laptop syncs your contacts, passwords, preferred settings, payment details, and more, just like it would when you switch from one Android phone to another.

Googlebook OS is built on Android’s codebase, but its interface is a blend of Android and ChromeOS. The layout mostly feels like a Chromebook, but the details of the UI are drawn from Android, specifically the Material 3 Expressive design language found primarily across Google’s own Pixel phones. Everything from widget design to the notification tray looks and feels like Android, only blown up a little to fill the space.

Widgets and other parts of Googlebook OS look identical to the software on Google’s Pixel phones.

Connect a Googlebook to your phone and each is supposed to feel like an extension of the other. Notifications are shared, and dismissing or reading them on one device will carry through to the other. You can also use the laptop to send in-line replies to messages sent to your phone.

File sharing is intended to be just as simple. The Googlebook file browser lists a paired phone among the hard drives, letting you go straight in to browse, open, edit, and copy files. No more uploading and downloading files with Google Drive or sending them as email attachments just to move them to the laptop.

There’s a version of Continue On, an Android 17 feature first introduced for tablets this year. It allows you to start using an app on your phone and pick it up on your laptop, though only certain apps are compatible. You can also open any phone app directly from the laptop via a dedicated app drawer. Apps are run on the phone itself, and simply cast to the laptop, where they’re displayed in a floating portrait window — though you can’t mirror the full phone itself, only individual apps. It’s less flexible, but also less fiddly.

A dedicated app drawer lets you cast specific apps from your phone.

They appear in portrait windows, and Google expects people to use them for quick tasks rather than extended work.

The most exciting features here — Continue On, app casting, file browsing — all require a phone running Android 17. For the moment that’s most Pixels and a handful of flagships from Samsung and other manufacturers, so Android’s fragmented updates will throttle immediate demand for Googlebooks. Future features may require more advanced Android versions of course, but Google says this core set should keep working even if your phone software gets a little behind. That’s reassuring, since the laptops will likely outlast your phone, with Google promising 10 years of software support.

Much of this isn’t new to Googlebooks. ChromeOS has been steadily adding integrations with Android over the years, and these new laptops build on that work. Chromebooks have been able to sync notifications, share passwords and payment cards, and even stream or emulate Android apps. Even Windows delivers its own version of these features via Phone Link, with notification syncing, screen mirroring, and a basic version of handoff. Googlebooks make these features quicker and simpler to access, and make sure that they work across every Android 17 phone, rather than Pixels and a handful more. Making an Android phone work with a Chromebook or Windows laptop has always taken a little effort; making it work with a Googlebook should require almost none.

Shifting Googlebook OS to Android’s tech stack means it can run Android apps without any emulation, and gets full access to the Play Store. If you can run an app on your phone, you can run it on your Googlebook. Google has worked with major players to ensure support already, including streamers Netflix, Disney Plus, and HBO Max — and because these are technically still mobile apps, you can download series and films to watch offline, unlike on most other laptops.

Netflix delivers offline downloads (!) but its optimization is still mixed — while most pages fill the screen, occasionally it shifts to this portrait view.

One worry is that all of this might get a little confusing. Some apps will run in small, phone-shaped windows with a vertical UI, some will scale dynamically for the big screen, and others will have dedicated desktop versions optimized for a laptop layout. Some of those desktop-optimized apps can be shrunk down to a phone UI if you prefer, some can’t. Sometimes apps will run natively on the laptop hardware, other times you’ll cast them from your phone. Some apps will support Continue On’s handoff between devices, most (at least at launch) won’t — though a Google rep told me it’s “a couple lines” of code to add support, and so they’re optimistic about uptake.

Google is trying to manage the possible confusion with new Play Store tags that let you know if an app is designed or optimized for desktop, or whether you’re better off using the web version instead. The app store homepage will also default to promoting apps that should run well on a laptop, so phone-first apps will only show up when you search for them.

The Play Store will let you know if an app has been designed with a Googlebook in mind.

These are the three tags apps can have.

My bigger concern is that as many Android apps as there are, they’re still only Android apps. Google has secured new desktop versions of CapCut and Fantastical, but much of the software available on Windows or Macs still doesn’t exist for Googlebooks. The Adobe apps are an obvious example — missing the full, desktop versions of Photoshop and Lightroom is a dealbreaker for me. For you, it might be something different: a crucial productivity app, an enterprise app or creative tool, or simply a favorite game. Googlebooks launch with access to over 20,000 games through the Play Store, but the vast majority are still basic mobile games; as my colleague Antonio Di Benedetto points out, it’s jarring to see a $1,000 laptop running Asphalt Legends with post-race ads.

A lack of “proper” apps has been the chief downside to Chromebooks for years. It’s been forgivable given the price point: Many Chromebooks cost well below $500. So far, Googlebooks are different, with the cheapest at $899, and even that price is “available for a limited time.” More expensive models start at $1,299. At that price you’re competing with the MacBook Air. Google’s launch partners have delivered competitive hardware, but it’s up to app developers to complete the equation.

I want to believe.

I’ll be waiting. I went into Google’s briefing curious and left almost convinced. I’ve spent over a decade waiting for a laptop that can make the most of my Android phone, and a Googlebook might just be it. But right now these look like laptops built on Android just as much as laptops built for it. It’ll take a serious rollout of desktop-class software to change that, and I really hope Google delivers it.

fullText:
Welcome to Indie App Spotlight. This is a weekly 9to5Mac series where we showcase the latest apps in the indie app world. If you’re a developer and would like your app featured, get in contact.

In this day and age, gas prices fluctuate quite a lot. If you want to have a better idea of how things are flowing, GasPulse is a great tool – giving you trends, historical prices, and an outlook to follow on your iPhone.

Top features

Using the weekly averages published by the Energy Information Administration, GasPulse shows you prices for each state or region. It’s not an app that’ll show you the cheapest gas station, but it shows you the trends with charts and a nice interface. It also has up to five years of historical prices.

Beyond that, it also offers an Outlook feature that gives you an idea of what to expect in the future. These are estimates, but it gives you a little bit of insight on whether or not things will go up or down. GasPulse also offers state-by-state comparisons, allowing you to see how things compare around you.

If you want price alerts, GasPulse also offers them for free for up to 6 areas, though it relies on iOS background refresh.

Lastly, GasPulse offers home screen and lock screen widgets, allowing you to keep an eye on things without opening the app. There’s also Siri support.

Download the app

GasPulse is available for free on the App Store for iPhone users running iOS 18 and later. There’s no requirement for a subscription, and it’s ad-free.

title: iPadOS 27.2 adds convenient new feature from the Mac
snippet: iPadOS 27.2 arrived in beta this week, and beyond adding the redesigned Health app, Apple has also brought over a recent Mac feature: a Siri popup when text is selected. more…
fullText:
iPadOS 27.2 arrived in beta this week, and beyond adding the redesigned Health app, Apple has also brought over a recent Mac feature: a Siri popup when text is selected.

Siri AI is the tentpole addition to iOS 27, iPadOS 27, and companion releases. And as such, Apple offers lots of ways to access the new, supercharged assistant.

On iPad you can invoke Siri via a “Siri” or “Hey Siri” voice prompt, pull down from the top of the screen, use the new Siri option in the edit menu, open the new Siri app, or my personal favorite: use CMD + Space to open Spotlight and ask Siri a question from there.

But iPadOS 27.2 adds yet another option that’s borrowed directly from the Mac.

In macOS 27 Golden Gate, in many situations when you select some text, a small Siri icon appears in the top-left corner of the selection. When you hover over the icon with your cursor, it expands to offer an ‘Ask Siri’ text box.

This wasn’t available in iPadOS 27. But now, if you have a trackpad connected to your iPad, that same behavior is available in iPadOS 27.2.

As seen in the images above, the new Siri icon starts out small and stays out of the way, but it’s very convenient to just hover over it to make the ‘Ask Siri’ box appear.

If you don’t have a trackpad attached, selecting text will still reveal the full edit menu where you can tap to open Siri. But it’s a more smooth and seamless experience with a trackpad.

macOS is full of small productivity-focused features like this that speed up everyday interactions, yet are missing from iPadOS. So it’s exciting to see such a recent Mac feature be brought over to the iPad.

title: CarPlay just got better, here’s everything new in iOS 27
snippet: iOS 27 has arrived, and with it a handful of improvements for CarPlay. Here’s everything new for CarPlay in iOS 27. more…
fullText:
iOS 27 has arrived, and with it a handful of improvements for CarPlay. Here’s everything new for CarPlay in iOS 27.

Siri AI and new Siri app

Apple’s Siri overhaul is the tentpole addition to iOS 27. And the new ‘Siri AI’ capabilities on the iPhone are available in CarPlay too if you have a compatible iPhone.

Siri AI offers a new design that’s more like the pre-iOS 18 look, but with less color. It appears as a glowing orb at the bottom-center of the screen.

Siri in CarPlay is now much better at answering questions of any kind, similar to ChatGPT and Google Gemini. In my testing, it’s also able to retain the context of your current conversation better than ever before. Here are 100+ examples of what Siri AI can do.

In a nice touch, conversations you have in CarPlay are automatically synced to the Siri app on iPhone. You can browse the full Siri history in the app, and there’s a car icon marking conversations you had via CarPlay.

Video app support

Apple added video in the car with iOS 26, but it was limited to AirPlay streaming. But with iOS 27 developers can now make dedicated video apps for CarPlay, so that users can browse videos right on their CarPlay display.

From Apple’s WWDC video that’s targeted toward developers:

With iOS 27 you can create apps to browse and play videos in new cars that support the video in car feature. If your app supports AirPlay video streaming, no changes are needed. People can already watch videos from your app on their CarPlay display when they aren’t driving. To do so, they simply select the car’s display when playing the video on iPhone. Now you can take it to the next level and let people browse their favorite videos from iPhone right on their CarPlay display.

Automakers need to sign on to support the feature, so unfortunately it won’t be available automatically in every car.

New design updates and wallpapers

iOS 27 has a handful of design-related updates for CarPlay too. 

As seen above, media apps feature a new MiniPlayer in CarPlay. Available in the top-right corner of the app, the MiniPlayer provides artwork and player controls—a nice upgrade with more utility than the previous waveform icon offered.

You can now do audio scrubbing on the Now Playing screen when listening to music, audiobooks, or podcasts. There’s a larger progress indicator that’s similar to the iPhone design, making it easy to grab and drag.

App icons have been refreshed with updated Liquid Glass designs in iOS 27, and those new icons extend to CarPlay.

Finally, there are new CarPlay wallpapers available now that resemble what’s included across iOS 27 and macOS Golden Gate.

title: Google fully details Googlebooks: $899+, October launch, & more
snippet: Following the May preview, Google today fully announced Googlebooks ahead of the consumer launch in October. more…
fullText:
Following the May preview, Google today fully announced Googlebooks ahead of the consumer launch in October.

Googlebook OS hands-on: It’s Android, stupid

Software

Google’s main pitch is that Googlebooks should be the laptop of choice for those with Android phones:

Today, we often switch between starting tasks on our phones and finishing them on our laptops. To make that experience better for Android users, we teamed up with the best laptop makers in the industry to deliver top-tier hardware alongside Google’s software experience that connects effortlessly with your phone.

Following phones and watches, Material 3 Expressive is coming to desktops. Quick Settings and notifications, which are nearly identical in design to what you’d find on Pixel, can be found in the top-right corner, while you have the time and date at the left. The bottom dock is center-aligned with the ‘G’ opening your app drawer. 

	

Upon signing in to a Googlebook, your Android phone’s settings, saved passwords, Wi-Fi, and messages will appear. Cross-device continuity includes Android 17’s “Continue On” capability and Cast My Apps if you don’t want to install the Android application on your laptop.

Additionally, Google touts a first-class Files app that can show what documents and photos are available on your phone. One good use of on-device AI is automatically generating file descriptions that aid search.

Gemini Intelligence is led by Magic Pointer and the wiggle gesture to bring up Gemini and enter a prompt, like adding dates to your Calendar. There’s also Rambler, like on the Pixel 11 series, to dictate a stream of consciousness, while Create My Widget is billed as letting you “customize your desktop by describing what you need in plain language.”

You get a “desktop-class” Chrome browser with support for extensions, the Gemini side panel, vertical tabs, and more. Most features found on Mac and Windows are available here.

The application story is a combination of Android and the web, with Google noting how 70% of time spent on laptops is in a browser. The company ultimately thinks it is up to developers to choose whether an Android app or the web is better for their application. There is a growing number of desktop-class Android apps, and the Play Store will highlight them with a new badge. 

On the gaming front, 20,000 mobile and PC titles will run on Googlebooks. They are optimized for keyboard, mouse, and touchscreen, with Google’s existing Play Games Level Up program resulting in monthly title launches. For everything else, Google offers a year of Nvidia GeForce Now.

For developers, Google very notably created an Antigravity app for Googlebooks that offers a native UI and interacts with the Linux environment. You can also install the Linux version of Antigravity if you wish, along with Claude Code and OpenAI’s Codex. For Android app development, Antigravity allows you to deploy directly to the Googlebook.

Under the hood, Google is integrating the multi-window performance and full browser capabilities of ChromeOS with a native Android stack that offers power and battery efficiency.

On the security front, Google touts the same security architecture as ChromeOS. There’s a Google Titan security chip and on-device malware detection. Additionally, a Level 5 security-certified hypervisor powered by pKVM isolation allows for the isolated Linux environment with full terminal access. This lets you “safely run any Linux developer tools, pull code repositories, access networks and the ports, or execute autonomous agents.”

Googlebooks get 10 years of automatic updates with quarterly feature drops similar to Pixel.

Hardware

On the hardware front, there are five flagship Googlebooks at launch, with Google mandating several key specs across the lineup. All devices are powered by Intel Core Ultra Series 3 or Snapdragon X Elite with NPUs (40+ TOPS). As such, Googlebook OS is optimized for ARM and x86, with MediaTek-powered devices coming in the future.

There’s a baseline of 16 GB of RAM with 32 GB variants available. All have a touchscreen with up to 2.8K LCD or OLED. Devices have up to six speakers with Dolby Atmos surround sound and “studio-quality, background noise-canceling” microphones.

Googlebooks are made from “premium materials” like aluminum, magnesium, or carbon fiber.

There are also backlit keyboards and large glass trackpads with haptic feedback and support for gestures. Google touts up to 14 hours of video playback and 16 hours of web browsing.

Finally, all devices have a Glowbar on the cover that lights up in the Google colors when you open and close the lid. When you plug in a charger, there’s a current charge level indicator and “playful” animation when you talk to Gemini. Notably (unlike Pixel Glow), third-party apps can access it to “build custom, interactive animations.”

title: I got to see Google’s wild ideas about the future of laptops
snippet: Googlebooks look like fancy Chromebooks at first, but there are interesting software ideas. | Photo: Antonio G. Di Benedetto / The Verge There are a few things about using a Googlebook that immediately feel just right. The hardware is polished (since it's based on current laptops). The OS is familiar (if you've ever used a Chromebook). But most impressive, it integrates your Android phone with your PC so they feel more like one device. It's the culmination of a series of new ideas that blur the two devices together. After my first look, I went from doubtful to excited by the prospect of Google pulling it all off. After an initial barebones announcement in May, Google is finally launching Googlebooks - its new line of Android-based laptops. The initial five Googlebook models … Read the full story at The Verge.
fullText:
There are a few things about using a Googlebook that immediately feel just right. The hardware is polished (since it’s based on current laptops). The OS is familiar (if you’ve ever used a Chromebook). But most impressive, it integrates your Android phone with your PC so they feel more like one device. It’s the culmination of a series of new ideas that blur the two devices together. After my first look, I went from doubtful to excited by the prospect of Google pulling it all off.

After an initial barebones announcement in May, Google is finally launching Googlebooks — its new line of Android-based laptops. The initial five Googlebook models from Dell, Lenovo, HP, Acer, and Asus all launch October 4th, with preorders available now and starting prices ranging from $899 to $1,299.

So what are Googlebooks?

In a nutshell, they’re laptops running a new operating system that’s a blend of Chromebooks and Android — with a whole lot of Gemini AI stuff built in. They look quite like Chromebooks, but with Android’s Material Three Expressive UI stylings on the software side and higher-end materials for hardware. There doesn’t seem to be a baseline spec for Googlebooks, but at launch they’re all thin-and-light laptops ranging from 13 inches to 15 inches with 16GB of RAM or more, touchscreen displays (most of them OLED), metal chassis, backlit keyboards, either fingerprint or facial recognition unlocking (or both), and a Google-y Glowbar light strip on their lids.

Powering the initial lineup of Googlebooks are Intel Core Ultra Series 3 “Panther Lake” and Qualcomm Snapdragon X Elite chips, with MediaTek options expected to come later. While the first wave of Googlebooks are similarly sized and all have “Googlebook” in their name, there are some variations: haptic or mechanical trackpads, port offerings, even a 2-in-1 convertible. Check out our roundup of all the hardware here.

I spent a bit of time prodding all the Googlebooks during my demos, and each one felt pretty nice. They each have their own unique qualities: the Asus was incredibly lightweight, the Lenovo has plenty of ports and an optional mouse with a matching Glowbar light, the Acer’s convertible form factor allows some tablet-like use (and it’s pretty affordable for a Panther Lake laptop). The HP had a great looking screen and a latticeless keyboard I surprisingly didn’t hate, and the Dell is basically a gold XPS 13 (which is excellent) but with a different chip.

1/5The Asus Googlebook 14.

But everything really special about Googlebooks comes down to software. They run Googlebook OS, which is built with the native Android stack atop a Linux kernel and supports both x86 and Arm architectures (as implied by the chip offerings). It’s an Android desktop interface that runs Android apps and feels much like ChromeOS, but it’s got some handy features when paired with an Android phone.

You can cast apps from an Android phone directly to a Googlebook, even without touching your phone. Googlebooks essentially have two app drawers: a G-logo start menu for installed Googlebook apps and a second one beside it that pulls up mobile apps from your phone. Click a phone app and you can fully use that app with the mouse and keyboard or the Googlebook’s touchscreen. It’s a bit like iPhone Mirroring on macOS, but the apps are individually extracted to the desktop OS instead of showing your whole phone interface.

1/2You can cast any app from your phone via a second app drawer on Googlebook OS. Here you see both drawers open.

Googlebooks also have a nifty feature called Continue On where the icons of apps you’re currently using on your phone appear in the bottom bar — allowing you to click it on the laptop and hand it off to the Googlebook. These app handoffs can transition to a native app or a web app, depending on how developers have programmed it. A Google rep informed me at my in-person briefing that Continue On is fairly simple for Android developers to add to their apps, and casting apps to a Googlebook doesn’t require anything extra.

The other big way Googlebooks interact with an Android phone is Quick Access, allowing you to see and access all the files stored on your phone right in the desktop Files app. The paired Android phone is listed in the sidebar of a Googlebook’s Files window, just like any other drive or home folder, and you can directly search it and share files from it without physically picking up your phone. This is pretty handy stuff, but of course it all requires you running an Android phone. If you have an iPhone then you’re limited to a Link to iOS app that just does some message syncing and replying.

1/2Quick Access treats your paired phone like another local drive. Image: Google

As Google first showed back in May, the Googlebook mouse cursor is called a Magic Pointer — allowing you to wiggle it to summon Gemini. Doing so allows you to ask Gemini questions or have it look at things on your screen to get further info. One of Google’s live demos was asking Gemini “Is this legit?” on a Spotify account authentication email, or adding a multi-week exercise routine for marathon training to a Google Calendar. Some tasks run locally, while many will go up to Gemini in the cloud — and it wasn’t clear when that was happening during any of Google’s demos. Googlebooks also have recent Android features like Create My Widget (for creating custom widgets from natural language prompts) and Rambler (speech transcription that can parse stream of consciousness-like wordiness).

And while thin-and-light laptops aren’t really built for gaming, since Googlebooks run Android they work with 20,000 games at launch. Many of these are free-to-play mobile games with microtransactions, of course, but the Play Store does have many indie titles that should play fine on a laptop. I briefly demoed a Googlebook running Dead Cells and Balatro — indie staples that are well worth playing on any platform. But it was also jarring to see a demo of Asphalt Legends offer me the option to watch a post-race ad for an in-game currency reward. That felt icky and weird on a laptop. But when it comes to mainline gaming, Nvidia’s GeForce Now service is also coming to Googlebooks, and the first year is free with one of Google’s new laptops.

Love me some Dead Cells.

Seeing ads after a race in a mobile game? Don’t love that.

A big draw of Googlebooks is that by being Android-based they can follow software developments that move at a much quicker pace than ChromeOS. Chromebooks will continue on, especially for education use where they’re widely adopted, but it’s pretty easy to feel like their days are numbered as the focus shifts to Googlebooks. Just like Chromebooks, Google is promising Googlebooks will get 10 years of OS support.

I kept asking who Googlebooks are for during Google’s media briefing, and Android president Sameer Samat told me they’re aimed at users who own a phone like a Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 that don’t particularly want to use Windows or a Mac. Googlebooks’ initial prices completely overlook direct competition with the MacBook Neo (at least, for now) but considering the state of Windows 11 and frequently voiced frustrations with Microsoft (I see you, Verge commenters) another competitor in the space could help mix things up.

1/2It’s not the Lightroom I want, but it’s a Lightroom and it’s “Optimized for desktop.”

One thing I found comforting was the work Google put into flagging apps as desktop-compatible in the Play Store. Kind of like how Valve verifies games for Steam Deck and Steam Machine compatibility, Google has three designations for Play Store apps on Googlebooks: Made for desktop, Optimized for desktop, or Better on the website. It’s cool to see an “Optimized for desktop” version of Lightroom I can install on a Google laptop, though I know it’s the mobile version and not the Lightroom Classic I regularly use on Windows and macOS.

But while that hints at Google taking this initiative pretty seriously, and all the Android integration tricks seem cool, there are many open questions for Google and its new OS that remain to be answered.

Even if Chromebooks continue on strictly for education, what will happen as that software ages with the development attention turned to Googlebooks?

Do people want to trust Google with their whole computer these days?

Do people want a laptop built with Gemini in mind? There’s an ongoing AI backlash, and Googlebooks puts Gemini at the forefront — even in the cursor.

Will developers like Adobe further optimize its mobile creative apps for desktop use? Or bring desktop-only apps like Lightroom Classic to Android? (Please?)

Are these laptops ready for showtime? Not to get too inside baseball, but Google isn’t sending out review units ahead of the launch. And some OEM reps told me they just got the hardware shortly before our briefing — deferring all software questions to Google. Maybe that’s no big deal, but it doesn’t instill much confidence.

What will future cheaper Googlebooks look and feel like? And just how cheap (or expensive) might they get — especially in the age of RAMageddon?

After seeing what Googlebooks can do I went from having no idea why they even exist to feeling at least adequately whelmed and looking forward to seeing some new ideas and competition in the laptop space (even if it might be just another Trojan Horse for Gemini). It’s not every day we get a new player in the desktop operating system and laptop spaces. There seems to be a higher ceiling of potential with Googlebooks than there was with Chromebooks, along with some cool features, but Google has a lot to prove at higher prices than people are used to paying for its laptops.

Photography by Antonio G. Di Benedetto / The Verge

title: Apple releases Xcode 27.1 beta, enabling iPhone Duo app development
snippet: Apple has released Xcode 27.1 beta 1 for developers. This version specifically enables app development that targets the new foldable iPhone Duo. more…
fullText:
Apple has released Xcode 27.1 beta 1 for developers. This version specifically enables app development that targets the new foldable iPhone Duo.

While iPhone Duo doesn’t launch until October, today’s Xcode release gives developers a chance to prepare for initial iPhone Duo support. 

Properly optimizing most apps for iPhone Duo will probably take more than a few weeks for most apps. However, Xcode 27.1 meets Apple’s promise to release dev tools before the end of September.

Apps built against Apple’s iOS 26 SDK will need to be updated for iOS 27 for basic iPhone Duo support.

Apps made for iOS 27.1 and later will take full advantage of the larger display. Still, there are a lot of sizing and layout considerations that developers need to consider when shipping proper app support.

While the device isn’t out yet, Xcode 27.1 beta also gives developers the chance to virtually experience their apps on the iPhone Duo simulator.

Xcode 27.1 beta is available to download from Apple’s developer webpage here.

The release follows the introduction of Xcode 27.2 beta earlier this week. Apple is shipping iOS 27.2 as the next software update for iPhones running iOS 27.0 with the exception of the iPhone Duo.

 It will run iOS 27.1, a version designed for the foldable device, before syncing up with the rest of the iPhone lineup in a later version.

iPhone Duo will be available for pre-order on October 16 and ships October 23. Pricing starts at $1999.

title: Samsung Phone Users Can Now Sync Photos and Video to Google
snippet: Syncing to Microsoft OneDrive will end on Sept. 30.
fullText:
One cloud in, one cloud out. Samsung phone users can now sync photos and videos in their Gallery app to Google, as native Microsoft OneDrive integration ends Sept. 30. The update will roll out over the coming days, and availability may vary depending on account type, device model or region.

Tech insider Ice Universe viewed the new feature and posted images on X, noting that you may now see a new “Sync photos and videos” option in Gallery Settings.

As detailed on this Google page, you must have a compatible Samsung device running Android 13 or newer and a personal Google account. To find out which Android version you have, go to Settings > About phone > Software information, then look for the Android version. If you need to create a Google account, the details are here.

After syncing Gallery to Google Photos, users can view and share multimedia from their Samsung devices, the Google Photos app and photos.google.com. But there are limitations. Google Workspace accounts can’t use it, and synced items can’t be viewed in Google features such as memories and highlights, live albums or search unless you back up photos and videos via Google Photos.

Also, Google Accounts supervised by parents are ineligible to use the feature.

Google says that you can back up photos, videos, albums, device folders such as downloads or screenshots, and metadata such as timestamps, location, and favorites status.

Representatives for Samsung and Google did not immediately respond to requests for further comment.

Syncing Samsung Gallery to Google Photos is optional, but storing photos and videos only in the Gallery will quickly eat up phone storage space. Open the Samsung Gallery app on your phone, then tap the three-line hamburger menu at the bottom right. Select Settings, then Sync Photos and videos. Choose a Google account from the instructions and grant permission to sync media.

Deleting items from either Samsung Gallery or Google Photos will remove them from both apps and from your cloud storage. Editing photos in either app will also show up everywhere.

Users can also turn off syncing at any time, and previously backed up items remain safely stored in their Google Account.

title: TechCrunch Mobility: How do we know when an AV is safe enough?
snippet: Welcome back to TechCrunch Mobility, your hub for the future of transportation and now, more than ever, the role AI is playing in it. To get this in your inbox, sign up here for free — just click TechCrunch Mobility!
fullText:
Welcome back to TechCrunch Mobility, your hub for the future of transportation and now, more than ever, the role AI is playing in it. To get this in your inbox, sign up here for free — just click TechCrunch Mobility!

One of the stickier problems for autonomous vehicle developers, regulators, and the public is determining when self-driving technology is safe enough for the road. So far, that question has largely fallen to industry to answer — companies that are applying their autonomous vehicle technology to self-driving trucks, robotaxis, and maybe someday personally owned passenger vehicles. 

Today, there is no standardized test for judging how well an automated driving system performs in the real world. We require people to pass a driver’s test before getting a license, but there isn’t an equivalent test or system for autonomous vehicle technology. 

So how do we know whether an AV is a safe driver? The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration says it’s working on an answer. 

Federal motor vehicle safety standards (FMVSS) already govern the vehicle automakers sell today. But those FMVSS rules weren’t designed for vehicles like the Tesla Cybercab and Zoox robotaxi, which lack traditional, and federally required, equipment like pedals, steering wheels, and design features like side mirrors and rearview mirrors.  

The NHTSA is working on a federal automated vehicle framework that it says will put safety at the foundation without stifling innovation, or as Administrator Jonathan Morrison put it this week, force the agency to play “whack-a-mole” with policy decisions or try to predict how the technology will evolve. That’s a tricky recipe to get right. 

The agency took a notable step toward that goal this week by reaching an agreement with SAE to launch ASCEND, a government-industry initiative aimed at speeding up the development of data-driven AV performance standards. 

“Our top priority for this consortium is ADS competency, which will inform and accelerate a corresponding federal motor vehicle safety standard,” Morrison said at the AI Horizons Summit in Pittsburgh. “Ultimately, our ADS performance rulemaking will provide federal leadership in this space. By delivering an AV competency standard, we hope we’ll be able to address the burgeoning past patchwork of inconsistent state and local level requirements, and continue to encourage American innovation and promote the safe deployment and development of these vehicles on the road.”

There is no timeline yet for when this consortium will produce ADS standards. But I bet the AV industry is already weighing in.

Note: Want to hear Morrison’s complete comments? Check out this video of the AI Horizons Summit, and fast-forward to the 04:36:00 mark.

A little bird

Image Credits:Bryce Durbin

We have a few things cookin’ but nothing quite ready to share. This is a reminder that you can send us tips!

Email Kirsten Korosec at kirsten.korosec@techcrunch.com or my Signal at kkorosec.07, or email Sean O’Kane at sean.okane@techcrunch.com.

Deals!

Image Credits:Bryce Durbin

Will Wall Street invest in a pure-play robotaxi company? We’re about to find out. 

Autonomous vehicle company May Mobility plans to go public through a merger with special purpose acquisition company ACP Holdings Acquisition Corp. in a deal that could raise more than $300 million at a valuation of $1.4 billion. 

There are other publicly traded companies working on autonomous vehicle technology: Aurora and Kodiak, which are both focused on self-driving trucks; Rivian; and Tesla. And while Waymo is not (yet) publicly traded, its parent company Alphabet is. It’s the same story for Amazon-owned Zoox. 

But May Mobility, which operates autonomous Toyota Siennas in three locations, says it will be the first public company in the U.S. focused entirely on autonomous ride-hailing vehicles. Senior reporter Sean O’Kane notes this will also be a test of May Mobility’s “asset-light” and “partnership-first” approach to autonomy.  

Other deals that got my attention …

Autonomous vehicle company Beep has merged with Freebee, an on-demand public transportation firm based in Miami. The combined company will be called Beep and will be led by Beep co-founder Kevin Reid as chair and CEO. Freebee co-founders Kris Kimball and Jason Spiegel will join as chief operating officer and president and chief growth officer, respectively.

Lucid Motors struck a partnership with European mobility platform Bolt to “deploy at least 25,000 fully autonomous vehicles” built on the EV maker’s upcoming midsize EV architecture, which is supposed to be smaller and cheaper than its current offerings.

R3 Lithium, a battery recycling startup based in Georgia, raised $15 million in a Series A round that included funding from TDK Ventures, Integral GlobalTech Partners, and Axial Partners.

Notable reads and other tidbits

Image Credits:Bryce Durbin

Cybersecurity teams with the U.S. Coast Guard and FBI boarded two U.S.-bound oil tankers after hackers reportedly compromised at least one of the ship’s networks and took control of its navigation, propulsion, and cargo systems.

GM unveiled a new user interface for its full-size pickups, the Chevy Silverado and GMC Sierra, a makeover that includes picture-in-picture displays for Apple CarPlay and Android Automotive. 

An aircraft equipped with Joby Aviation’s autonomy technology flew more than 3,100 miles across the United States without a human pilot taking control at any point. As I noted in my article, this should be viewed as more than a splashy demo.

ShinyHunters hacking group published hundreds of thousands of files from a Florida state database of vehicles and driver information. 

U.S. automakers may be forced to build AM radio into new vehicles within the next year after the House overwhelmingly approved the AM Radio for Every Vehicle Act. EV makers have eschewed AM receivers because the electromagnetic interference generated by electric motors can affect the frequencies used by AM radio.

Volkswagen unveiled a new prototype electric vehicle with record-breaking efficiency.

Waymo restarted its robotaxi service in San Antonio, Texas, five months after one of its vehicles was swept away during a flash flood. The company also launched a new robotaxi service in Las Vegas and announced it was headed to Singapore, where it would begin mapping and eventually testing its AV tech.

Wayve hired Elisa de Martel as its next CFO, an executive who has held several top financial jobs at tech companies, including Waymo. 

Zoox is currently under a 100-vehicle cap in Las Vegas, the only market in which it operates a commercial service. That cap expires September 25, clearing the way for the Amazon-owned company to expand its commercial fleet of custom-built robotaxis.

title: Google confirms Pixel phones were exploited in ‘targeted’ attack related to modem
snippet: Google has confirmed that a “limited” number of Pixel phones were attacked by a vulnerability related to the modem on the device. more…
fullText:
Google has confirmed that a “limited” number of Pixel phones were attacked by a vulnerability related to the modem on the device.

As part of the September 2026 security update, Google patched over 200 security vulnerabilities, but specifically calls out that one of those was actively exploited in the wild.

Note: There are indications that CVE-2026-58704 may be under limited, targeted exploitation.

The issue is related to the modem, with a bypass that requires no user interaction. CVE-2026-58704 is described as follows:

In Cellular Modem, there is a possible permission bypass due to a logic error in the code. This could lead to remote (proximal/adjacent) escalation of privilege with no additional execution privileges needed. User interaction is not needed for exploitation.

Exact details of how the vulnerability was exploited are unclear – as well as which models were affected – but CISA (via The Hacker News) says that it was exploited on Pixel phones, explaining that “Google Pixel devices contain an improper authorization vulnerability in the cellular modem.” Combined with Google’s announcement, this was used in the wild, apparently to hack “targeted” devices. CISA issued a notice that this is a “known exploited vulnerability,” explaining that “this type of vulnerability is a frequent attack vector for malicious cyber actors and poses significant risks to the federal enterprise.” TechCrunch notes that this is called a “zero-click” attack, adding that Google hadn’t replied to a request for comment around the vulnerability being exploited and who was exploiting it.

	

If you’re on a Pixel phone, updating to the September 2026 patch, rolling out now, fixes the issue.

title: The Mac Mini is still mighty, just not as cheap
snippet: Apple’s little computer gets a little spendy. There are lots of compact desktop computers out there, but none match the Mac Mini's small size and big power. 2024's redesign reduced the Mini to 0.82L, a chassis so minimal you can easily mount it behind a monitor or under a desk. But despite being tiny, the Mini maintains a bunch of speedy ports - even a front-facing headphone jack. Along with that comes another beefier version, replacing the M4 … Read the full story at The Verge.
fullText:
There are lots of compact desktop computers out there, but none match the Mac Mini’s small size and big power. 2024’s redesign reduced the Mini to 0.82L, a chassis so minimal you can easily mount it behind a monitor or under a desk. I’ve used gaming laptop charging bricks that are nearly as large and definitely heavier than this whole computer. But despite being tiny, the Mini maintains a bunch of speedy ports — even a front-facing headphone jack.

The 2026 Mini is the first Mac to get Apple’s new M6 chip, with more cores — and more kinds of cores — than the outgoing M4 model. Along with that comes another beefier version, replacing the M4 Pro model with an M5 Pro. It’s a chip bump year, and that’s just fine. But it’s also a price bump year: While the M4 Mac Mini started at $599, the new model starts at $899. In spite of that, the Mac Mini remains the best value in the Mac lineup, because just about everything costs more these days.

Since May, the cheapest M4 Mini was the model with 512GB storage, for $799; Apple discontinued the $599 model with 256GB of storage due to supply constraints — in part because of people buying up Mac Minis en masse for use with OpenClaw. So while the base M6 model with 16GB / 256GB is technically only $100 more than the last available M4 Mini, it’s really a $300 increase.

Component report card

Keyboard: BYO

Number of ugly stickers to remove: 0

We have two specced-up units in for review. One is a $1,299 M6 model with a 12-core CPU / 12-core GPU, 24GB of unified memory, 512GB of storage, and 2.5Gb ethernet. The M5 Pro config is a very pricey $2,899 for an 18-core CPU / 20-core GPU, 48GB of RAM, 1TB SSD, and 10Gb ethernet. As powerful as the M5 Pro is, this is a bit overkill for a Mac Mini. Spending $2,899 puts you well into M5 Max Mac Studio territory.

Like all the latest M-series Macs, both the M6 and M5 Pro Mac Mini are absolute speed demons for raw performance. They even benefit from Apple’s recent push to faster storage, doubling the storage speeds of the M4 / M4 Pro Mac Mini. The M6 is Apple’s newest chip, and it’s now the head of the pack in single-core performance. Not just the Mac pack, either; the entire pack. The M6 chip’s jump to a 12-core CPU and 12-core GPU over the M4’s 10-core / 10-core makes it faster on all fronts.

The M6 contains all three of Apple’s current core types: two super, four performance, and six efficiency. (The super cores are the fastest ones, which Apple called performance cores until earlier this year; the performance cores are new and meant for multithreaded work.) The M4 had four of the old performance cores and six efficiency cores. The M5 Pro Mac Mini has six super cores, 12 performance cores, and zero efficiency cores.

In single-threaded work, the M6’s super cores are about 10 percent faster than M5’s performance cores, and a little more than 20 percent faster than the performance cores in the M4. The super and performance cores in the M5 Pro are both slower than the M6’s, and so are the GPU cores, but what they lack in speed they make up for in number, not to mention memory bandwidth. The M5 Pro is 40 to 50 percent faster in multi-threaded CPU and GPU benchmarks than the M6.

It’s just so dang tiny.

Looking at a real-world benchmark like our Adobe Premiere 4K export test, the M6 Mac Mini finishes in 2 minutes and 34 seconds — 40 seconds faster than the M4 we tested in the iMac with the same amount of RAM. The M5 Pro did it in 1:51, almost a third faster than the M6 and even faster than our recent re-test of the 10-core / 32-core M1 Max (which took 2:03).

What does all of this feel like in everyday use? These Mac Minis are more than capable for lots of multitasking and content creation, with the M5 Pro of course having more headroom. I was able to import a batch of 1,253 50-megapixel RAW images (all my recent photos still living on my SD card) from my full-frame Sony camera into Lightroom Classic on the M6 Mac Mini in about 6 minutes and 13 seconds. The same import only went about 30 seconds faster on the M5 Pro Mac Mini. But doing some heavy batch editing with AI subject detection across a selection of 188 photos showed the performance advantage of the M5 Pro. The M6 Mac Mini was decently fast, but even with 24GB of RAM this little torture test hit swap memory and slowed mid-processing. The M5 Pro sailed through and stayed speedier the whole way through.

The M5 Pro model should come in black.

If you’re doing video editing, visual effects, or 3D rendering then you’re best served looking at the M5 Pro Mac Mini — or maybe even the Mac Studio if you have the budget. The M6 Mac Mini is more for generalists who do creative work on the side or want an everyday desktop they could use for a very long time, like up to a decade. When I bought a Mac Mini for myself in 2023 I opted for the cheapest M2 Pro. (Yes, I’m plenty jealous of how small the current models are.) It served me well, but these days I’d probably be fine with an M6 Mac Mini. While I often deal with lots of high-res images in Lightroom Classic, photography isn’t my full-time work. If I were editing thousands of photos for hours a day I’d definitely consider the M5 Pro Mac Mini or M5 Max Mac Studio — and then I’d also get my precious SD card slot.

And yes, the Mac Minis are great for local AI compute, thanks in part to fast unified memory, and Apple’s leaning into that with the new models. The press release announcing the M6 and M5 Pro chips mentions AI capabilities nearly 40 times.

1/2Lots of ports.

Hardware-wise, these Mac Minis are nearly identical to the older ones. They have the same ports as the last-gen model, with two 10Gbps USB-C ports and a headphone jack on the front. On the rear, there are three Thunderbolt ports (TB4 on the M6 model; TB5 on the M5 Pro), plus HDMI 2.1 and an ethernet port. The ethernet has been bumped from 1 gigabit to 2.5Gbps; you can upgrade to 10Gb for $100.

Sure, the power button is still on the bottom, but it remains mostly no big deal since the Mini is designed to sip power when idle; you can just put it to sleep instead of turning it off. Apple even added a software feature to somewhat alleviate this by having the Mac Mini turn itself back on after the power is cut.

The other thing that’s still the same are the Mac Mini’s crummy little speakers. I’ve owned and used the older, larger M2 Pro Mac Mini for years so I know how you can get by with the built-in speakers when you’re too lazy to put on headphones, but they should only be relied on for hearing the beeps, boops, and “knock brushes” of notifications.

There’s now Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6 support on the 2026 Mac Minis, which is a nice small upgrade. Just like annual phone releases, the new Mac Mini will best serve newcomers and people still running much older models. Do you still have an Intel-based Mac that’s now run out of OS updates with the introduction of macOS 27 Golden Gate? Boy, are you in for a treat.

On the software side, I feel the same way about macOS 27 Golden Gate as I did during the  developer beta: the visual refinements that tone down Liquid Glass transparency, increase window sidebar legibility, and fix window corner radii are all welcome changes. Golden Gate is an overall nice improvement over macOS 26 Tahoe, even if Siri AI and Apple Intelligence on the Mac are just kinda Fine.

The bottom power button remains weird, but it’s rarely an issue. It could pose a problem if you mount the Mini somewhere hard to reach.

Since this year’s upgrade to the Mac Mini is mostly a chip bump, it’s of course a bummer it’s much more expensive. But then again, so is everything else these days. RAMageddon shows no mercy for any manufacturer. Apple’s computers are pricier. Intel and AMD chip costs are rumored to rise soon. Laptops are launching at one price and then changing shortly after. In terms of mini PCs, Minisforum raised its prices and the Framework Desktop is more expensive now than when it launched last year. There are cheaper mini PCs, and there are smaller ones, but none of them truly compete with the Mac Mini’s balance of performance, price, and size — even with the price increase. (Gaming is a different story, of course.)

This is our new normal. The Mac Mini is still a great deal; it just doesn’t feel like the steal it used to be. But with the recent price increases hitting MacBook Airs and MacBook Pros, the new Mac Minis remain much cheaper than getting similar chips in a laptop (especially if you already have a monitor, mouse, and keyboard). The base M6 Mac Mini is $400 cheaper than the cheapest M5 MacBook Air, and the base M5 Pro model is $800 less than the MacBook Pro with the same chip and memory.

Sadly it doesn’t seem likely we’ll ever see a Mac Mini start at a price like $599 ever again. It’s still an easy recommendation if you want a tiny desktop computer that runs circles around comparably priced PCs and will last for years, but it’ll take time to forget the gut punch that is these price increases.

M6 / M5 Pro Mac Mini specs (as reviewed)

CPU (M6): Apple M6 (12-core CPU / 12-core GPU)

CPU (M5 Pro): Apple M5 Pro (18-core CPU / 20-core GPU)

Unified memory (M6): 24GB

Unified memory (M5 Pro): 48GB

Storage (M6): 512GB SSD

Storage (M5 Pro): 1TB SSD

Connectivity: Wi-Fi 7, Bluetooth 6

Ports (M6): 2x USB-C (10Gbps), 3x Thunderbolt 4 / USB-C (DisplayPort 1.4), 1x HDMI 2.1, RJ45 2.5Gb ethernet, AC power

Ports (M5 Pro): 2x USB-C (10Gbps), 3x Thunderbolt 5 / USB-C (DisplayPort 2.1), 1x HDMI 2.1, RJ45 10Gb ethernet, AC power

Weight (M6): 1.5 pounds / 0.67kg

Weight (M5 Pro): 1.6 pounds / 0.73kg

Dimensions: 5 x 5 x 2 inches / 127 x 127 x 50mm

Price (M6): $1,299

Price (M5 Pro): $2,899

excerpt:
There are lots of compact desktop computers out there, but none match the Mac Mini’s small size and big power. 2024’s redesign reduced the Mini to 0.82L, a chassis so minimal you can easily mount it behind a monitor or under a desk. I’ve used gaming laptop charging bricks that are nearly as large and definitely heavier than this whole computer. But despite being tiny, the Mini maintains a bunch of speedy ports — even a front-facing headphone jack.

The 2026 Mini is the first Mac to get Apple’s new M6 chip, with more cores — and more kinds of cores — than the outgoing M4 model. Along with that comes another beefier version, replacing the M4 Pro model with an M5 Pro. It’s a chip bump year, and that’s just fine. But it’s also a price bump year: While the M4 Mac Mini started at $599, the new model starts at $899. In spite of that, the Mac Mini remains the best value in the Mac lineup, because just about everything costs more these days.

title: Snap announces Specs Intelligence app for iPhone and Mac, cellular variant of Specs
snippet: After unveiling the design of its consumer-grade Spectacles back in June, Snap is now announcing that they’ll be available for pre-order starting today with a new 5G carrying case. The company also introduced a new proactive AI agent called Specs Intelligence, which despite being Specs branded, will be available on iPhone and Mac regardless of if you own a pair. more…
fullText:
After unveiling the design of its consumer-grade Spectacles back in June, Snap is now announcing that they’ll be available for pre-order starting today with a new 5G carrying case. The company also introduced a new proactive AI agent called Specs Intelligence, which despite being Specs branded, will be available on iPhone and Mac regardless of if you own a pair.

Cellular Specs, in partnership with Verizon

Snap today announced that it’ll be releasing a cellular carrying case for the Snap Specs, allowing you to use your Specs away from home. This case will be available as a separate purchase, or you can purchase it bundled with the glasses for an additional $200, or $2395.

The cellular plan for Specs will cost $10/month for Verizon customers, and $20/month for non-Verizon customers. Outside of the US, Orange in France and EE in the UK will also offer cellular plans for Specs.

Specs remain on track to ship to customers later this fall, though an exact date isn’t available. That said, Snap is opening a demo experience at Westfield Century City in LA starting on October 1st for eager customers who want to try them out early. Verizon stores will also offer demos at a later date.

You can preorder Specs today, with a $200 refundable deposit here.

Specs Intelligence

Snap is also throwing its hat in the personal AI agent race, with a new Specs Intelligence app for iPhone and Mac. Despite being Specs branded, you won’t need to own a pair of Specs to use it – though they do integrate nicely with Specs. Here’s how the company describes the service:

It builds an understanding of your goals, priorities, relationships, and routines from the apps and tools you choose to connect, helping you focus on what matters now while making progress towards your longer-term goals.

Rather than waiting for a prompt, SPECS Intelligence is designed to anticipate when help would be useful and surface relevant information and actions at the right moment. On SPECS AR glasses, it is designed to extend that personal context into the physical world by bringing relevant information directly into view.

The app will be available starting today with a waitlist on their website.

title: The US Navy just told us what’s on its tech wish list for the next several years
snippet: Navy CTO Justin Fanelli talks co-investing alongside VCs instead of funding early research himself, recent buys like a $562 million autonomous refueling deal, and the Navy's updated wish list — from AI to quantum — for where founders should be building next.
fullText:
Justin Fanelli, the Department of Navy’s chief technology officer, has spent the last three and a half years trying to make the U.S. Navy easier to do business with. When we first talked to him last year, he described a shift away from what he called “your granddaddy’s government” — a “spaghetti chart” of entry points for startups — into something closer to a funnel, where companies that show strong results get pulled into the Navy’s technology base as enterprise services.

This week, we caught up with him again on a video call, and this time, he wasn’t just looking again to further streamline the procurement process, he was sprinting, literally, to catch a flight he’d just been ordered onto with no destination shared.

“You have an hour and 15 minutes to get on a plane,” Fanelli said, recounting what he’d just been told, speaking into his phone as he walked, the sun shining behind him. “I’m like, ‘Where?’ Oh my God! And they were like, ‘We’ll figure [the logistics], we’ll tell you as you get there.’ And I’m like, ‘For more than overnight?’ And they were like, ‘Yes.’” As he was walking to his car, he was still unsure what he’d packed for or where he was headed. “I will figure that out in the next 20 minutes,” he said, sounding excited about the adventure ahead.

Fanelli reached out because the “demand signal” he sent to investors last year had only grown, and it was making an impact, he said. When the Navy first published its longer-term technology priorities, investors told him it changed how they thought about the Navy’s buying plans, which is part of why he’s doing it again — sharing a fresh list of what the Navy wants to buy in the next several years, this time vetted by a handful of (unnamed) venture investors before release.

How much money the Navy actually puts to work each year depends on what counts as spending, Fanelli said. “We spend in the $150 billion range every year,” he said, though he was careful to separate that number — total Navy purchasing — from something narrower, like direct equity investment. 

Indeed, while most of that spending still flows through traditional channels, Fanelli said the Navy is trying to inch further toward what he calls co-investment — putting money behind companies alongside private capital rather than writing a check to an established prime contractor. Taking an equity stake, he said, is the most aggressive version of that and remains rare. More often, co-investment means the Navy waits for companies to mature a product on their own before buying it, rather than funding early research itself.

The stage of company the Navy buys from has shifted, too. “We mostly buy Series D through F type companies,” Fanelli said, adding that the Navy used to fund its own early-stage research to cover the seed-through-Series-B gap. It’s trying to hand that job to commercial investors instead, which is part of why the priorities document exists at all. “The cost of that, or the responsibility, is for us, if we’re not going to do it ourselves, to cast a cleaner signal,” he said.

As for recent purchases, Fanelli — a former Air Force cadet whose career has spanned roles across defense, intelligence, DARPA, and open source initiatives — rattled off a handful. A contract worth $562 million was awarded this month for the MQ-25 Stingray, an autonomous refueling drone that extends the range of manned fighter jets flying off carriers.

The Navy has also been buying edge compute hardware from Armada, described loosely as shipping containers packed with servers meant for ship or remote deployment. It brought in Gecko Robotics to handle inspection work that used to be done manually and dangerously; Fanelli said the move drew little pushback because almost nobody wanted that job in the first place. Domino Data Lab is now running the Navy’s machine learning pipeline. 

And in a case Fanelli seemed to particularly enjoy sharing, the Navy swapped a defense contractor’s years-delayed shipboard camera system for commercial cameras paired with software from Applied Intuition, cutting roughly four years off the timeline and expanding to more ships than expected.

Given the Strait of Hormuz has been a flashpoint this year — tanker strikes, a seized vessel, ceasefires that have broken down over shipping-route disputes — it seemed worth asking whether any of that commercial technology is showing up there now. Fanelli was cautious. “I often don’t know what’s classified and unclassified because I’m normally talking to people with clearances,” he said, adding that he’d have to check. (We’ll let you know if he gets back to us.)

Interestingly, not many people sign off on a purchase like that, according to Fanelli. Buying decisions run through what he called a source selection committee, a small group rather than the sprawling review process outsiders might picture. He described the goal as keeping the process merit-based rather than adding layers of approval.

He didn’t get into why technologies typically fail once they’re inside the Navy — he’d arrived at his car and needed to figure out next steps for travel. But when we talked last year, Fanelli explained that the most common reason promising technologies fail isn’t technical, but rather budgetary. The Navy runs on long planning cycles, and a new tool only sticks around if it replaces or “turns off” something the Navy is already paying for. 

Either way, before we parted ways, Fanelli shared an updated internal list of the technology areas the Navy is prioritizing, jointly issued by his office and the Portfolio Acquisition Executive for Mission Systems. It breaks down into five broad categories, for those of you either developing or funding defense tech.

The first is applied AI, covering machine learning and increasingly agentic software meant to turn raw data into decisions — sensor fusion, targeting support, autonomous behavior, and cyber operations built on software rather than hardware. 

Quantum information science comes second, focused less on owning quantum hardware and more on applying quantum or quantum-adjacent techniques to navigation, secure communication, and cryptography. 

Advanced networking is third, aimed at moving data securely across environments where connections are degraded or intermittent, whether that’s a ship at sea or a coalition partner’s network. 

Fourth is electromagnetic spectrum operations, technology that senses and manages the spectrum itself, built to adapt in contested conditions rather than rely on fixed configurations. 

The fifth category, digital engineering and interoperability, covers the plumbing: open APIs, model-based systems engineering, and zero-trust architecture meant to let different Navy systems talk to each other without custom integration work every time.

None is a funding commitment, the memo notes, and none of it ranks individual programs. It also adds as a reminder that its priorities “will change based on emergent, near-term, and long-term needs.” In short, don’t take it as gospel. Instead, it’s meant to be read the way Fanelli talked about last year’s list — as a roadmap that companies and investors can plan around, so that decisions made now about where to put money have somewhere to go inside the Navy in a couple of years.

title: PDF Expert update adds handwriting recognition, expands Apple Pencil support, more
snippet: Readdle updated PDF Expert for iOS 27 and iPadOS 27 this week, adding several new features, including searchable handwriting in 29 languages. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
Readdle updated PDF Expert for iOS 27 and iPadOS 27 this week, adding several new features, including searchable handwriting in 29 languages. Here are the details.

PDF Expert now indexes handwritten notes

Readdle’s classic PDF editor, PDF Expert, was updated this week with several features that leverage new possibilities introduced with iOS 27 and iPadOS 27.

Chief among them is a new Handwriting Recognition feature, which works both within individual PDFs and across the user’s entire library, including existing handwritten annotations and notes added in other apps.

PDF Expert now indexes these notes as regular text, making it easier to find something the user might remember jotting down but can’t quite recall where it was.

The company notes that Handwriting Recognition currently works with 29 languages, matching the language support offered by Apple’s new PKStrokeRecognizer API. Presumably, as Apple expands language support for the API, PDF Expert and its users will benefit as well.

Importantly, Handwriting Recognition and library-wide search are available to PDF Expert Premium users. Free users can still use the Text tool to write by hand and have their handwriting converted to typed text as they write.

Additionally, the update adds support for the Apple Pencil Pro’s squeeze gesture, which opens PDF Expert’s tool palette.

Here’s Readdle:

Users can switch between pens, markers, highlighters, shapes, stamps, signatures, and measurement tools. They can also adjust color, thickness, and opacity, access recent or favorite tools, switch to the eraser, or undo and redo an action.

The company notes that this feature requires an Apple Pencil Pro and a compatible iPad, and that users can enable it by selecting “Show Tool Palette” in Apple Pencil settings if the squeeze gesture is currently assigned to another action.

Finally, this week’s update also expands the Liquid Glass look across the app’s interface, “including the sidebar, document viewer and its toolbar, and Presentation mode,” Readdle notes. Users can now also access dedicated undo and redo buttons directly from the document view.

title: Googlebook hands-on: What makes a laptop, a laptop? [Video]
snippet: After a protracted wait, the first wave of Googlebooks is now official. Having spent a brief period testing, here’s what it’s like to use one. more…
fullText:
After a protracted wait, the first wave of Googlebooks is now official. Having spent a brief period testing, here’s what it’s like to use one.

I didn’t quite spend as much time with the software as my colleague Abner, so for a full set of impressions on these laptops running Googlebook OS, please read his extensive thoughts. This is a little more focused on the hardware side, with a sprinkle of software.

The good news right up top: My initial worries have almost completely been washed away, save a few minor complaints about two specific devices; there’s more here to like than I ever expected. Notice I said “almost” as there are still concerns in the back of my mind, but despite lots of, I guess, negativity surrounding and preceding this launch, the entire lineup of Googlebooks has exceeded my fairly low expectations.

For more video content, subscribe to 9to5Google on YouTube.

	

I do believe that this is largely due to my mixed experience with various Chromebooks across the entire price spectrum, combined with the ultimately lackluster or barebones “Desktop mode” that was added to Pixel devices over the past year.

This time, we have fewer SKUs to deal with, and of the five Googlebook devices, there appear to be fewer pinch points – save the pricing. These are not going to be cheap, with prices “starting at” $899 and, in most cases, are going to be more expensive. That is likely where a portion of you are going to stop reading and just dismiss these entirely. I can completely understand why.

Without glossing over or forgiving the frankly inflated asking price, I do believe this comes with one distinct benefit. There is less compromise in quality, which is something that worried me, given the mixed history of Chromebooks and the pitfalls of the cheapest model becoming the flag-bearer for the “default” experience.

I spent around 45 minutes prodding and poking the lineup, and there are two standouts.

Right off the bat, the Dell XPS and the HP Googlebook were the most impressive launch devices here. That said, each of the five laptops has its own merits.

ASUS’ Googlebook, Lenovo’s Googlebook 15, and Acer’s Googlebook 14 offer, in my opinion, are marginally lesser but still fairly decent takes on the first wave of hardware. The Lenovo in particular takes some design cues from previous Chromebooks and pairs with a bright HDR display. It was really easy to see despite lots of glare and jostling in the testing area.

I will state that I am personally not a fan of 2-in-1 laptops, but Googlebook OS, as it’s being styled, just turns the Acer model into arguably the best touchscreen laptop-tablet hybrid on the market. In fact, all of these laptops have excellent touchscreens that run at 120Hz. I was worried ahead of time that we’d get 60Hz screens, so it was very good to see a baseline of 120Hz.

Windows and ChromeOS have always struggled with touch inputs, while MacOS doesn’t allow for user interface control with your hands – or stylus. How many elite touchscreen experiences exist on a laptop? I wager until now, none. This is where Android, in my opinion, is being leveraged in the potentially best way possible. Swipes, taps, prods, it’s all just like using your phone or a tablet.

Just dipping back into a specific device in the lineup for a second, the matte display on the Acer Googlebook 14 was a great touch. It just eliminated glare almost entirely and reminded me of the recently released iPhone Duo. My only gripe was that it was covered in greasy fingerprints and smudges after a few minutes of usage.

Lenovo, ASUS, and Acer are utilizing Intel Core Ultra “Pantherlake” chips, while Dell and HP are going with the Snapdragon X Elite chipset. All come with at least 16GB of RAM for optimal performance. Some SKUs might offer up to 32GB of RAM, but my session made no mention of storage capacities, and there is no way to expand storage using external storage like a microSD card. There could be a really easy way to get people onside by offering these in future SKUs; for now, it’s business as usual.

More good news: The performance is excellent. Every Googlebook felt especially snappy. These are desktop-level chips running Android, which sort of is to be expected.

If anything, I was shocked at how responsive the experience was. It helps that each device has almost identical specifications. You can pick the laptop that suits your specific needs and still expect performance parity. Given my trepidation due to how Chromebooks have been treated by OEMs, this was very refreshing. It’s a good sign right at launch, but let’s hope Google holds more cards this time to almost force device makers to hit base specifications once cheaper models arrive.

The touchpads on all of the models are genuinely impressive. There’s some level of haptics, but MacBooks still reign supreme here. Every keyboard felt tight and responsive, and I liked stabbing away at the keys however briefly. None of the five models felt mushy or squishy under my fingers, and the layouts were instantly familiar to my battle-worn MacBook Pro battered fingertips. I didn’t have too long to test out the two unique keyboard G and odd Caps Lock keys, but they’ll no doubt take a while to get used to if you’re coming from Windows or Mac.

We saw ahead of launch that the lightbar is a key branding differentiator on the Googlebook. Sure, it looks nice, but it didn’t seem to do much beyond, well, look kind of cool. Google is planning on opening this LED strip up to developers in the coming months, so I’m sure we’ll get various takes on notifications, DND mode, and more that I probably haven’t thought of.

Something that I hope isn’t missed here is that the XPS Googlebook from Dell is the first such laptop from the company to come without Windows pre-installed. I think, given how mediocre the Dell Chromebook line was, this feels like a real statement of intent for a product line that is widely heralded as the best alternative to a MacBook. The company wouldn’t stake the XPS line on a mediocre product. It’s a gorgeous small-form-factor laptop, and one I really hope to spend some extended time with soon.

Can Android fill in the gap Chromebooks leave behind?

There are so many question marks over the Googlebook lineup, most notably who the platform is going to suit best or how it’ll fit into someone’s existing computing lineup. Some will ship with HDMI ports; there’s no room for a single SD card slot, or at least one that I remember spotting. I’d love to know what the experience is like using a secondary display or taking that experience elsewhere.

I feel like the software is much better than I had anticipated for a launch product. Yes, we’re missing a few top-level professional tools, but the full desktop Chrome browser might dispel some pre-launch detractors. I installed an extension I use every day, and it wanted to track my cashback while I was visiting a few of my favorite online shopping haunts. That reduced some of my initial fears of mobile Chrome on a laptop form factor.

What I cannot fault is the launch hardware. It is solid.

I went in with some preconceptions likely based on some of the leaks and, I’ll be honest, a mediocre unveil during the Android Show earlier this year. The devices have done a lot of the talking, which is an interesting prospect, as they already feel like a fluid expansion of Android into a new form factor.

Right now, I am likely not the target market. I need certain pieces of software, but ask yourself: do you have one key piece of software that is locking you into your current laptop or tablet? If that is the case, you probably were never looking at making a switch to a new desktop platform on launch day anyway.

My overriding early thought is that a Googlebook is an option for someone who has no allegiance to a desktop OS, but has a strong urge for their phone to expand into a bigger, more competent portable display. That might be a tiny portion of the market, but it could also be huge given that many people still use a phone for 95% of their day-to-day tasks. I don’t have a crystal ball or next week’s lottery numbers, but we have a new operating system to choose from, and I can’t be too negative about it. Any challengers to Windows, Mac, or Linux are good in my book. We just need things to start moving fast right out of the gate.

I think back to the early era of the smartphone. I imagined being able to take my phone, plug it into a screen, and have access to everything I need or use most. If that really worked, we’d all be using Samsung DeX, but we’re all still using separate laptops and desktops instead.

The modern smartphone is a hub for payments, photos, emails, entertainment, and the “right hand” of most people. Here’s what is different: The Googlebook takes your Android phone and turns it into a laptop. Whether you want it is ultimately up to you.

title: You can now claim your payout from Apple’s $250 million Siri settlement
snippet: The major class action lawsuit against Apple over Siri and Apple Intelligence delays continues to progress. Apple is expected to pay $250 million to settle the lawsuit, and you can now submit your claim to get a chunk of that payout. Here’s how. more…
fullText:
The major class action lawsuit against Apple over Siri and Apple Intelligence delays continues to progress. Apple is expected to pay $250 million to settle the lawsuit, and you can now submit your claim to get a chunk of that payout. Here’s how.

How to claim your payout from Apple’s Siri settlement

Verita Global, the Settlement Administrator behind the case, has set up the website where you can submit claim information.

The eligible class includes people in the United States who purchased an Apple Intelligence-capable iPhone between June 10, 2024 and March 29, 2025. That covers the window between when Apple announced the first Apple Intelligence features at WWDC and when it officially delayed the “more personalized” version of Siri.

Apple is paying $250 million to settle the lawsuit, while also admitting no wrongdoing. Legal fees and lawyers will take a chunk of the settlement. For iPhone users, the payout is expected to be $25 per eligible device. That number, however, could vary. If more users than expected file a claim, it could be less. If fewer claims are filed, the maximum payout is $95 per eligible device.

On the settlement website, you’ll be asked to submit your contact information as well as the serial number of the qualifying iPhone. You can then choose whether you’d like to be paid by check, PayPal, Venmo, or ACH. The deadline to submit a claim is December 21, 2026. 

The settlement website explains (via MacRumors): 

The Settlement will provide a cash payment if you purchased an iPhone 15 Pro, iPhone 15 Pro Max, iPhone 16, iPhone 16e, iPhone 16 Plus, iPhone 16 Pro, or iPhone 16 Pro Max that you purchased between June 10, 2024 and March 29, 2025 in the United States.

You must fill out and submit a complete and accurate Claim Form below by December 21, 2026. If your Claim Form is incomplete, contains false information, or is not submitted by the deadline, your claim will be rejected and you will waive all rights to receive a payment under this Settlement. The information you provide will be treated as confidential and used for the purpose of this Settlement only.

While the settlement website is now live, it will still be more than a year until payouts are sent. The final approval hearing for payouts is September 29, 2027, and payments will begin at least 60 days after that. 

Are you submitting a claim to get your $25? Do you think this is a fair settlement? Let us know down in the comments.
