title: Samsung Gallery is adding Google Photos backup to replace OneDrive
snippet: New updates are starting to roll out that will let Samsung Gallery replace its OneDrive integration with Google Photos support. more…
fullText:
New updates are starting to roll out that will let Samsung Gallery replace its OneDrive integration with Google Photos support.

Earlier this year, Samsung Gallery removed integration with OneDrive and, in turn, also removed native cloud backup for Galaxy users. Users could, of course, use apps from Microsoft, Google, Amazon, or any other number of providers, but there was nothing built into Samsung’s own Gallery app anymore.

Now, Samsung is confirming its replacement.

In an update to the “Gallery Cloud Sync” app on Samsung devices, the company says:

	

Gallery Cloud Sync is a service that safely backs up your precious memories to Google Cloud, allowing you to enjoy them seamlessly on all your devices at any time. View photos taken on your smartphone right away on your tablet.

Easy and secure backup: Safely store your Gallery photos, videos, and albums in the Cloud.

Seamless multi-device sync: No matter which device you use, your Gallery is always kept identical and up to date.

Google Cloud-based reliability: Provides a fast and stable environment through Google’s trusted cloud storage.

Edited for formatting

The mention of “Google Cloud” here is a bit misleading, as Samsung Gallery is adopting direct Google Photos integration, as shown by an early preview of this functionality by @WigettaGaming and SammyGuru writer “That Josh Guy” on Twitter/X. It’s not live just yet – at least in our testing – but Samsung Gallery will offer support for “Sync with Google,” including the ability to see available storage via the Gallery app, choosing which albums to sync, and what data conditions must be met to sync.

Samsung requires the “Gallery Cloud Sync” app and “Samsung Cloud” to both be updated, but it seems a Gallery app update or perhaps even a full system update will be required to get this working fully.

Google Photos integration like this has existed for a few years now, previously being added to the OnePlus Gallery app in 2024 and on devices from Xiaomi and select other brands. Google’s support page on the topic does not yet mention Samsung.

Samsung Gallery will still let existing OneDrive users sync their photos through September 30, but it’s great to see a replacement lined up.

fullText:
Google today is rolling out Android Canary 2609 with another update to Quick Settings that lets you require an unlock before making changes.

ZP11.260821.010 with the September 2026 security patch is available for the Pixel 10a, Pixel 10, Pixel 10 Pro, Pixel 10 Pro XL, Pixel 10 Pro Fold, Pixel 9a, Pixel 9, Pixel 9 Pro, Pixel 9 Pro XL, Pixel 9 Pro Fold, Pixel 8a, Pixel 8, Pixel 8 Pro, Pixel 7a, Pixel 7 Pro, Pixel 7, Pixel 6a, Pixel Fold, and Pixel Tablet.

As always, “Canary builds are highly experimental and are NOT recommended for general use.”

	

Require unlock for Quick Settings

Go to Settings > Display & touch > Lock screen for the new “Require unlock for Quick Settings” toggle that is off by default: “To prevent unauthorized changes, you must unlock your device to use Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, Mobile Data, and Airplane Mode.”

When enabled, you can still open the Quick Settings panel from the lockscreen, but tapping on those key Tiles will prompt you to fingerprint or PIN unlock. The flashlight, rotation, dark theme, etc. don’t require authorization.

Audio streams Quick Settings Tile

Additionally, the “Voice broadcast” Tile moves from system apps to Connectivity.

title: A small but growing number of founders are betting on bringing people together offline
snippet: On the surface, a game console and a leathercraft school don't appear to have much in common. But both founders think there's money in fostering the kind of connection that technology has eroded over the last couple of decades.
fullText:
Brynn Putnam and Tristan Walker have already done something that most founders only dream about: created companies so compelling that bigger outfits bought them. Putnam, a trained ballerina with a small chain of boutique studios, built the connected-fitness company Mirror and sold it to Lululemon for $500 million in cash less than three years later. Walker, who interned at Twitter while at Stanford business school, built the popular men’s grooming brand Walker & Company Brands, selling it five years later to Procter & Gamble for undisclosed terms (reportedly in the range of $20 million to $40 million).

That both of them are at it again is less surprising than the fact that their dramatically different new startups share the same north star: bringing people together, offline, in the same room.

Putnam’s new company, Board, which makes a 24-inch touchscreen table that recognizes physical game pieces as well as gestures, was built explicitly for a group sitting around it together rather than one person alone with a screen.

Walker’s Heirloom Craft is buying up and scaling fine-craft trade schools, starting with a leatherworking school in San Francisco founded by Hermès’ first American artisan-ambassador. (Walker is also running Collaborative Holdings, a fund carved out by the venture firm Collaborative Fund built to give founders more time to build their businesses.)

On the surface, a game console and a leathercraft school don’t appear to have much in common. But both founders think there’s money is fostering the kind of connection that technology has eroded over the last couple of decades.

The timing isn’t accidental. In June of last year, the World Health Organization’s Commission on Social Connection formally classified loneliness as a defining global health challenge, estimating that one in six people worldwide are affected and linking the condition to roughly 870,000 deaths a year.

The opportunity to address that challenge is expanding, too, for those paying attention to it. In a Harris Poll survey sponsored by Marriott Bonvoy earlier this year, two-thirds of Americans said they were prioritizing experiences, like travel, over material purchases this year. (The same percentage said retail shopping today feels too generic, with all retailers looking and feeling the same.)

For now, East Coast entrepreneurs seem to be gravitating more naturally to the space, if it can be called that. Along with Putnam and Walker, two other founders whose newest businesses are focused on connection include Bonobos founder Andy Dunn and Audrey Gelman of The Wing.

Pie, Dunn’s now five-year-old company, has moved from friend-matching app to event-discovery tool to what he now calls a “social life operating system,” anchored by “Community Homes” — a permanent digital hub for recurring social groups like run clubs or watch parties.

Gelman tried this once before. Her last company, The Wing, built a business on bringing women together and folded during the pandemic amid accusations that it didn’t treat its own staff equitably. Now she’s found a different way to do something similar. Her current venture, The Six Bells Countryside Inn, an 11-room guesthouse in the Hudson Valley, hosts a monthly murder-mystery dinner where actors seed the crowd and, by dessert, someone turns up dead. The mystery itself is a little ridiculous by design, but the effect it has on guests is reportedly substantial. (According to a New York Times feature on the inn this summer, its visitors routinely linger in the bar past midnight, trading numbers with strangers.)

All of these new businesses come from a personal as well as a professional place. At one of TechCrunch’s recent StrictlyVC evening events, held in New York’s West Village, Putnam was candid about the fact that Mirror was built around her own life. She was pregnant with her first child, running brick-and-mortar fitness studios, and trying to bring that experience home through a screen using technology, as she put it, to work on “myself, my body, my fitness, my reflection.”

Board was built with the opposite in mind. Now a mother of five in a blended family — the household went from three people to seven — Putnam said she kept running into the same problem: no product on the market let people of wildly different ages and abilities play together. “How can we use tech to create a shared experience?” is the question she said drove the pivot. It wasn’t a “movement from digital to analog,” as she put it, “so much as how can we use tech to bring people together rather than take them apart.”

It’s why Board’s touchscreen recognizes the physical objects placed on it — a spaceship triggers an action, a knife performs a cut — instead of relying on the buttons and joysticks of a traditional controller; this way, a child and a grandparent can play the same game without a shared learning curve.

Walker had the same instinct, but his came from anxiety about what AI is doing to work and to community. He started Heirloom, he said, because he was worried about AI “stealing knowledge work” and pulling people away from each other. If he was going to build something after Walker & Company, he wanted it to bring people back together.

It’s an interesting bet. Speaking at the same StrictlyVC event, Walker said he believes the U.S. has forgotten how to transmit mastery, including leatherworking, watchmaking, and fragrance design. For 50 years, he argued, America has broken the chain from master to apprentice, offshoring production and stripping the prestige from manual skill to the point that apprenticeships became something people did when they couldn’t get into a four-year college.

Heirloom is a wager that that’s now reversing, and Walker had a number to back it up, telling a room full of founders and investors that roughly half of Gen Z and Gen Alpha say they don’t want a four-year degree at all. In fact, more than half of the capacity at Heirloom’s first location in San Francisco is currently filled not by career-changers or retirees but by young tech workers looking for what he calls a “phones-down creative outlet.”

So far, the dollars involved are relatively small for these venture-backed startups. Putnam has raised $35 million from VCs for three-year-old Board. Pie has raised $24 million. Six Bells has raised roughly $3.8 million. Heirloom, founded 11 months ago, hasn’t disclosed its funding.

One possible exception is WeWork co-founder Adam Neumann, whose new residential real estate venture Flow — marketed around the same premise of solving loneliness through physical space — has raised more than $450 million, largely from Andreessen Horowitz, dwarfing everyone else in this story combined.

Indeed, right now it’s unclear whether “togetherness” becomes its own sizable investment category. Getting strangers to show up for each other — as good as that may be for society — isn’t nearly as scalable as shipping software. 

What’s notable is who’s building these companies: Putnam, Walker, Dunn, Gelman, and Neumann have all built a real brand once before. That makes it easier to raise capital and gives investors some confidence these are founders who know how to build something people actually buy. They’ve each guessed right about where the puck is headed once before. We’ll know more in another year or two whether enough customers follow along again this time.

title: Google goes in-depth, and a bit NSFW, on Noto 3D emoji as Android rollout expands
snippet: Google Design published a more detailed explanation of Noto 3D today as it expands beyond Pixel devices. more…
fullText:
Google Design published a more detailed explanation of Noto 3D today as it expands beyond Pixel devices.

Google explains that the design process for Noto 3D involved “drawing, sculpting, and debating every single character by hand so that dimension never came at the cost of soul.”

Noto 3D prioritizes “emotional clarity” over “treating emoji as miniature scans of the natural world.”

Our job was to preserve the vibe behind each symbol: using 3D to give the character a body, but illustration to give it a soul.

Research found that “highly anatomical details like irises or nostril depth actually slow down how fast our brains process emotion,” so the aim was to remove “extraneous detail and [keep] facial geometry minimal.” Additionally, “excessive props and texture destroy comprehension,” with “background features and accessories” becoming “visual static” at 18×18 pixels.

	

The design team ultimately decided that “every emoji gets at most three essential details to communicate what it is.”

In going from flat assets to three dimensions, Google asked: “What does the back of a smiley face look like?” NSFW (truly) joke aside, the team found examples like how the poodle emoji only had three legs.

Meanwhile, the same research found that “people empathize far more with complete silhouettes — especially when it comes to depicting real animals.” As such, Google moved away from floating heads. 

Seeing an animal’s stance, paws, and posture helps communicate intent. Upon learning this last year, we updated a few animal emoji, like the raccoon, to embrace its full mischievous self — and now in 3D.

Following the Pixel 11 launch, Noto 3D is now “rolling out across Google apps, Android, and select devices from partners including Nothing, Lenovo, Xiaomi, OPPO, OnePlus, realme, vivo, iQOO, HONOR, TECNO, Infinix, itel, [and] Motorola.” You can also browse the entire collection on Google’s dedicated page.

title: Android Auto update lets you customize your Google Maps ‘driving avatar’ via car display
snippet: Google is rolling out an update for Maps on Android Auto that gives users the ability to edit their “driving avatar” directly from the car’s display. more…
fullText:
Google is rolling out an update for Maps on Android Auto that gives users the ability to edit their “driving avatar” directly from the car’s display.

The ability to change the classic blue arrow navigation icon in Google Maps itself is not new, but it’s only been available on car displays for about a year. In May 2025, Google Maps rolled out support for showing your chosen icon on Android Auto and CarPlay, but it needed to be set on the phone itself. 

Now, Google is rolling out an on-car picker for your Google Maps “driving avatar” on Android Auto.

The change is rather simple. Through Google Maps on Android Auto, a new “driving avatar” setting appears alongside settings for home/work and alerts. Tapping it gives you the option to pick your avatar and change it to the color of your choice. It’s the same functionality found on your phone, just now accessible directly via the car’s display.

	

This appears to be going live with a server-side update. Android Authority spotted the change with Android Auto 17.8.163744 and Google Maps 26.38.01.980791571 but, despite using those same versions, we’re not seeing the option just yet. Sound off in the comments below if you have it.

In our teardown of Android Auto 17.8, we also noticed that Google has removed the neat little “Jimothy” Easter egg which, as we predicted, was clearly never meant for a public-facing rollout.

title: I’ve Used iOS 27 for Months. Here Are 7 Things I Like and 3 I’m Still Confused About
snippet: The new OS consistently nudges things in a good direction, even if it doesn’t feel like a total overhaul.
fullText:
The latest iOS update is out now. Apple released iOS 27 on Monday, Sept. 14 (just as I predicted). The updated Siri AI is the centerpiece of the update, but the OS also brings several other features to your iPhone — even if those features aren’t especially groundbreaking.

You can download iOS 27 now by going to Settings > General > Software Update > Update Now and following the prompts on your screen.

I’ve been using iOS 27 betas since June, and found a handful of useful new features, including a new Liquid Glass slider, and even started testing the revamped Siri after avoiding the digital assistant for a decade. Overall, my phone feels snappier and opening apps is almost instantaneous. 

Apple’s iOS 27 brings a lot of quality of life upgrades to your device without as many standout new features as previous iOS updates — similar to Liquid Glass in iOS 26. There are also a few questionable changes, such as a new way to access your Notification Center, which isn’t unusual for these annual upgrades. Overall, iOS 27 is an inoffensive update filled with subtle improvements that you might not notice unless they’re pointed out.

As the official pointer-outer person, that’s my cue to give you a virtual tour around Siri AI and some of my favorite changes, as well as a few updates that left me scratching my head.

Note that my experience with these features is based on beta versions of iOS 27, so it’s possible some of them work differently on the public release. Siri AI is still in beta, even after the public release of iOS 27, and remains an opt-in experience.

iOS 27’s best improvements

Siri gets an AI overhaul

The latest iOS update has convinced me to turn over some daily digital chores to Siri, such as looking up driving directions or checking my schedule. Despite a few flaws, Siri worked well when I asked it to plot my route in CarPlay, find a cake recipe and perform a number of other simple tasks. The result? I’m now comfortable using Siri for small jobs.

In iOS 27, Siri AI is disabled by default, so you have to enable it if you want to use it. Here’s how to do so. 

Tap Settings.

Tap Siri. 

Tap Try New Siri.

It can also take time to go from being waitlisted to being able to ask Siri AI for a gift recommendation for your friend based on a text thread. Don’t forget: Siri AI is also still in beta in iOS 27, so you could run into bugs or have odd experiences with the digital assistant. Plus, Siri AI is only available in Apple Intelligence-compatible devices. iPhone 14 models or older (or the iPhone 15 or 15 Plus models) can’t access the enhanced assistant.

New Liquid Glass slider, and one questionable option

Screenshot by Zach McAuliffe/CNET

After Apple launched Liquid Glass in iOS 26, the company added ways to adjust transparency to address readability issues. With iOS 27, you can get as close to disabling the design as possible thanks to a new Liquid Glass slider. After installing iOS 27, you’re given an option to adjust just how liquidy or glassy you want things. But if you skip that screen, here’s where to find the Liquid Glass slider.

Tap Settings.

Tap Appearance. 

Tap Liquid Glass. 

From here, you can make Liquid Glass elements on your device more or less transparent by dragging the slider to the right. If you want more see-throughness, so elements are more transparent, drag it left. I find it difficult to tell menus and background items apart — I don’t understand who would want this option, but it’s there if you do. 

I’ve been happily using the totally frosted look (slider all the way to the right) for a few weeks now. While I didn’t mind Liquid Glass as much as other folks, the frosted setting ensures I can read and see the text, menus and icons properly. 

Safari gets an upgrade, too

My CNET colleague Jason Chun has been enjoying the Safari upgrades in iOS 27, including favorable UI tweaks. He noted that the All Tabs icon replaces the three-dot menu in Safari’s Compact toolbar. He also likes the return of the Bookmarks icon to the top of a new tab next to Reading List and History, and that Safari can automatically organize tabs. 

“It’s a super useful feature,” Chun wrote. “Especially if you keep as many emotional support tabs open as I do (currently 72).” 

More volume control across your device

Screenshot by Zach McAuliffe/CNET

Apple finally gives you the choice to adjust the volumes of your ringtones, alerts and alarms independently. This has been greatly helpful, ensuring my alarm isn’t so loud that it wakes up my infant son at night, yet keeping my ringtone loud enough during the day that I can hear it over him crying. 

To separate the volume levels, you have to disable two switches:

Tap Settings.

Tap Sounds & Haptics.

Disable the switches next to both instances of Match Ringtone Volume.

You can then use the sliders beneath those switches to change the volume of your alarms and your alerts without affecting your ringtone volume. 

Pasting photos and links into messages is easier

Screenshot by Zach McAuliffe/CNET

There’s also an easy way to paste photos, links from social media and more into Messages in iOS 27. If you copy one of those things and go into a chat, Messages will display an option above your keyboard to paste the item into your message before you start typing. 

It’s a simple adjustment that streamlines texting assets to folks. Before, you had to long-press on the text box and tap Paste. That’s not a lot of steps, but tapping the option above the keyboard is faster.

I also appreciate how this makes it easier to ensure I’m pasting the intended photo or link into a message instead of another link or text from hours ago. I’ve pasted unrelated gibberish into texting fields many times before iOS 27.

The Weather app shows different elements

Screenshot by Zach McAuliffe/CNET

The Weather app gets another small tweak, showing more weather elements throughout the day. You can see hour-by-hour forecasts for rain and winds in your area by tapping water drop and wind symbols in the Conditions bar in the app. You can also see those conditions for the coming days of the week.

This is a welcome feature that helps me plan my day before stepping out the door with just a glance. 

New on-screen timer

Screenshot by Zach McAuliffe/CNET

You also don’t need to go into your clock app to set a timer in iOS 27. If you open the timer in your Control Center, a new timer window will appear at the top of your screen with a horizontal dial you can pull left or right to get the exact countdown you need (down to 15-second increments). You can set and start a timer from here and access it while in other apps. 

I like being able to quickly set and keep track of a timer without switching apps — a small but mighty improvement.

Three changes I’m still lost on

A standalone Siri app is now a thing

Screenshot by Zach McAuliffe/CNET

Apple Intelligence-compatible devices get a new Siri app in iOS 27 that lets you interact with the digital assistant in a similar way to other chatbots, such as Gemini on Android, and access past conversations or requests within the app.

I struggle to see the appeal of this app over the regular Siri voice assistant. It feels easier to use Siri without the app in most instances, such as asking the assistant to look up the hours of a local bookstore.

Even if you’re using the Siri app as a search engine, it feels easier to, you know… use a search engine. I asked Siri to check the news, for example, and the app would regularly give me news that was at least a few days old. This is better than when I tested an earlier beta version of iOS 27 and the app gave me news from about a month prior, but it’s still not what I’m looking for.

It does give you links at the bottom of queries to verify information, which is good if you use the app as such. However, a search engine such as DuckDuckGo could give me those links without forcing me to wade through a preamble that might be full of outdated or incorrect information.

Notification Center has a new home thanks to Siri AI

If you do enable the new Siri AI, your iPhone’s Notification Center gets a new home — much to my dismay. Instead of two sections for the drag-from-the-top touch shortcuts, now there are three. Instead of dragging down from the center of your home screen to see your notifications, now you have to drag down from the top-left corner of your home screen. If you drag down from the center, you open a new Search or Ask bar. 

I’m right-handed and this is dreadful. It’s one of the more annoying things about iOS 27. It messes with my muscle memory and my expectations of where things are located on my phone.

The good news is that if you don’t enable Siri AI (or later disable it), you can still access your Notification Center by dragging down from the top center of your home screen. It does mean you’d need to sacrifice using Siri AI — it all comes down to your UX preference. 

The tiny clock is tiny and morally wrong

Screenshot by Zach McAuliffe/CNET

You can shrink your lock screen clock in iOS 27 when customizing your lock screen. Tap the highlighted button in the picture above and the clock shrinks down into the date bar across the top of your screen. 

Sure, that option lets you see more of your lock screen background. However, I’m an advocate of the lock screen’s big clock and therefore consider the tiny clock to be heresy. Tiny clock feels too small to be comfortably legible. People who like this setting: Can you see Pluto on a clear night without a telescope?

iOS 27 is a step in the right direction

Siri AI is the centerpiece of the update, and Apple has improved on the digital assistant enough that if you don’t already use it, I’d suggest giving it another chance. Most of the other new features are small improvements and upgrades that make for a pleasant, if sometimes underwhelming, experience.

For more on the operating system, you can check out how to change some of the most annoying features on the OS and how I learned to stop worrying and began to enjoy Siri. You can also check out what could land on your device with iOS 27.2.

	

			

				

					

						

													

					

					

						

Zachary McAuliffe
						

						

							Senior writer						
					

											

								

											Zach began writing for CNET in November, 2021 after writing for a broadcast news station in his hometown, Cincinnati, for five years. You can usually find him hanging out with his wife, son and dog. You can reach him at zmcauliffe@cnet.com.

title: Elon Musk’s latest Boring Company pitch involves a Hyperloop between Austin and San Antonio
snippet: Many of The Boring Company's announced projects have not materialized.
fullText:
In Brief

Posted:

12:38 PM PDT · September 20, 2026

Image Credits:Benjamin Fanjoy / Getty Images

		

							

											
									

					

	

Elon Musk recently claimed that his tunneling startup The Boring Company is working on “a simple precursor Hyperloop” between Austin and San Antonio that will reduce the journey between the two cities to less than 30 minutes.

The Boring Company account shared Musk’s statement and said it “would be excited and honored to build this massive infrastructure project.”

Many of The Boring Company’s announced projects — including tunnel systems in Chicago, Los Angeles, and between New York City and Washington, D.C. — have not materialized. However, it does operate a transportation system combining tunnels and surface routes in Las Vegas, and it recently raised a $3 billion round led by the United Arab Emirates.

Musk’s comments about a potential Austin-San Antonio Hyperloop were actually in reply to an AI-generated video depicting a generic science fiction future with human colonies on other worlds. Musk re-posted the video and declared, “This is the future we shall bring into being”.

Musk’s critics have argued that his vision of the future is apparently inspired by pulp science fiction and comic books; historian Jill Lepore recently told me that he seems to favor sci-fi that “completely defeats and defies all of his political beliefs.”

title: iPhone 18 Pro Launch Could Be the First of Many for Apple’s New CEO This Year
snippet: The iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max may be the first phones to go on sale under new Apple CEO John Ternus, but today’s launch hinted at even more hardware launches to come.
fullText:
New Apple CEO John Ternus welcomed buyers of the new iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max to the company’s flagship Fifth Avenue store in New York on Friday, and it’s likely to be just the first of several major product launches for the former hardware lead’s first year in the top job.

Dressed in a dark gray shirt and blue jeans, Ternus immediately took to taking selfies, giving handshakes and signing phone boxes for the hundreds of fans who chose to preorder the new iPhone or Apple Watch. 

	

			

Ternus, formerly Apple’s senior vice president of hardware engineering, took a casual and personable approach to the launch — even gently laughing as one excited Apple fan accidentally dropped his iPhone 17 Pro Max onto the concrete while walking into the store.

“It’s fine, it’s got a little ding, no crack, thank you, Ceramic Shield,” Dallen Frutchey, 18, from Virginia, said about the accidental drop just ahead of moving his data to his new iPhone 18 Pro Max. This is his fourth time attending one of Apple’s Fifth Avenue store openings, where he had met prior CEO Tim Cook a number of times. At today’s event, he got a selfie with Ternus just before the phone drop.

“I’m excited to have someone who is down in the details with the products working on things now,” Frutchey said, wearing a blue sweater that matched his new glacier blue phone.

Dallen Frutchey, 18, with his new iPhone 18 Pro Max in glacier blue.Mike Sorrentino/CNET

The very first person to come out of the Apple store — Harry Sun, 21, from New Jersey — walked out with a burgundy phone while wearing a Believe pin from the Apple TV show Ted Lasso. Eric Morgan, the second person in line, came all the way from Guatemala. He was buying several phones for his family, who also made the trip but were staying at their hotel, away from the iPhone launch-day madness.

Harry Sun, 21, was the first person to walk out of Apple’s Fifth Avenue store with a new iPhone in hand.Bridget Carey/CNET

The glacier blue hue appeared to be an early crowd favorite at this store, and Apple’s flagship location had a number of visible changes to mark the occasion. The outside of the store had a color blend of burgundy along with that shade of blue — giving no love to the more traditional silver and black color variants that are also available for the 18 Pro and Pro Max.

Apple decorated the entrance to its Fifth Avenue store for the launch.Mike Sorrentino/CNET

Inside, the Apple store took on more of a party vibe as it filled with the crowds that had been waiting outside. A DJ booth spinning Lady Gaga songs blasted in front of a large blue carpet area that served as a showroom for the new phones, as well as the Apple Watch Series 12 and Apple Watch Ultra 4.

The blue carpet showroom area for Apple’s iPhone 18 Pro phones, Apple Watch Series 12, Apple Watch Ultra 4 and the AirPods 5.Mike Sorrentino/CNET

At the opposite end of the store, without many passersby, a small photography exhibit featuring photos taken on the iPhone 18 Pro was on display in an area that formerly served as the Apple HomePod demo area. We will see over the next few months whether new products will take over that real estate, since today’s event also marks a shift in how Apple conducts its iPhone launches.

Apple has a photography exhibition spotlighting images taken on the iPhone 18 Pro at its Fifth Avenue store.Mike Sorrentino/CNET

Apple’s set to do at least one more store launch like this when the iPhone Duo goes on sale on Oct. 23 — marking the company’s first entry into the foldable phone space. It’s also rumored to be launching a number of new home entertainment products, with the decreased floor space for the HomePod possibly hinting at a relaunch of the speaker now that the new Siri AI assistant is rolling out to the iPhone 15 Pro and later.

And that’s not to mention the rumors hinting that a non-Pro iPhone 18 and an iPhone Air sequel may be set up for a spring launch, anchoring what could be a new annual launch event early in the year to contrast with premium phones coming later in Apple’s typical September window.

Apple’s current lineup consists of (left to right) the iPhone 17, iPhone Air, iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max. Not pictured but also available are the iPhone 17E and iPhone 16.Mike Sorrentino/CNET

So while this is the first iPhone launch under Ternus, it’s likely that several more of these are to come over the next year.

Bridget Carey contributed to this story.

title: Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4 missing one health-focused feature
snippet: Well, this is odd. The handwashing timer feature is currently absent from the new Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4 hardware. more…
fullText:
Well, this is odd. The handwashing timer feature is currently absent from the new Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4 hardware.

Handwashing detection and timer feature not currently supported by Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4

Handwashing detection is still a feature in watchOS 27. It also remains a category in Apple Health, including the iOS 27.2 version. Handwashing detection works on Apple Watch Series 11 and Ultra 3, and it’s still included in the watchOS 27 guide.

However, Apple’s newest watches aren’t included in the supported hardware list. It’s unclear if that’s an omission or a hardware difference.

In theory, there’s no reason to even mention supported hardware if Apple planned to continue supporting the feature on its newest watches. 

Handwashing detection arrived in 2020 as part of watchOS 7. It’s likely this pandemic-era feature is just no longer supported by Apple’s 2026 hardware. Series 12 and Ultra 4 include the first overhauled processor for the first time in a few years. It features new Audio Intelligence features like Siri Recap and Live Rewind. Handwashing detection may have just been left out.

We’ll update our coverage if we learn more about the missing feature.

Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4 are both available now. You can read the 9to5Mac review here.

title: Motorola teases high-end ‘Signature 27’ with a wild-looking design
snippet: Ahead of more information coming tomorrow, Motorola has teased its wild-looking “Signature 27” phone on social media. more…
fullText:
Ahead of more information coming tomorrow, Motorola has teased its wild-looking “Signature 27” phone on social media.

In a post on Instagram, Motorola ditches much of the smoke and shadows surrounding its upcoming “Signature 27” smartphone, showing off most of the phone’s design. And it looks wild, with four camera lenses across two rows on the top of the device, curving down to a thinner overall design further down that’s mostly out of view.

It’s a big design departure from the previous Motorola Signature, and also something we haven’t seen in other smartphones available today.

Motorola says that this device – which, based on prior teasers, is the “Signature 27” – is “engineered to the highest standards.” The teaser also mentions Qualcomm’s Snapdragon Summit event, all but confirming the device will be powered by one of the latest Snapdragon chips.

title: Can John Ternus find Apple’s next big thing?
snippet: Today, I’m talking with Mark Gurman, who is the world’s best-sourced Apple reporter — both as Bloomberg’s chief Apple correspondent and the host of the upcoming podcast Power On. Earlier this month, Apple hosted its annual iPhone hardware event, virtually every detail of which was reported ahead of time by Mark. But this event was special, for a number of reasons. It was new Apple CEO John Ternus’ first major product launch since he took over for former CEO Tim Cook less than two weeks prior. It was also the debut of the iPhone Duo, Apple’s first foldable smartphone. The timing of those two things was not at all coincidental, as you’ll hear Mark explain. Apple takes these hardware events — and the stories they tell — extremely seriously. This year’s story actually says a great deal about what’s happening at Apple, how Cook managed in wholesale leadership ranks over the past year, and how all of that might change Apple’s culture. Furthermore, what all that tells about Ternus’ plan to navigate Apple from what you might call the iPhone era into the AI era. Okay: Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman on the future of Apple. Here we go. This interview has been lightly edited for length and clarity. Mark Gurman, you’re the chief Apple correspondent and the managing editor of consumer technology at Bloomberg. Welcome to Decoder. Good to be here finally. Thanks for having me. And it’s been a while, so it’s good to catch up on all things Apple. Yeah, I’m really excited to talk to you. Obviously, Apple just had its big event. They announced the iPhone Duo. It was John Ternus’s first event as CEO. This is a Decoder episode, so we’ve got a new CEO, and we’ve got a new org chart inside of Apple. There’s been a lot of shuffling. You’ve been chronicling them very, very deeply over the past few years. Let’s just start with the event. I have a very basic question for you. Sure. Do you ever get nostalgic for a time when you didn’t know what was going to happen at the iPhone event? Do I ever get nostalgic? Do you ever wish that you, Mark Gurman, were about to be surprised? Honestly, I never think about it that way. I’m just fixated on delivering the goods and delivering the news. And people love their Apple. People want to know everything that’s coming down to the last minute, so I’m here to provide it for them. The thing with me, and I don’t know if most people know this about me, but I hope people know this about me, is that I’m a huge Apple fan through and through, and I’ve always been. And I’m so lucky to be able to cover a company that I love, a company that I am obsessed with, and a company whose products I use. There are so many people who cover companies that they couldn’t care less about. That’s not me. So I do what I do because I love Apple and I love covering Apple. I love the community around it, and I love talking about it. And it’s always fun to get a peek at the future and help keep not only myself informed, but people informed around me. That actually leads me to a lot of things because I’ve known you forever. We’ve been working in and around the same spaces forever. You got your start as an Apple blogger at the Apple rumor sites. There’s a whole culture around Apple that has grown up and changed over the years, and you can trace it to different eras of hardware, to different CEOs, to different sizes of the company. This was the first event with John Ternus as CEO. Apple announced a big new product in the iPhone Duo. Do you sense that the community is changing? How do you think that community has changed over the years? And do you think Ternus is going to lead to a difference in what that community feels like? I have to say, this event really didn’t feel much different than a Tim Cook event. They felt pretty interchangeable. It could have been Tim up there introducing it. It could have been Ternus up there introducing it. The one thing I will say that did feel slightly different is that Ternus came out swinging with a point of view on AI. The first thing he came out with was about the intelligent personal hub. Now, here’s the big difference between Tim Cook and John Ternus in terms of their management style. You’re inside Apple, you’re an executive, you’ll come to him with an idea, you’ll come to him with a viewpoint, a decision, an opinion, and he’ll just pepper you with more questions. He won’t make a singular decision in many cases. It’s very much communal decision-making, collaborative decision-making. John Ternus, if you come to him and you want him to make a decision, he’ll make a decision. He’ll have an opinion. Now, you may hate his opinion; you may completely disagree with him, but he has a viewpoint. But that’s the big difference between talking to people about Ternus and Tim. Ternus comes out talking about his view on AI. I may disagree with it. A lot of people may disagree with it. They may think the OpenAI or Anthropic approach is superior, but at least he came out and had a viewpoint. Apple’s been at this AI game now for two years since they launched Apple Intelligence at WWDC in 2024, and it’s been a mishmash of things. They haven’t really come out with a very strong narrative and viewpoint, and they finally did. So, as I said, whether you agree with it or not, they did do that. And I thought that was a really interesting way to kick off the keynote. All right, we’re just going to get into the weeds of Apple nerds disagreeing about things. Okay, let’s do it. I sat through that event, and I appreciated the same thing that you saw, which is, “Oh, we’re telling a story.” John Ternus is on the stage, and the first thing he’s doing is telling a story about this product and how it fits into the universe of technology. And then I took a beat, and I was like, oh, but they’re also just making sure that he’s successful at his first event by playing Apple’s greatest hits. Because an “intelligent personal hub” is just a replay of Steve Jobs saying the iMac was the digital hub. At the very end of the event, Ternus said, “There’s one more thing, and it’s the iPhone Duo.” There was just a part of all of that that, to me, felt like Apple saying, “Look, our new CEO can put on the clothes of the old CEO. He can do this same dance that you’re expecting.” Underneath it, what I felt was, to your point, that I don’t buy the story about the intelligent hub. No, I don’t buy it either. Because any of the things we’re seeing AI do are happening in cloud services. It’s the same week that Meta launched Muse, right? Right. You can feel what you want about Meta launching Muse, but Mark Zuckerberg is giving everybody 8GB of storage and 8GB of RAM in the cloud, and Muse can go do a lot of things that AI on the iPhone absolutely cannot do at this point in time. I just felt like there was a part where they were playing it really safe with John by having him basically show up and be the new lead singer of Journey. You can’t get it wrong if you’re going to do “Lights.” If you’re going to show up on stage and do “Don’t Stop Believin’,” you’re going to be fine for a minute. And it’s all the stuff that comes after that’s going to really show his real personality. But it sounds like you thought that that’s his point of view. Well, it’s a couple of things. At a very high level, Apple’s going to tell a story around what they have. If Apple invented ChatGPT, they would’ve invented ChatGPT, and they would’ve told a good story around that. Apple has gone as far as it’s able to, at least for now, on AI. So it’s telling the story, the best version of that story that they can with what they have to work with, with the bird they have in hand. So that’s the one thing. I agree with you on the intelligent personal hub, and how that compares to the iMac back in ’98. And it feels like they’re trying to sell this pivot from the Mac as the center of everything with the peripherals around it; then you got to iCloud in 2011, the center of everything with the peripherals around it. Now, it’s this Intelligence right at the center with everything around it. But what’s so fascinating is that Apple held a major product launch event in September of the year 2026 and did not introduce a single notable new AI feature. The first 15 minutes or so of the keynote was simply a replay, a re-narrativization of what they introduced over the past two years with Apple Intelligence. And so they tried to just tell that story in a more concrete way. The other thing is they don’t have any AI devices at the very core, and so they need to prop up the iPhone as their AI device because they don’t have an alternative. But of course they’re only going to do that until they have that killer device, and then they’re going to change that whole narrative. So it’s a very narrative PR and marketing-driven company. And I’m not saying that to be critical. I mean, if I ran the company, obviously I’m going to tout what I have. I’m not going to veer from that. But it is interesting how they’re playing this. And I agree, they did play it very safe. There’s nothing safer than John Ternus introducing a new iPhone. It’s like the safest thing you can do. No major new AI product, no smart home hub, nothing in the spatial space, just straight down the middle. Yeah, it seems like that next wave of smart home products, which we’re expecting later this year… I say, “We’re expecting.” I’m expecting it because that is something you have reported. [Laughs] I am expecting it, yes. Mark Gurman is expecting new products from Apple. That is the first cut at some truly AI-native devices. Because you have Siri AI and it is functional now in a way that it previously was not functional, you can try some new classes of devices. There are about a half dozen AI-native devices coming in the next year and a half or so. The first will be the smart home hub, which is basically an Amazon Echo Show but Apple-style. It will have a square screen and an entirely new operating system. The idea is: what would a Siri AI operating system look like? This is that: intercom, video conferencing, proactive intelligence. So you walk up to it, it recognizes who you are, and it will show content personal to you. It will know who is speaking. Obviously, the Amazon Echo can do that, but Apple’s doing it in its own Apple-y way with AI-based Face ID. They’re working on a home security system. They’re working on another version of the smart home hub that I just talked about that is attached to a robotic arm. So you put it on your desk, and it can move around. It’s actually a category that’s pretty popping in Asia and in China right now. Then you’ve got the wearables, the smart glasses. I still believe those are going to be introduced and shipped in 2027, so not too far from now. Trust me, you’ll be wearing them. Within 365 days, you will be wearing them and have video footage of you wearing them at the Steve Jobs Theater. And if that is not the case, either something went horribly wrong for you or something went horribly wrong for Apple. You’ll also have the AirPods with cameras. That’s an interesting thing that we should talk about, but they’ll have the AirPods with cameras and then a few other wearables that I won’t get into. So this is what I was talking about when I said there were eras at Apple and people’s relationship with the company really changed. The Steve Jobs era was defined by devices, and in particular, Steve Jobs himself getting up and doing a keynote and famously putting up pictures of all the existing smartphones and saying, “Well, these all suck. And here’s the reason they all suck, and here’s the iPhone and here’s why it’s better.” That created one kind of relationship between Apple’s enormous community of fans, its leader, and the products. I think that was very successful. I think the Tim Cook era has been meaningfully different. I think it’s largely a story about scale. To some extent, it’s a story about values. To a huge extent, it’s a story about privacy. Apple has marketed itself as the privacy company. It fought the FBI to keep the iPhone encrypted. There’s a lot there with Tim Cook’s version of the company, but it’s more corporate. Certainly, it’s just a vaster company. It’s safer. It’s not as rough around the edges as Jobs’ Apple, but it wasn’t as device-based. I don’t think the Vision Pro has the same kind of mainstream cultural impact as even the hockey puck mouse that Jobs put out. There was a thing that he could do with products that Tim Cook Apple could not quite do with products. And that just feels really different to me. Well, I didn’t have the briefings. Yeah. But according to the literature on their website, when you’re doing that feature, it lights up with a microphone icon when you do the live rewind. Maybe it doesn’t light up for the Siri Recap — I don’t think it does for the all day listening — but the last 15 seconds things, it supposedly shows a microphone. But Nilay, is this podcast a video? Yeah. Okay. I’m wearing an Apple Watch. Can you see anything on my screen? Right, it’s crazy to me. So I can’t believe they did that because, really, you’re going to take a backlash like this and then do it again with a visual intelligence six, nine months from now? And then you’re going to do it with a pair of smart glasses, and you’re going to walk into all of the other things. Yeah. It feels like Apple knows that there’s a next generation of user interfaces coming that is AI-powered that requires an amount of ambient capture, whether that’s just listening so you can talk to it or whether it’s visual so you can see the world around you. And they haven’t solved the social privacy aspect. Nope. There are white papers about how Apple might have solved the technical database privacy aspect, right? Yep. They’ve got Private Cloud Compute, and they’re going to encrypt the data. They’re not going to store this and that. And I don’t think any of that’s going to overcome the social privacy aspect. They didn’t do a good job on articulating the social aspect of it at all. They could’ve shown more demos. They could’ve discussed it a bit deeper. I know they only have very limited time in the keynote, but I don’t think they spent enough time breaking things down here. I quite frankly think they did not do a good job rolling this feature out. I ask myself, would I be comfortable using this feature? Yeah. But then if I tell everyone around me in the last week, “Hey, I’ve been recording you the whole time,” they’re going to freak out, and they’re not going to trust Apple. So it’s a really interesting one. I’m pretty shocked they did it. What are the net new Apple Watch buyers because of this feature? What is the bigger challenge, doing this feature or not doing this feature? And I think that doing this feature is a bigger drawback than not doing the feature. Here, there is no cost of not doing something. Well, there is a cost if you think there’s about to be a wave of AI devices that are doing always-on transcripts and meeting recordings, and OpenAI is going to do something. I mean, we have seen a wave of startups that do this. But we’re not there yet, right? Right. This could’ve waited six months. So you can just foreclose it. This is like Microsoft stuff. You’re like, “Here’s a preview of a feature. Don’t even consider that stuff. Eventually this will get good,” and you’ve just foreclosed the competitor. Well, the other thing is they had nothing else for the watch, so they had to just do something, right? This is the weakest Apple Watch update we’ve seen in a long time, and they’re lost as to what to do next. Now they’re recalibrating it. They’re going to have a major watch revamp at the end of next year and so forth, but they have to do something. If it were me, I would have ripped off the bandaid at the same time with all the audio plus visual intelligence stuff next year. Do it all together and have a really coherent privacy story. But do you think that stuff is compatible with Apple’s reputation for privacy? This is the real question I’m getting at: they might not have told the right story about the Apple Watch. Apple is going to have to tell the right story about AirPods with cameras in them in a world where people are shooting spray foam at Flock cameras because they don’t want them in their communities. There’s a connection between these two ideas, and it doesn’t seem like Apple knows how to tell that story. Well, clearly not, because they haven’t done it. But here’s the story on the AirPods. They can’t record actual video. They can’t take actual pictures. They have an extremely low frame rate. I’m talking about a few frames per second. The actual data that gets input into them, it’s like… Have you ever used a Roomba, and when you look at the app, what does the Roomba see? It’s like wireframes of the environment. It would not be able to tell you and me apart. It’s just seeing two people. Then how can it do the brands of tomato sauce in the aisle? Well, in terms of non-people, it’d be able to do that, and it could read text. So it’d be pretty heavily reliant on reading text and seeing color and whatnot. But being able to differentiate between two people would be very difficult. It’s almost like a fake reproduction of what’s around you. I don’t have a good explanation for it, but I’m sure if they wanted to, they’ll give a good one. I’m not sure they’re going to break it down. They might just say, “Just trust us. We’re Apple. It’s not taking pictures. It’s not taking video. It doesn’t know what it’s seeing to some extent.” So we’ll see how they play it. But I would’ve done all this stuff together, ripped off the bandaid and spent a lot of time focused on it. There was no need to do this audio intelligence feature at the end of ’26 when you could have done it at the end of ’27. Unless you’re trying to slowly boil the frog, right? You’re going to get people mad about this, and then you’re going to do the next one the next time. Right. It just seems like this next generation of devices involves some kind of ambient listening that we are not ready for as a society. People are really mad about Meta glasses. What are you going to do about it? They soiled the water for Apple and a lot of other companies. Meta being the first mover on this created an industry-wide problem. And I think even though Apple has such a strong privacy stance, there are people who don’t believe them. There are people who don’t care what they have to say. There are people who are going to be angry about the Apple glasses and whatnot. I think Apple, to some extent, is on such a high horse with its privacy message that it came away surprised that there would be some backlash to Apple doing this. They think, I believe, that people are overblowing it when it comes to Apple and everyone should just be focused on Meta. And just because Meta has done a poor job protecting people’s privacy doesn’t mean we’re going to. So we’ll see what happens. One thing: when I talk to the folks there, they never make the connection between Apple and Meta in the sense that Meta’s apps run on Apple’s phones. People are mad about Meta, and they still think the phones, Apple’s phones, are listening to them, and they can’t quite make that connection because it undoes a lot of their own messaging. If you believe your iPhone is listening to you, that’s not just Meta’s problem. It is also Apple’s problem. They kind of have to actively ignore that relationship because otherwise everything else falls apart. And I think that’s why there’s this blind spot. If people’s watches start generating transcripts, it’s exactly the same relationship as “my iPhone is listening to me, and that’s why I saw an ad for a vacation that I only talked to my friend about.” I’m curious what they’re going to do. I have a feeling they’re just going to bulldoze their way through it. They’re going to just try to tell a good story. They’re going to do a ton of PR briefings about it. They’re going to do a ton of white papers about it, and get as nerdy and in-depth as they can on this stuff. You know what they’re going to do? They’re going to throw out a lot of comparisons. I even heard Ternus do this in one of the interviews, in Apple’s statement on some of these features. I could totally imagine them saying, “Why is it any different recording from smart glasses if you could just hold your phone up and record people?” With the audio intelligence feature, one thing I didn’t even think of is the Apple Watch- It’s very funny you just mentioned that because that is exactly what Mark Zuckerberg just said to our friend Alex Heath. Oh, that’s funny. “How is it different from a phone?” This is the industry’s approach. I think the answer is that people are like, “Yeah, I can see you doing that, and I feel very comfortable telling you to stop.” There’s something different about that. I didn’t even realize this. Someone pointed this out to me the other day. It’s like your Apple Watch has had the Voice Memos app for, I don’t know, eight years at this point. Who stopped anyone from recording their whole day with the Voice Memos app on the Apple Watch anyway? This is just a more privacy-centric version of that. So Apple’s solving a problem here. They’re not creating one. So it just depends on how you look at these things. I think they’ll bulldoze their way through it. It’s going to be a problem, but I think they’ll be fine. All right. Last two before I let you get out of here. We’ve talked around the iPhone Duo a lot. We’ve mentioned it a lot. It’s the thing that just came out. We haven’t talked about it. What do you think of it? I think it’s incredible. I think, and this is a bold take, that foldables will become the new normal within a decade. If you look at the market share of smartphones at the end of 2006, smartphones had like 6 percent of the market. Now they have 85 percent of the market. It went over 50 percent of the market after five to six years. The iPhone itself was not the source of that, but the iPhone got everyone into the smartphone game. I think the iPhone Duo is going to do the same for the phone market. I think it’s going to become the new normal. Even though Apple is a late mover to foldables? Yeah. I think the Apple brand is that strong, really. I really do. I think the fit and finish, the software integration, is going to get people really excited about this category. I think that the Apple Upgrade program, the leasing program, will eventually expand internationally. I think that’s going to get people in it. I think that at some point they’re going to stop advertising sticker prices and focus on the monthly prices, and they’re going to get people locked into this thing. They’re going to have a family of iPhone Duos over time. You’ll see every phone maker just transitioning, transitioning to foldables. Samsung: half the line is already foldables. Very soon the candy bar style is going to become legacy. That’s a big prediction. Although I will say their iPhone handoff feature, where you can move a number between phones, seems to point to a future where I, for example, have the folding phone for work and then a much smaller, lighter phone for the weekends with the family. You can see that vision taking shape only because it’s now easy to port a number between devices, just whenever you want, which I think is incredible. Last question. We’ve talked a lot about Apple, its culture, and its set of products. What do you think its biggest challenges are in the new era under John Ternus, and what do you think its biggest opportunities are? I would say that I think the biggest challenge and the biggest opportunity are the same thing. Ternus’ Apple for the next three to five years is still Tim Cook’s Apple, right? That’s just the reality. He’s still going to be there in the background. He’s still going to loom large, and the product pipeline is still going to be coming out of an era that started under Tim Cook. But in five years from now, they are going to need to start thinking of what actually replaces the iPhone as the next thing. We went from the Mac to iCloud to AI as the center. What is Apple’s new thing after the phone? What is Apple’s new thing after the current generation of AI? And Ternus’ tenure as CEO, I think, will go down as a success if he’s able to find that next new centerpiece. He’s got a few years before he needs to start cooking on that, but I’m talking about something that can be in development for 5 to 10 years. Tim Cook never had the opportunity to have his new centerpiece of the company. He never had the opportunity to put his stamp on products at the company for two reasons. Both things that he tried to do as his centerpiece failed spectacularly. Obviously the Vision Pro, but the car — the car, that was Apple’s multi-trillion-dollar market cap opportunity, and they just blew it. Ternus will need to successfully hit that. I’d actually put a third thing on that list. It was the very beginning of the Cook era, with Jobs literally on his deathbed, and he said he’d figured out TV. Oh, yes. He had to spend however long pretending he knew what that meant because I don’t think it had been solved. And so there was this first wave of “Apple’s going to redefine TV” because the last page of the Isaacson biography had a Jobs quote on it. They haven’t even done a new Apple TV box in four years. That’s a long time. It’s funny because you don’t need one. It never occurs to me that I need to upgrade this thing, but maybe there’s going to be some AI feature. Well, Siri AI. They’ve been waiting for the Siri AI update. This could be a whole other podcast, but Siri AI has been the gate to all of these new product categories. The AirPods were supposed to be out already, the Apple TV, the HomePod, the smart home hub… all these devices were supposed to come out. Apple couldn’t do any of them until Siri AI. Now Siri AI is here, so the floodgates are open. All right. Well, Mark, we’re going to have to have you back on the show to talk about those floodgates and all these new products very soon. I can’t believe you haven’t been on until now. Thank you so much for being on Decoder. Yeah. And obviously I’d love to have you on my new podcast, Power On Podcast, launching very shortly. So thanks in advance. Questions or comments? Hit us up at decoder@theverge.com. We really do read every email!
fullText:
Today, I’m talking with Mark Gurman, who is the world’s best-sourced Apple reporter — both as Bloomberg’s chief Apple correspondent and the host of the upcoming podcast Power On.

Earlier this month, Apple hosted its annual iPhone hardware event, virtually every detail of which was reported ahead of time by Mark. But this event was special, for a number of reasons.

It was new Apple CEO John Ternus’ first major product launch since he took over for former CEO Tim Cook less than two weeks prior. It was also the debut of the iPhone Duo, Apple’s first foldable smartphone. The timing of those two things was not at all coincidental, as you’ll hear Mark explain. Apple takes these hardware events — and the stories they tell — extremely seriously.

This year’s story actually says a great deal about what’s happening at Apple, how Cook managed in wholesale leadership ranks over the past year, and how all of that might change Apple’s culture. Furthermore, what all that tells about Ternus’ plan to navigate Apple from what you might call the iPhone era into the AI era.

Okay: Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman on the future of Apple. Here we go.

This interview has been lightly edited for length and clarity. 

Mark Gurman, you’re the chief Apple correspondent and the managing editor of consumer technology at Bloomberg. Welcome to Decoder.

Good to be here finally. Thanks for having me. And it’s been a while, so it’s good to catch up on all things Apple.

Yeah, I’m really excited to talk to you. Obviously, Apple just had its big event. They announced the iPhone Duo. It was John Ternus’s first event as CEO. This is a Decoder episode, so we’ve got a new CEO, and we’ve got a new org chart inside of Apple.

There’s been a lot of shuffling. You’ve been chronicling them very, very deeply over the past few years. Let’s just start with the event. I have a very basic question for you.

Sure.

Do you ever get nostalgic for a time when you didn’t know what was going to happen at the iPhone event?

Do I ever get nostalgic?

Do you ever wish that you, Mark Gurman, were about to be surprised?

Honestly, I never think about it that way. I’m just fixated on delivering the goods and delivering the news. And people love their Apple. People want to know everything that’s coming down to the last minute, so I’m here to provide it for them.

The thing with me, and I don’t know if most people know this about me, but I hope people know this about me, is that I’m a huge Apple fan through and through, and I’ve always been. And I’m so lucky to be able to cover a company that I love, a company that I am obsessed with, and a company whose products I use. There are so many people who cover companies that they couldn’t care less about. That’s not me.

So I do what I do because I love Apple and I love covering Apple. I love the community around it, and I love talking about it. And it’s always fun to get a peek at the future and help keep not only myself informed, but people informed around me.

That actually leads me to a lot of things because I’ve known you forever. We’ve been working in and around the same spaces forever. You got your start as an Apple blogger at the Apple rumor sites. 

There’s a whole culture around Apple that has grown up and changed over the years, and you can trace it to different eras of hardware, to different CEOs, to different sizes of the company. This was the first event with John Ternus as CEO. Apple announced a big new product in the iPhone Duo.

Do you sense that the community is changing? How do you think that community has changed over the years? And do you think Ternus is going to lead to a difference in what that community feels like?

I have to say, this event really didn’t feel much different than a Tim Cook event. They felt pretty interchangeable. It could have been Tim up there introducing it. It could have been Ternus up there introducing it.

The one thing I will say that did feel slightly different is that Ternus came out swinging with a point of view on AI. The first thing he came out with was about the intelligent personal hub. Now, here’s the big difference between Tim Cook and John Ternus in terms of their management style. You’re inside Apple, you’re an executive, you’ll come to him with an idea, you’ll come to him with a viewpoint, a decision, an opinion, and he’ll just pepper you with more questions. He won’t make a singular decision in many cases. It’s very much communal decision-making, collaborative decision-making.

John Ternus, if you come to him and you want him to make a decision, he’ll make a decision. He’ll have an opinion. Now, you may hate his opinion; you may completely disagree with him, but he has a viewpoint. But that’s the big difference between talking to people about Ternus and Tim.

Ternus comes out talking about his view on AI. I may disagree with it. A lot of people may disagree with it. They may think the OpenAI or Anthropic approach is superior, but at least he came out and had a viewpoint.

Apple’s been at this AI game now for two years since they launched Apple Intelligence at WWDC in 2024, and it’s been a mishmash of things. They haven’t really come out with a very strong narrative and viewpoint, and they finally did. So, as I said, whether you agree with it or not, they did do that. And I thought that was a really interesting way to kick off the keynote.

All right, we’re just going to get into the weeds of Apple nerds disagreeing about things. 

Okay, let’s do it.

I sat through that event, and I appreciated the same thing that you saw, which is, “Oh, we’re telling a story.” John Ternus is on the stage, and the first thing he’s doing is telling a story about this product and how it fits into the universe of technology. And then I took a beat, and I was like, oh, but they’re also just making sure that he’s successful at his first event by playing Apple’s greatest hits. 

Because an “intelligent personal hub” is just a replay of Steve Jobs saying the iMac was the digital hub. At the very end of the event, Ternus said, “There’s one more thing, and it’s the iPhone Duo.” 

There was just a part of all of that that, to me, felt like Apple saying, “Look, our new CEO can put on the clothes of the old CEO. He can do this same dance that you’re expecting.” Underneath it, what I felt was, to your point, that I don’t buy the story about the intelligent hub. 

No, I don’t buy it either.

Because any of the things we’re seeing AI do are happening in cloud services. It’s the same week that Meta launched Muse, right?

Right.

You can feel what you want about Meta launching Muse, but Mark Zuckerberg is giving everybody 8GB of storage and 8GB of RAM in the cloud, and Muse can go do a lot of things that AI on the iPhone absolutely cannot do at this point in time. 

I just felt like there was a part where they were playing it really safe with John by having him basically show up and be the new lead singer of Journey. You can’t get it wrong if you’re going to do “Lights.” If you’re going to show up on stage and do “Don’t Stop Believin’,” you’re going to be fine for a minute. And it’s all the stuff that comes after that’s going to really show his real personality. But it sounds like you thought that that’s his point of view.

Well, it’s a couple of things. At a very high level, Apple’s going to tell a story around what they have. If Apple invented ChatGPT, they would’ve invented ChatGPT, and they would’ve told a good story around that. Apple has gone as far as it’s able to, at least for now, on AI. So it’s telling the story, the best version of that story that they can with what they have to work with, with the bird they have in hand. So that’s the one thing.

I agree with you on the intelligent personal hub, and how that compares to the iMac back in ‘98. And it feels like they’re trying to sell this pivot from the Mac as the center of everything with the peripherals around it; then you got to iCloud in 2011, the center of everything with the peripherals around it. Now, it’s this Intelligence right at the center with everything around it.

But what’s so fascinating is that Apple held a major product launch event in September of the year 2026 and did not introduce a single notable new AI feature. The first 15 minutes or so of the keynote was simply a replay, a re-narrativization of what they introduced over the past two years with Apple Intelligence. And so they tried to just tell that story in a more concrete way.

The other thing is they don’t have any AI devices at the very core, and so they need to prop up the iPhone as their AI device because they don’t have an alternative. But of course they’re only going to do that until they have that killer device, and then they’re going to change that whole narrative.

So it’s a very narrative PR and marketing-driven company. And I’m not saying that to be critical. I mean, if I ran the company, obviously I’m going to tout what I have. I’m not going to veer from that. But it is interesting how they’re playing this. And I agree, they did play it very safe. There’s nothing safer than John Ternus introducing a new iPhone. It’s like the safest thing you can do. No major new AI product, no smart home hub, nothing in the spatial space, just straight down the middle.

Yeah, it seems like that next wave of smart home products, which we’re expecting later this year... I say, “We’re expecting.” I’m expecting it because that is something you have reported.

[Laughs] I am expecting it, yes.

Mark Gurman is expecting new products from Apple. That is the first cut at some truly AI-native devices. Because you have Siri AI and it is functional now in a way that it previously was not functional, you can try some new classes of devices.

There are about a half dozen AI-native devices coming in the next year and a half or so. The first will be the smart home hub, which is basically an Amazon Echo Show but Apple-style. It will have a square screen and an entirely new operating system. The idea is: what would a Siri AI operating system look like? This is that: intercom, video conferencing, proactive intelligence.

So you walk up to it, it recognizes who you are, and it will show content personal to you. It will know who is speaking. Obviously, the Amazon Echo can do that, but Apple’s doing it in its own Apple-y way with AI-based Face ID.

They’re working on a home security system. They’re working on another version of the smart home hub that I just talked about that is attached to a robotic arm. So you put it on your desk, and it can move around. It’s actually a category that’s pretty popping in Asia and in China right now.

Then you’ve got the wearables, the smart glasses. I still believe those are going to be introduced and shipped in 2027, so not too far from now. Trust me, you’ll be wearing them. Within 365 days, you will be wearing them and have video footage of you wearing them at the Steve Jobs Theater. And if that is not the case, either something went horribly wrong for you or something went horribly wrong for Apple.

You’ll also have the AirPods with cameras. That’s an interesting thing that we should talk about, but they’ll have the AirPods with cameras and then a few other wearables that I won’t get into.

So this is what I was talking about when I said there were eras at Apple and people’s relationship with the company really changed. The Steve Jobs era was defined by devices, and in particular, Steve Jobs himself getting up and doing a keynote and famously putting up pictures of all the existing smartphones and saying, “Well, these all suck. And here’s the reason they all suck, and here’s the iPhone and here’s why it’s better.” 

That created one kind of relationship between Apple’s enormous community of fans, its leader, and the products. I think that was very successful. I think the Tim Cook era has been meaningfully different. I think it’s largely a story about scale. To some extent, it’s a story about values. To a huge extent, it’s a story about privacy. 

Apple has marketed itself as the privacy company. It fought the FBI to keep the iPhone encrypted. There’s a lot there with Tim Cook’s version of the company, but it’s more corporate. Certainly, it’s just a vaster company. It’s safer. It’s not as rough around the edges as Jobs’ Apple, but it wasn’t as device-based. 

I don’t think the Vision Pro has the same kind of mainstream cultural impact as even the hockey puck mouse that Jobs put out. There was a thing that he could do with products that Tim Cook Apple could not quite do with products. And that just feels really different to me.

I’m going to correct you on that because every time I put an article or a post out about the Vision Pro being on life support, I get what amounts to basically a notch or two below a death threat from dozens of people. So people are passionate about it.

Dozens? Dozens?

Well, honestly, I think what it is is that people have created businesses around spatial computing and apps, and they’re just pissed off that they’ve invested all this time and money in a category that’s probably going to die out.

And then you have consumers who spent four grand on this product, and they’re like, “I saved up for this thing, I’m living with this thing, and I’m pissed off to hear the realities.” But if you have another hour, we can talk about the Vision Pro.

No, the comparison there is good. People have invested in it. They care deeply about it. The comparison I’m making is that the relationship people have to Apple in the Cook era is as an institution. It’s just like this big thing that spans the globe on a massive scale. 

It’s IBM.

Yeah, and in the Jobs era, it was all about really, really innovative new products that redefined categories over and over again. You’re describing a whole bunch of new products that came up in the Cook era that John Ternus is going to launch. How do you expect the culture of Apple to change around its products or its relationship to the culture to change as we go from one CEO to another?

But think about what they did. You’ve got the coolest new iPhone and Apple product in maybe 10, 20 years introduced one week after Tim Cook steps down. And then for the next 12 to 18 months, you’ve got, I don’t know, six or seven new product categories. Maybe you have 25 pretty breakthrough things.

So Tim Cook made a decision that, even though his tenure at a product company was pretty limited in major new things, the Apple Watch turned out to be a success, even though it started as a complete dud, as you remember. The AirPods are a unique beast in that they’re an accessory, but it’s not a platform on its own yet. It’s going to get there. And the Vision Pro is a failure.

Tim Cook could have ended his tenure as CEO with the iPhone Duo. He could have just waited. Typical transitions at Apple happen mid-October or mid-April; they happen on January 1st. It was a specific decision that was made for John Ternus to be the one to introduce the iPhone Duo. It was a specific decision made for John Ternus to be the one to introduce this whole new product roadmap. Even though, as you know, because of the length of hardware development cycles and R&D, these things were in the oven for five to 10 years.

So it’s really interesting that this decision was made to let Ternus be the face of this whole new era of products rather than allow Tim Cook to take the credit for it. And I think that’s to your point where they’re trying to draw the line in the sand of this new era. If Cook is already going to step down in the next three years, let’s just do it now and let Ternus take the credit for everything.

Take me inside that. You’ve obviously done a lot of reporting. I think you were the first to break the news that Cook would be searching for a successor. You were, I think, among the very first to break that it would be Ternus. Tell me about that process. 

This is a big decision; Cook is going to play a huge role at the company. He has a massive compensation program tied pretty much to having to talk to Xi Jinping and Donald Trump. It seems like that’s his job: to just manage that relationship. 

For $47 million a year, I would talk to Trump and Xi Jinping on the phone every day.

[Laughs] I would need at least 50, but that’s just me. That’s his job: to go do politics much the same way that Eric Schmidt at Google was in charge of governments after Larry Page became CEO. There’s a whole pattern here. 

Brad Smith at Microsoft, even though he wasn’t CEO, but yeah.

He’s the president of the company. Yeah, there’s a parallel here. Tell me about this decision of Tim Cook wanting to elevate his position to something like that, and of making John Ternus the face of the product side of the company in this new role.

So 2023 rolls around and Tim Cook starts every executive team meeting, all high-level meetings with people at Apple at the executive levels, with, “We need to start taking succession seriously. We need to start thinking about who the next people are.” At that time, there was a really strong realization that many of the people at the top of Apple either had half a billion dollars in the bank or were already billionaires, and that this era would start to age out really quickly.

And so Tim Cook knew that he wanted to take a step back. Jeff Williams, the number two as the COO, knew he wanted to retire. The CFO, Luca Maestri, wanted to retire, too. The general counsel, Kate Adams, also wanted to retire. They were all about the same age, give or take a few years. So they basically came up with this plan that would go one by one over the next few years.

It started with the CFO. Luca retires at the very end of 2024, and he’s replaced by the new CFO, Kevan Parekh. Then 2025 rolls around, and Jeff Williams, the COO, retires and is replaced by his deputy, Sabih Khan. Then in 2026, they had the transition for the general counsel, and they got a great replacement for her from Meta, Jennifer Newstead. And then at the end of 2026, the big one: Tim Cook to John Ternus. So they played this out very, very slowly.

What Tim Cook has done, and I do think this is going to change in the Ternus era as we progress here, is that he came up with this strategy that I call “Hotel California.” You never want to leave. Tim Cook, he’s staying around as executive chairman. The general counsel had her stay around an extra six to nine months to run government affairs.
