Unless you’re trying to slowly boil the frog, right? You’re going to get people mad about this, and then you’re going to do the next one the next time. 

Right.

It just seems like this next generation of devices involves some kind of ambient listening that we are not ready for as a society. People are really mad about Meta glasses. What are you going to do about it?

They soiled the water for Apple and a lot of other companies. Meta being the first mover on this created an industry-wide problem. And I think even though Apple has such a strong privacy stance, there are people who don’t believe them. There are people who don’t care what they have to say. There are people who are going to be angry about the Apple glasses and whatnot.

I think Apple, to some extent, is on such a high horse with its privacy message that it came away surprised that there would be some backlash to Apple doing this. They think, I believe, that people are overblowing it when it comes to Apple and everyone should just be focused on Meta. And just because Meta has done a poor job protecting people’s privacy doesn’t mean we’re going to. So we’ll see what happens.

One thing: when I talk to the folks there, they never make the connection between Apple and Meta in the sense that Meta’s apps run on Apple’s phones. People are mad about Meta, and they still think the phones, Apple’s phones, are listening to them, and they can’t quite make that connection because it undoes a lot of their own messaging. If you believe your iPhone is listening to you, that’s not just Meta’s problem. It is also Apple’s problem.

They kind of have to actively ignore that relationship because otherwise everything else falls apart. And I think that’s why there’s this blind spot. If people’s watches start generating transcripts, it’s exactly the same relationship as “my iPhone is listening to me, and that’s why I saw an ad for a vacation that I only talked to my friend about.”

I’m curious what they’re going to do. I have a feeling they’re just going to bulldoze their way through it. They’re going to just try to tell a good story. They’re going to do a ton of PR briefings about it. They’re going to do a ton of white papers about it, and get as nerdy and in-depth as they can on this stuff.

You know what they’re going to do? They’re going to throw out a lot of comparisons. I even heard Ternus do this in one of the interviews, in Apple’s statement on some of these features. I could totally imagine them saying, “Why is it any different recording from smart glasses if you could just hold your phone up and record people?” With the audio intelligence feature, one thing I didn’t even think of is the Apple Watch-

Oh, that’s funny.

“How is it different from a phone?” This is the industry’s approach. I think the answer is that people are like, “Yeah, I can see you doing that, and I feel very comfortable telling you to stop.” There’s something different about that.

I didn’t even realize this. Someone pointed this out to me the other day. It’s like your Apple Watch has had the Voice Memos app for, I don’t know, eight years at this point. Who stopped anyone from recording their whole day with the Voice Memos app on the Apple Watch anyway? This is just a more privacy-centric version of that. So Apple’s solving a problem here. They’re not creating one. So it just depends on how you look at these things. I think they’ll bulldoze their way through it. It’s going to be a problem, but I think they’ll be fine.

All right. Last two before I let you get out of here. We’ve talked around the iPhone Duo a lot. We’ve mentioned it a lot. It’s the thing that just came out. We haven’t talked about it. What do you think of it?

I think it’s incredible. I think, and this is a bold take, that foldables will become the new normal within a decade. If you look at the market share of smartphones at the end of 2006, smartphones had like 6 percent of the market. Now they have 85 percent of the market. It went over 50 percent of the market after five to six years.

The iPhone itself was not the source of that, but the iPhone got everyone into the smartphone game. I think the iPhone Duo is going to do the same for the phone market. I think it’s going to become the new normal.

Even though Apple is a late mover to foldables?

Yeah. I think the Apple brand is that strong, really. I really do. I think the fit and finish, the software integration, is going to get people really excited about this category. I think that the Apple Upgrade program, the leasing program, will eventually expand internationally. I think that’s going to get people in it.

I think that at some point they’re going to stop advertising sticker prices and focus on the monthly prices, and they’re going to get people locked into this thing. They’re going to have a family of iPhone Duos over time. You’ll see every phone maker just transitioning, transitioning to foldables. Samsung: half the line is already foldables. Very soon the candy bar style is going to become legacy.

That’s a big prediction. Although I will say their iPhone handoff feature, where you can move a number between phones, seems to point to a future where I, for example, have the folding phone for work and then a much smaller, lighter phone for the weekends with the family. You can see that vision taking shape only because it’s now easy to port a number between devices, just whenever you want, which I think is incredible. 

Last question. We’ve talked a lot about Apple, its culture, and its set of products. What do you think its biggest challenges are in the new era under John Ternus, and what do you think its biggest opportunities are?

I would say that I think the biggest challenge and the biggest opportunity are the same thing. Ternus’ Apple for the next three to five years is still Tim Cook’s Apple, right? That’s just the reality. He’s still going to be there in the background. He’s still going to loom large, and the product pipeline is still going to be coming out of an era that started under Tim Cook.

But in five years from now, they are going to need to start thinking of what actually replaces the iPhone as the next thing. We went from the Mac to iCloud to AI as the center. What is Apple’s new thing after the phone? What is Apple’s new thing after the current generation of AI? And Ternus’ tenure as CEO, I think, will go down as a success if he’s able to find that next new centerpiece. He’s got a few years before he needs to start cooking on that, but I’m talking about something that can be in development for 5 to 10 years.

Tim Cook never had the opportunity to have his new centerpiece of the company. He never had the opportunity to put his stamp on products at the company for two reasons. Both things that he tried to do as his centerpiece failed spectacularly. Obviously the Vision Pro, but the car — the car, that was Apple’s multi-trillion-dollar market cap opportunity, and they just blew it. Ternus will need to successfully hit that.

I’d actually put a third thing on that list. It was the very beginning of the Cook era, with Jobs literally on his deathbed, and he said he’d figured out TV. 

Oh, yes.

He had to spend however long pretending he knew what that meant because I don’t think it had been solved. And so there was this first wave of “Apple’s going to redefine TV” because the last page of the Isaacson biography had a Jobs quote on it.

They haven’t even done a new Apple TV box in four years.

That’s a long time. It’s funny because you don’t need one. It never occurs to me that I need to upgrade this thing, but maybe there’s going to be some AI feature.

Well, Siri AI. They’ve been waiting for the Siri AI update. This could be a whole other podcast, but Siri AI has been the gate to all of these new product categories. The AirPods were supposed to be out already, the Apple TV, the HomePod, the smart home hub… all these devices were supposed to come out. Apple couldn’t do any of them until Siri AI. Now Siri AI is here, so the floodgates are open.

All right. Well, Mark, we’re going to have to have you back on the show to talk about those floodgates and all these new products very soon. I can’t believe you haven’t been on until now. Thank you so much for being on Decoder.

Yeah. And obviously I’d love to have you on my new podcast, Power On Podcast, launching very shortly. So thanks in advance.

Questions or comments? Hit us up at decoder@theverge.com. We really do read every email!

title: World model companies are keeping a lot of secrets
snippet: Everyone in the world-models space is sitting on a pile of cash and a ton of buzz, but good luck getting anyone — from the founders to their own data suppliers — to tell you what they're actually building.
fullText:
This week, I moderated a panel on world models at the All In conference (no relation to the podcast), and it gave me a chance to dig into one of the most mysterious corners of the AI world. The big players in the space are Yann LeCun’s AMI Labs and Fei-Fei Li’s World Labs — and while both have accumulated a lot of buzz and funding, they also rank pretty low on the trying-to-make-money scale.

At their core, world models are about automating spatial intelligence, so the field could head in lots of exciting and lucrative directions, from robotics to interactive video to more complex self-driving systems. 

But when I started to press on where we would actually see the tech commercialized, things got foggy. The closest thing I found to an authority was Michael Rabbat, a co-founder of AMI Labs and the company’s VP of World Models, who joined me on the panel. But when I pressed him on exactly what the company was working on, he was cagey. “We’ll talk about it when we’re ready to talk about it.” Over email, he clarified, “We’re still in a research and building phase, so we’re not talking publicly about any product plans or timeline.”

To be fair, AMI is less than a year old, so it’s fair enough to keep quiet. But this sort of caginess extends to the whole world-modeling space. World Labs’ Marble is probably the most fully developed product in the space, and its demos range from straightforward media creation, building explorable environments for video games, or CGI effects. There are robotics use cases too, but the whole platform seems more designed to demonstrate capabilities. 

That secrecy even extends to these companies’ suppliers. On the sidelines of the same conference, I spoke to Alex de Vigan, CEO of Physicl — a data supplier for the burgeoning world model business. He says he knows Physicl’s data has been useful for whatever they’re building, but he’s still in the dark about what exactly that is. “I wish they would tell us more. We could build more useful data if we knew what they were working on,” de Vigan told me.

Part of the mystery comes from how versatile world models are as an idea. The simplest version is a navigable map of the world, similar to the AI models that power self-driving cars. But the same modeling approach that helps a Waymo weave through traffic could also help a humanoid robot carry boxes, or turn a few minutes of video footage into an explorable environment. AMI has already dipped its toe in manufacturing, biomedicine, robotics, and even AI software for doctors through its Nabia partnership. Surely it won’t pursue all of those — but maybe one or two of them are standing out?

No one doubts that there are lots of viable businesses to be built on world model tech — and as long as it’s easy to fundraise, there’s no particular pressure to focus on one. In fact, there’s good reason not to. If AMI announced tomorrow that they had built a humanoid OpenClaw or a next-generation Hollywood rendering system, a lot of other labs would suddenly be very interested in the space. Soon, the lab would face potential competition from the other world model companies, the neolabs, and even OpenAI and Anthropic. 

In some ways, it’s the flip side of all that easy fundraising. Your competitors can fundraise, too — and the same money that lets you build under the radar is also funding lots of potential rivals once the path to market becomes clear. But even if that competition is inevitable, it’s best if you delay it for as long as possible, which means keeping quiet about exactly what you’re building.

Cixin Liu fans will recognize this as a dark forest scenario: If you don’t know who else is in the woods, it’s best not to attract attention.

This post was first published on September 18, 2026.

title: Google Keep update tweaks the homescreen widget on Android
snippet: Google Keep for Android has rolled out a small tweak to the “Note collection” widget that shows a feed on your homescreen. more…
fullText:
Google Keep for Android has rolled out a small tweak to the “Note collection” widget that shows a feed on your homescreen.

The Material You-era sidebar on the right with shortcuts to add a text note, list, audio, drawing, or photo has been removed. It has been replaced by a circular FAB (floating action button) — like on “Single note” — that opens a pop-up. 

Introducing a second tap for note creation, this menu matches the behavior of the smaller, pill-shaped “Quick capture” widget.

Old vs. new

	

As such, there’s now an edge-to-edge design and you get to see a bit more of each note. By comparison, the previous design left considerable empty space, especially if you went for a full-width homescreen layout. 

Version 5.26.365.x of Google Keep is rolling out via the Play Store.

This follows the rollout of Keep Live for Google AI Plus, Pro, and Ultra subscribers.

title: The iPhone 18 Pro Is Tricky to Repair, According to an iFixIt Teardown
snippet: A teardown of the iPhone 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max shows that most repairs require removing the screen, which has a delicate plastic frame backing.
fullText:
On the outside, the iPhone 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max look identical and have the same dimensions as last year’s iPhone 17 Pro and 17 Pro Max. But on the inside, the 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max are quite different, with bigger batteries, a new A20 Pro chip, a significantly larger vapor cooling system and tiny mechanical aperture blades in the main camera’s lens.

As the new Apple pro phones make their way into people’s pockets, they’re also appearing in durability testing and teardown videos. 

Tech reviewer Zach Nelson dropped a pair of iPhone 18 Pro videos on his YouTube channel, JerryRigEverything: one showing how the new pro phone did in a scratch and durability test, and the other showing him dismantle Apple’s new handset.

On Sunday, the tech repair and advocacy site iFixIt did a teardown of the iPhone 18 Pro, and not all of it went according to plan. Taking off the back glass panel was relatively straightforward, but there’s not much that a person can repair aside from the panel itself.

Of the four 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max models that iFixIt took apart, the plastic frame behind the display broke on three. Apple doesn’t sell the plastic frame part, so if it’s damaged, it can only be replaced by getting a whole new display module. You could put the display back on without the plastic backing frame, but it wouldn’t sit flush with the body. I should note that in Nelson’s teardown, he didn’t suffer the same calamity and gave Apple a “thumbs up for repairability” after removing the display.

“Four phones are too few to establish a failure rate. Adhesive strength, heating, technique or a difference in the plastic could all matter. That plastic frame has been present since the 15 Pro. But it hasn’t given us nearly as much trouble in previous years,” wrote Liz Chamberlian and Carsten Frauenheim, iFixIt’s director of sustainability and repairability engineer, respectively, in a blog post. “Using isopropyl alcohol might make display removal more consistent, but we’ll have to do more testing to be sure.”

Nelson and iFixIt’s teardown, along with Apple’s Ireland site, gives us a complete picture of the battery capacity for the new iPhone Pro models, SIM card and eSIM only models. Both the iPhone 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max have larger batteries compared to last year’s 17 Pro and 17 Pro Max. The variants sold outside the US have a slightly smaller battery to afford room for a SIM card tray. 

Phone

SIM card or eSIM only

Battery capacity

iPhone 18 Pro

SIM card + eSIM

4,056 mAh

iPhone 18 Pro

eSIM only

4,288 mAh

iPhone 18 Pro Max

SIM card + eSIM

5,391 mAh

iPhone 18 Pro Max

eSIM only

5,567 mAh

The new variable aperture on the main camera of the 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max is another curiosity. It’s made of six tiny mechanical blades. For CNET’s iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max review video, our cinematographer, Celso Bulgatti, filmed it in action.

There are six paper-thin aperture blades inside the main camera lens of the iPhone 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max.Celso Bulgatti/CNET

If any of the rear cameras on the iPhone 18 Pro or 18 Pro Max break, you’d likely need to replace the entire camera array, which includes the new mechanical aperture.

“We dismantled the main camera and concluded that an aperture-only repair isn’t going to be feasible: If your aperture gets stuck, you’ll be looking at replacing the entire main camera assembly,” noted Chamberlian and Frauenheim.

On the whole, iFixIt gave the iPhone 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max a provisional repairability score of 7 out of 10, the same as the 17 Pro and 17 Pro Max and 16 Pro and 16 Pro Max.

You can watch more of iFixIt’s findings in the company’s full teardown video below.

title: New all-glass iPhone 20 Pro rumor reveals another design change
snippet: Apple’s major 20th-anniversary iPhone refresh is in the works for next year. A new rumor today reiterates expectations that the iPhone 20 Pro and iPhone 20 Pro Max will have even bigger screens than the current models. more…
fullText:
Apple’s major 20th-anniversary iPhone refresh is in the works for next year. A new rumor today reiterates expectations that the iPhone 20 Pro and iPhone 20 Pro Max will have even bigger screens than the current models.

The rumor comes from Weibo leaker Digital Chat Station, who has a track record of sharing accurate iPhone leaks. Here are the screen sizes of next year’s iPhone 20 Pro models, according to the latest leak:

iPhone 20 Pro: 6.41 inches

iPhone 20 Pro Max: 6.96 inches

For comparison, the iPhone 18 Pro features a 6.27-inch display measured diagonally, which Apple markets as 6.3 inches. The iPhone 18 Pro Max has a 6.86-inch display, which Apple rounds to 6.9 inches in its marketing materials.

This means the iPhone 20 Pro and iPhone 20 Pro Max could have the biggest iPhone screens ever — save, of course, for the 7.6-inch inner display on the looming iPhone Duo.

Today’s rumor adds that Apple is testing a “borderless quad-curved design” with a hole-punch display design, featuring a smaller Dynamic Island. The design is widely expected to be made primarily from glass.

In August, Bloomberg reported that this 20th-anniversary iPhone is still on track for next year. Mark Gurman described the design as using glass on the front and the back, and that the material “will curve into the sides of the devices, with a metal band in the middle.”

title: M6 Mac mini review: Apple’s most versatile Mac continues to shine
snippet: Over the last several years, the Mac mini has become one of the most compelling Macs in Apple’s lineup. It combines impressive performance with a compact footprint, making it versatile enough for all kinds of workflows. I’ve spent the last week using the M6 Mac mini, and it pushes that formula even further. Here’s everything you need to know. Buy the M6 Mac mini: from $879.99 (Reg. $899) Buy the M5 Pro Mac mini: from $1,669.99 (Reg. $1,699) more…
fullText:
Over the last several years, the Mac mini has become one of the most compelling Macs in Apple’s lineup. It combines impressive performance with a compact footprint, making it versatile enough for all kinds of workflows.

I’ve spent the last week using the M6 Mac mini, and it pushes that formula even further. Here’s everything you need to know.

Buy the M6 Mac mini: from $879.99 (Reg. $899)

Buy the M5 Pro Mac mini: from $1,669.99 (Reg. $1,699)

Design

From the outside, the new Mac mini looks identical to its predecessor. Apple gave the Mac mini its first proper redesign in more than a decade in 2024, dramatically shrinking its footprint to just 5 by 5 inches. That same design persists today, and it’s still incredibly easy to love.

There’s something about having the small but powerful Mac mini on my desk that just makes me smile. The amount of power Apple has packed into this tiny footprint is nothing short of impressive.

It’s a delightful example of Apple’s design team at its best, without compromising performance or connectivity.

Connectivity

On the front, you’ll find two USB-C ports and a 3.5mm headphone jack. On the back of the M6 configuration, you’ll find three Thunderbolt 4 ports, while the M5 Pro version features three Thunderbolt 5 ports. There’s also an HDMI port on the back.

One nice change: 2.5Gb Ethernet is now standard on both the M6 and M5 Pro configurations. The M4 models started at gigabit Ethernet. 10Gb remains an optional upgrade.

The other two connectivity updates for the new Mac mini models include Wi-Fi 7 instead of Wi-Fi 6E and Bluetooth 6 instead of Bluetooth 5.3.

For external displays, both versions of the Mac mini support up to three displays, but specifics vary based on the chip:

M4

M6

1 display

8K/60, 5K/120, or 4K/240

8K/60, 5K/120, or 4K/240

2 displays

2× 6K/60 or 4K/144; or 8K/60, 5K/120, or 4K/240 + 5K/60

2× 6K/60 or 4K/165; or 8K/60, 5K/120, or 4K/240 + 5K/60

3 displays

2× 6K/60 or 4K/144 + 1× 5K/60

2× 6K/60 or 4K/165 + 1× 5K/60

Single TB port

Up to 2 displays

Up to 2 displays

DisplayPort

1.4

1.4

M4 Pro

M5 Pro

1 display

8K/60, 5K/120, or 4K/240

8K/60, 5K/120, or 4K/240

2 displays

8K/60, 5K/120, or 4K/240 + (6K/60 or 4K/144)

8K/60, 5K/120, or 4K/240 + (5K/120 or 4K/200)

3 displays

3× 6K/60 or 4K/144

3× 6K/60 or 4K/165

Single TB port

Up to 2 displays

Up to 3 displays

DisplayPort

2.1

2.1

Performance

My review unit is the M6 configuration of the Mac mini, so I’m going to focus on that for most of this review. The M5 Pro version is the same chip we’ve come to know and love since debuting in the MacBook Pro earlier this year.

Here are the specs of my review unit:

12-core CPU

12-core GPU

24GB unified memory

512GB storage

The M6 chip has two additional CPU cores compared to the M4 and M5 chips. It’s Apple’s first 2nm processor for the Mac. It’s also Apple’s first chip to use all three of its CPU core types: 2 super cores, 4 performance cores, and 6 efficiency cores.

The super cores prioritize maximum single-threaded performance, while performance cores are optimized for multithreaded workloads. The efficiency cores handle lighter background tasks.

Memory bandwidth has also increased significantly, from 120GB/s with the M4 to up to 170GB/s with the M6 (153GB/s on the 16GB configuration).

The M6 also features a new 12-core GPU, up from the 10-core GPU in the M4. Apple says graphics performance is up to 2x faster than the M4 Mac mini, including up to 2x faster ray-traced rendering in Blender. Each GPU core also includes a Neural Accelerator, helping the M6 deliver up to 4x faster AI performance than the M4 Mac mini.

I won’t pretend to regularly run local AI models or other on-device AI workflows, so I don’t have much real-world insight to offer here. But for people who do, Apple’s own testing suggests the gains are real.

Here’s Federico Viticci, whose AI opinion I trust, on the new Mac Studio: 

M5 Ultra Mac Studio Review: The Dream Mac for Local AI Agents

In Geekbench 7 testing, the M6 Mac mini scored 4,074 in single-core, 22,632 in multi-core, and 92,542 in the Metal GPU test. That puts it 24% ahead of the M4 in single-core performance, 48% ahead in multi-core performance, and 71% ahead in GPU performance.

Geekbench results, of course, aren’t necessarily indicative of real-world performance. Instead, they’re good for cross-reference comparisons to other Macs.

As you can see, the M6 also starts to encroach on M4 Pro territory, beating the 12-core M4 Pro in both single-core and multi-core performance, though the M4 Pro still has the edge in GPU performance.

Apple also says the M6 Mac mini offers up to 2x faster storage, and my benchmarking supports that. I consistently hit around 6,000-6,400 MB/s write speeds and 6,000-6,300 MB/s read speeds in Blackmagic Disk Speed Test. For comparison, 512GB M4 Mac mini configurations generally reached around 3,000 to 3,400 MB/s.

Pricing

When Apple debuted the redesigned Mac mini in 2024, we marveled at the price. It started at $599 with the M4 chip paired with 16GB of memory and 256GB of storage.

A lot has changed since then.

The Mac mini has become a go-to recommendation for people looking for dedicated machines to run AI agents and other AI workflows. We’ve entered what former Apple CEO Tim Cook has called a “100-year flood” in terms of memory prices, and there are no signs of that ending anytime soon.

In May, Apple stopped selling the 256GB storage configuration for the M4 Mac mini, making the base configuration 512GB. This raised the pricing floor from $599 to $799.

When Apple raised prices for most products over the summer, the 256GB Mac mini configuration returned, priced at $799 (up $200 compared to its launch price).

At the time, it was reasonable to think this was Apple insulating the Mac mini from any future increases (at least in the short term). Unfortunately, that wasn’t the case.

The M6 Mac mini starts at $899 for 256GB of storage and 16GB of memory. The M5 Pro configuration starts at $1,699, up $300 from the M4 Pro launch price and up $100 from the M4 Pro’s most recent price.

The thing that stands out to me, though, isn’t necessarily the $899 starting price. It’s that you still only get 256GB of storage. If the M6 Mac mini started with 512GB of storage, I don’t think there would be much room to complain about the price. Instead, upgrading to 512GB of storage costs an additional $200, pushing the price to $1,099.

So, the good news is the Mac mini is better than it’s ever been. The bad news is that it’s no longer the exceptional $599 value it was two years ago … it’s just a really good value instead.

9to5Mac’s Take

I love that we live in a world where the Mac mini is thriving. Apple’s smallest Mac, which has occasionally felt neglected, is having its well-deserved moment in the spotlight.

There’s a lot to love about the new Mac mini, including the faster performance and storage, all with the same great design. That combination of performance and design also makes it the most versatile Mac Apple sells, whether you’re using it as a desktop, an always-on server, a machine for running AI agents, or something else entirely.

Is it a little awkward that the Mac mini comes in M6 and M5 Pro configurations, as opposed to M6 and M6 Pro? On paper, sure, but practically I’m glad that Apple is focused on updating the Mac mini with whatever chips are ready at a given moment. That flexibility is one of the best things about the Apple Silicon era.

While the higher starting price changes the value equation, it doesn’t change my overall feelings about the Mac mini. It’s still an easy Mac to recommend for people who want a compact desktop Mac without spending substantially more for a Mac Studio.

title: iOS 27’s Wallet app adds feature that will make you want to use Apple Cash
snippet: Apple Wallet is better than ever in iOS 27 thanks to a handful of new features, including a clever solution for splitting bills with friends and family via Apple Cash. Here’s how it works. more…
fullText:
Apple Wallet is better than ever in iOS 27 thanks to a handful of new features, including a clever solution for splitting bills with friends and family via Apple Cash. Here’s how it works.

iOS 27 uses your iPhone’s camera and Apple Intelligence to make bill splitting seamless

Apple Cash has been part of iOS for years now, and I use it occasionally with a select few people in my life. But third-party services like Venmo and Zelle still tend to be preferred by most people I know for sending money.

In iOS 27 though, a new Apple Wallet bill splitting feature could make Apple Cash far more popular.

Here’s how the new bill splitting option works, per Apple:

With iOS 27, users can split bills using Apple Cash and Apple Intelligence, making it easy to settle up after meals with friends. Users can simply scan a receipt with their iPhone camera, or use a photo of a bill to split it with friends. This capability is available in Messages, in Apple Wallet, or by using Visual Intelligence onscreen and with the iPhone camera. For example, the new Siri mode in the Camera app lets users get information and take action on what’s in front of them. When users point their iPhone at a receipt using Siri mode, it can surface the relevant action to split a bill with Apple Cash and identify the items on the receipt. As users select their items, their total payment is calculated, including their share of tax and tip, so they can pay back exactly what they owe with Apple Cash.

The whole process is extremely simple and seamless. Just point your iPhone camera at a receipt, or choose an existing receipt photo, and Apple Intelligence does the work of identifying each item so you can mark what’s yours. It’s easy to add a tip too, with no math required as iOS 27 calculates common amounts like 18% and 20% automatically.

In my testing, bill splitting has proven an excellent addition to iOS 27 that delivers a very user-friendly experience. I love that it works from the standard Camera app in Siri mode, via the Messages app, and of course in Wallet directly.

The only real downside is that if you or your friends haven’t set up Apple Cash yet, that will be an extra step that slows you down. 

But once Apple Cash is set up, bill splitting is a great addition that I hope gains a lot of popularity over time because the experience is so seamless.

title: Samsung Gallery rolling out Google Photos sync, here are the details you need to know
snippet: As teased, Samsung Gallery is now rolling out support for Google Photos sync, though there are a few details worth noting. more…
fullText:
As teased, Samsung Gallery is now rolling out support for Google Photos sync, though there are a few details worth noting.

Through app updates earlier this week, Samsung confirmed it was replacing the Microsoft OneDrive backup integration in its Gallery app with Google Photos sync. The change wasn’t live at the time, but works similarly to integrations found in the pre-installed Gallery apps on other phones from other Android brands such as OnePlus and Xiaomi.

Now, it’s actually starting to roll out.

Following updates to the Gallery Sync and Samsung Cloud apps, a Samsung Gallery update is also now rolling out to some users, which enables Google Photos integration – we’re not yet seeing the update on our end. Ice Universe shared screenshots of the settings.

	

Samsung Gallery v15.9.01.7 seems to be the trigger for activating sync, despite other apps actually facilitating the sync.

On a support page, Google offers more details on how Samsung Gallery > Google Photos sync works. It requires your Samsung device to be running Android 13 or newer, doesn’t support Workspace accounts, and there are some restrictions on what media you can see and what features work.

Google says that images and videos synced from Samsung Gallery won’t work with Memories and highlights, Live albums, or Search in Google Photos. Samsung Gallery also won’t show content backed up directly through Photos – only content synced from Samsung Gallery via a Samsung device shows up in the app.

Samsung has access to the media items that were originally backed up from Gallery Cloud Sync, but not to other items in Google Photos that were not backed up from a synced Samsung device.

If your device has all of the needed updates, you’ll find the option to enable Google Photos sync in Samsung Gallery via Menu > Settings > Sync > Sync photos and videos.

Samsung Gallery’s integration with OneDrive ends on September 30 for those still using it.

title: ScrollEd wants to turn textbooks into TikTok
snippet: ScrollEd turns textbooks into a scrollable, Instagram-like feed with video, audio, and quizzes. The Palo Alto startup, founded by student co-founders (and spouses) Utsav Gupta and Rebecca Neff, pitches at TechCrunch Disrupt.
fullText:
Society has spent a lot of time bemoaning our digitally addled minds and goldfish-like attention spans, pointing the finger of blame at doomscrolling as the reason we can’t just sit down and read a book or study for exams. But what if the solution isn’t to stop scrolling, but to rethink what we’re scrolling through?

That’s the bet startup ScrollEd is making. The Palo Alto-based startup is pitching in the TechCrunch Disrupt Startup Battlefield 200 competition with the novel idea that if students won’t open a textbook, the textbook should open itself up to them — as a scroll.

ScrollEd has built an app that allows the user to turn any text file — including dry PDFs or text books — into a feed that feels a lot like Instagram Reels or TikTok. As you scroll, the content shows up as AI-generated video, audio, text, or even interactive quizzes. Swiping up surfaces a new topic, while swiping sideways lets you go deeper into the one you’re on, with a quiz waiting for you at the end. 

“The younger generation is increasingly going short form, vertical feed only (especially the 18 year olds we’ve spoken to!), and this poses challenges for any kind of media that requires depth,” Utsav Gupta, ScrollEd’s co-founder, told TechCrunch in an email. “We want to meet them where they are…We just have to be deliberate about how we use it and choose not to maximize engagement on the platform.”

“A short video can make you curious; following that curiosity can mean searching for another explanation or leaving the app,” Gupta continued. “We wanted going deeper to be as easy as moving to the next video.” 

Gupta bootstrapped ScrollEd this year alongside his co-founder and wife Rebecca Neff after the two both noticed feeling dissatisfied after doomscrolling before bed. Both are students — Gupta studies AI and human purpose at Stanford, and Neff studies computer science at the University of Pennsylvania. 

The startup is targeting educational institutions, corporate training programs, and individuals who “just want something better to scroll on,” according to Gupta. 

ScrollEd is following a freemium model, combining a free consumer feed with a paid ScrollEd Pro subscription and annual institutional licenses. Institutions pay to deliver educational material through the platform, in exchange for reports about engagement, lesson progress, and other data. 

In the coming months, ScrollEd intends to focus on its consumer launch, building its lesson library and source-checking workflow, and developing pilots for institutions. (The company will launch its consumer business at Disrupt, in fact. “We’re hoping to ‘disrupt’ social media and short form!” Gupta joked.)

The startup is also building infrastructure that will one day allow educators to assess individual learners and adapt to their needs. 

“The ambition is a social network that’s better for you,” Gupta said.

Check out ScrollEd and the other smart startups that TC’s editorial team has vetted and you’ll want to check out at TechCrunch Disrupt, coming up October 13-15 in downtown San Francisco. You can find many more details, and tickets, right here.

title: Android Bench 2.0 focuses on long-horizon tasks, agent evaluations
snippet: Google’s development of Android Bench continues today with a version 2.0 that reflects how AI can handle more complex development tasks. more…
fullText:
Google’s development of Android Bench continues today with a version 2.0 that reflects how AI can handle more complex development tasks.

The first version “focused on incremental changes to existing repositories,” like bug fixes or smaller feature requests. Android Bench 2.0 targets “tasks of great complexity that take an engineer multiple days or even a week to complete,” such as adding new features, building apps from scratch, and converting cross-platform apps to Android.

This new focus required “more nuanced evaluation and scoring” that goes beyond pass or fail grading. Google is moving from binary to continuous scoring:

We calculate this completion rate through a combination of factors like functionality, visual fidelity, and avoiding regressions. We also apply objective scoring penalties for deviations from evaluation instructions or structural constraints.

Google has rated Gemini 3.7/3.8 Flash, OpenAI GPT-6, Anthropic Fable 5.1, Kimi K3, and Qwen 3.8 Max. GPT-6 Astra is at the top of the benchmark with a 28% pass rate (compared to scores in the 90% range with the previous approach).

	

Google shared insights like how “porting cross-platform apps to Android remains an open challenge—no model hits a 100% pass rate, and frontier models reach at most a 80% completion rate.”

“…AI does a better job at writing new code rather than refactoring existing code. Refactors and migrations get trickier because success depends on architectural complexity rather than code volume.”

“Models show strong capabilities on well-established, deterministic transformations, such as converting Java to Kotlin, swapping Retrofit for Ktor, or introducing a ViewModel layer.”

“…models struggle when tasks require runtime validation (like missing dependency injection graphs), involve breaking framework changes, or run into knowledge gaps with unreleased libraries.”

With agent evaluations, Android Bench ran “agents from the corresponding model provider,” like Gemini 3.8 Flash on Google Antigravity and GPT-5.6 Sol with Codex. Google says “harness design positively impacts developer outcomes,” with Android Bench planning to include different model and agent combinations in the future.

title: Review: Satechi’s Thunderbolt 5 CubeDock pairs perfectly with the new M6 Mac mini
snippet: Apple just released a new Mac mini late last month, equipped with the new M6 and M5 Pro chips. If you’re looking for a perfect Thunderbolt 5 dock to pair with your new Mac mini (or your current M4/M4 Pro model) – Satechi has a great offering for you. more…
fullText:
Apple just released a new Mac mini late last month, equipped with the new M6 and M5 Pro chips. If you’re looking for a perfect Thunderbolt 5 dock to pair with your new Mac mini (or your current M4/M4 Pro model) – Satechi has a great offering for you.

Satechi’s Thunderbolt 5 CubeDock is shaped just like a Mac mini, making it a perfect companion, whether you have it side by side or stacked. It brings 8 additional ports, an M.2 NVMe SSD bay, and supports up to 140W of host charging if you’re pairing it with a laptop instead.

With Thunderbolt 5, there’s up to 120Gbps of throughput, allowing you to run up to three 6K@60Hz or 4K@144Hz displays with M5 Pro through a single cable, or two with any other chipset.

Beyond its display capabilities, it offers two 10Gbps USB-C ports and two 10Gbps USB-A ports, a 2.5G Ethernet port, an SD card reader, and a microSD card reader – with each supporting UHS-II. There’s also an additional 3.5mm combo audio jack if you need a second one.

The best part for me is the fact that it has an M.2 NVMe SSD bay, and the bay is large enough to fit SSDs that have a built-in heatsink – which can’t be said for every product with an SSD bay. The SSD bay sits within the enclosure and doesn’t expand the footprint. You can fit an 8TB SSD in it, at up to 6000MB/s – and it supports 2230, 2242, 2260, and 2280 drive sizes.

9to5Mac’s Take

If you want the best dock that can take advantage of Thunderbolt 5 capabilities and look right at home with your Mac mini, the Satechi CubeDock is undeniably the best option. I will say, it’s a bit pricey at $399.99, so it’s likely hard to justify for most people unless you’re super obsessed with running everything through one dock with an integrated SSD hub.

One thing of note is that it does get quite warm when you’re using it. It’s not to a concerning level, though you absolutely will notice it if you touch it. Is this an issue for something that sits on your desk? Probably not.

You can purchase the Satechi Thunderbolt 5 CubeDock for $399.99 on Amazon. Right now, there’s a promo where you can bundle an additional braided Thunderbolt 5 cable ($39.99) and unlock 10% off of your order, effectively making the second cable free with the purchase.

If you’re just interested in the new Mac mini, I’d also say they’re worth a purchase. They’re still readily available with delivery in September, compared to the previous M4 models which were incredibly hard to find:

Lepton is a tool for use with the Steam client which allows games which are exclusive to Android to run on the Linux operating system. Most users should use Lepton provided by the Steam Client itself.

title: Tim Cook keeping John Ternus away from controversy by attending White House dinner
snippet: One of the trickier parts of Tim Cook’s job when he was Apple CEO was walking the tightrope of upholding the company’s values without provoking the ire of the White House over things like immigration policy and DEI. His new role as executive chairman sees him retain responsibility for government liaison, offering replacement CEO John Ternus some degree of protection … more…
fullText:
One of the trickier parts of Tim Cook’s job when he was Apple CEO was walking the tightrope of upholding the company’s values without provoking the ire of the White House over things like immigration policy and DEI.

His new role as executive chairman sees him retain responsibility for government liaison, offering replacement CEO John Ternus some degree of protection … 

Past challenges

The challenges Cook faced in the past date back many years. For example, back in 2018, changes to US immigration policy and practice affected thousands of Apple employees. Tim Cook was among a number of CEOs who wrote to the administration stating that the changes were causing “considerable anxiety for many thousands of Apple employees,” as well as “threatening to disrupt company operations.”

Cook faced similar difficulties last year when Trump said that Apple should get rid of its DEI policies. He responded by saying the company would comply with any changes to the law but would not compromise its values.

Cook is now Apple’s official diplomat

Earlier this year, Apple confirmed that Cook’s new role includes responsibility for liaising with governments.

As executive chairman, Cook will assist with certain aspects of the company, including engaging with policymakers around the world.

Attending White House dinner next week

Bloomberg reports that Cook will be attending a White House state dinner for China’s president next week. The event takes place at a difficult time for US-China relations, especially over AI.

Apple Inc. Executive Chairman Tim Cook and OpenAI Chief Executive Officer Sam Altman are poised to attend a White House state dinner for Chinese President Xi Jinping next week […] The summit comes at a delicate moment for US-Chinese relations — and the artificial intelligence industry. Geopolitical tensions are simmering over the AI race, international trade and the Middle East.

9to5Mac’s Take

I would wager a large sum of money that the idea of the diplomatic role being Cook’s responsibility came from the man himself. It’s a self-sacrificing move intended to free his successor from unnecessary distractions and controversies.

Ternus will of course still be constrained in what he can say when it comes to Apple’s response to controversial policies and laws, whether in the US, China or elsewhere, but having official responses be the responsibility of someone else does give him more latitude than would otherwise be the case.

title: Google Home just became a power user’s paradise
snippet: Good morning. Today I’m finding some peace playing Lumines Remastered, deciding whether to get my kids one of the new 4th-gen Yoto players, and trying to figure out why everyone is freaking out about this recent Tom Cruise interview. more…
fullText:
Good morning. Today I’m finding some peace playing Lumines Remastered, deciding whether to get my kids one of the new 4th-gen Yoto players, and trying to figure out why everyone is freaking out about this recent Tom Cruise interview.

As a reminder, Inbox is the tech newsletter that goes beyond the news cycle. We cover the most important 9to5Google stories from the last couple of days along with a few highlights from around the web. We publish every Tuesday and Thursday, and if you like what you read, please subscribe.

Inbox is written by Daniel Bader. Read previous issues here, and then catch up with Ben Schoon’s excellent Weekender column published every Sunday.

⭐️ Starred

Over the past few months, I’ve been using MCP (Model Context Protocol) to connect with my bank, my to-do app (TickTick), my personal database (Obsidian), and anything else I can get my hands on. I find it intuitive to have a conversation with a chatbot about stacking tasks, performing a complex set of calculations, or just figuring out the answer to a difficult problem. 

	

Now Google is getting in on the MCP action with Home MCP, a way to connect coding agents like Claude, Codex, Antigravity, Hermes, and OpenClaw to Google’s Home ecosystem and the products connected to it.

Right now, the tool is limited to Google Home Premium Advanced subscribers in the US, but it’s an ambitious first step toward making it easier to interact with what is usually a digital rat’s nest of brands, categories, and compatibility layers. Google has already rolled out Gemini for Home in an attempt to make automation more straightforward, but I commend the company for dipping its toe into the DIY space and seeing what happens.

According to Google, MCP “gives your favorite AI agent real-world physical context—allowing it to analyze and answer questions about home activity, summarize camera footage across rooms, manage devices on your behalf, or even create your own smart home dashboards using everyday language.” I’m totally going to use it to teach my Nest Cam Outdoor that the cat who wanders onto my driveway every morning isn’t, in fact, a person. Wish me luck.

✉️ Inbox

GM just found the ‘sweet spot’ for supporting Android Auto & CarPlay. See, all it took was people loudly complaining for three years.

SwiftKey ‘AI voice’ is Pixel 11’s Rambler voice-to-text for other Android phones, works offline. I have my doubts that this is any good — SwiftKey’s been awful for years — but I guess it’s good that this exists?

Google just shared these fun Pixel 11 blueprint wallpapers. These are really fun.

Samsung Gallery is adding Google Photos backup to replace OneDrive. Good, no one uses OneDrive anyway.

Gemini 3.8 Live Extended Thinking powers Gemini Live, Gmail, & Keep. Google is the undisputed leader of text-to-speech, and Gemini 3.8 Live just extends its lead.

The new Boox e-ink devices get Android 16 out of the box, including Palma 3. The Palma 3 looks like an actual gadget, no longer a plastic toy like the previous ones, and I must have it.

Google confirms Pixel phones were exploited in ‘targeted’ attack related to modem. This is pretty concerning, especially because it was “zero-click,” but glad it’s been fixed.

Philips Hue Bridge Pro is now $139, with even bigger price hikes globally. Woof.

🍎 Roll call

It’s iPhone review season, and because this seems like an “S” year, the camera is rightfully getting the most attention. That’s why I watched basically every second of all the new iPhone 18 Pro reviews from channels like PetaPixel, Tyler Stalman, The Verge, and Matti Haapoja.

I’m still not sure what to think about the aperture control. Most reviews are saying that it has very little real-world utility, while others are claiming that it was the only way to offer an f/1.48 lens without sacrificing depth control (or overly relying on software bokeh). Either way, once Apple decides to offer a hardware feature it tends to stick around whether or not it’s any good (see Camera Control), so we’ll likely see a few more generations of this tech.

Sticking with the iPhone theme, two of my favorite podcasters convened this week to discuss the iPhone Duo and how it fares next to the multitude of Android competitors. 

(And if you enjoy the conversation with Stephen Radochia and want to hear more from him, he and I host a little podcast called Old’s Cool that looks at new tech from a vintage point of view.)

➡️ FWD:

This section has some of our favorite stuff from around the internet. Great videos, weird memes, fun reads, recommended apps, whatever. Send us your recommendations!

Tired of getting recorded against your will by other meeting attendees? Kalypta from Deveillance reportedly makes you “inaudible to AI” by “reshaping audio in real time” on your local machine. What a crazy world we live in.

OpenAI’s “Project Lily” tasks real humans with reading ChatGPT transcripts in order to make inference better and more accurate. According to 404 Media, which broke the story, “OpenAI is hiring hundreds of contractors who read a massive stream of real users’ ChatGPT prompts, with the prompts sometimes including sensitive personal information.” 

Snap finally let people try its $2,200 Specs smart glasses, a bulky and unwieldy computer that it’s inviting developers to test. The gadget has a 4-hour battery and can run real apps like Spotify while relying on a proactive AI assistant to do everything else. 

🤑 Action Items

Over the past couple of days, I’ve been trying out a new launcher on my Fold 8, a launcher unlike anything I’ve used on Android before. That’s because it’s defined by its adherence to the UX found on iOS — specifically the upcoming iPhone Duo.

From the demented mind of Reddit’s u/wolftech029, Folio is a love letter (for better or worse) to the way Apple’s home screen drastically differs from the ones found on various Android phones. From predefined grids to Apple’s App Library to the Duo’s funky blur effect, Folio has it all. 

I’m not sure it’s going to stay on my phone for long, but its existence (and the speed at which it was vibe-coded) is a testament to Android’s versatility and openness.

title: iOS 27.2 references new option to overwrite iPhone storage with blank data after erasing
snippet: Apple is working on a new option to more thoroughly wipe an iPhone’s storage when erasing the device, but there’s a catch. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
Apple is working on a new option to more thoroughly wipe an iPhone’s storage when erasing the device, but there’s a catch. Here are the details.

New feature exclusive to Chinese devices

References included in today’s iOS 27.2 beta 1 point to a new iPhone erasing option that will let the user overwrite the device’s entire storage with blank data, including storage that isn’t actively in use.

In addition to erasing the iPhone’s data, the feature can overwrite the device’s entire storage with blank data, including storage that isn’t actively in use. Apple warns that the process may take longer than a standard erase and could affect the device’s lifespan.

The move is interesting, as currently, when a user erases an iPhone, the device’s encryption keys are destroyed, effectively rendering the remaining data inaccessible. In fact, Apple is very clear about this in an Apple Platform Deployment support article:

On the device, erasing (or wiping) obliterates all the keys in effaceable storage and renders all user data cryptographically inaccessible.

While digging through today’s beta, 9to5Mac confirmed that, as currently implemented, the feature will only be available on iPhone models sold in China, where Apple appears to be adding it to comply with an upcoming data-erasure requirement.

That’s because a new Chinese standard taking effect on January 1, 2027, will require smartphones and other electronic devices to offer a way to more thoroughly erase stored data, including through methods such as overwriting it.

For semiconductor storage, such as the flash storage used in smartphones, one approved method involves overwriting storage containing user data at least once with meaningless data. That closely matches Apple’s description of replacing storage with blank data.

Finally, the new erasing option won’t be exclusive to iPhones, as code references also point to support for other devices, including the iPad, HomePod, and Apple Vision Pro.

To learn more about China’s upcoming GB 46864-2025 standard, follow this link.

Embattled surveillance technology company Flock Safety unveiled a “generous” severance package for voluntary employee departures on Friday, according to a report in Wired.

Flock reportedly expects a significant portion of its 1,500-person workforce to express interest in the buyouts, and said it will grant them to a majority of those who are interested. The company’s internal announcement described these packages as the “most generous” it has ever offered.

By letting employees depart voluntarily, Flock can say goodbye to team members demoralized by the ongoing backlash over the company’s license plate recognition technology. Wired also reports that without buyouts, the company would “almost certainly” need to lay off some staff.

title: I Got the Inside Scoop on Apple’s New Health App, Now in Developer Beta
snippet: I spoke with Dr. Sumbul Desai, Apple’s VP of Health and Fitness, to learn more about the redesigned Health app and its new features.
fullText:
Last week at Apple’s “Surprise and Shine” event, Dr. Sumbul Desai, Apple’s VP of Health and Fitness, announced the redesigned Health app and its fresh features. Between the new Insights tab with Apple Intelligence-powered suggestions, a Longevity tab that shows your Health Age, a readiness score, movement assessments, a blood panel and curated doctor videos, my head was swimming with questions. The following day, I sat down for a video chat with Desai for deeper insight into Apple’s reimagined health platform.

On Wednesday, the new Health app debuted in the first developer beta of iOS 27.2. Some announced features will be available in later betas, including personalized summaries under the Insights tab, personalized recommendations and the ability to order a blood panel from Quest Diagnostics. 

“Features will roll out progressively,” Apple said in an email. “Feedback during the beta period will help us continue refining it ahead of the public release in late 2026.”

Here’s everything you can expect to uncover in the Health app and the features you shouldn’t sleep on.

From data spreadsheet to intelligent experience

Launched in 2014, the Health app was initially intended to be like a spreadsheet, with data flowing in, Desai explained. However, the team realized they wanted more from the app, so it evolved over the past 12 years into what Desai now calls “an experience.”

Those at the helm of the Health app’s 2026 makeover considered how to leverage Apple’s machine learning and AI to help people live healthier, while also personalizing the app’s recommendations and turning it into an intelligent hub, not unlike the iPhone itself. For instance, as you open the app and move through your day, different screens appear to reflect your health status. 

Movement assessments have also been added to provide an even more complete picture of a user’s health and track progress or decline. Desai described them as a “mini physical” you can complete at home.

All assessments under the app’s Longevity tab are science-based and contribute to a rainbow-petal visual that illuminates your state of health. Some assessments rely on vision-based AI models that integrate the phone’s camera, marking the first time Apple has used the camera for health.  

The current iteration of the Health app is just the beginning and was designed to set in motion the next era of the team’s work in health and fitness, as Desai said those working on the app still feel they have more to do.

The Longevity tab’s rainbow visual.Apple

Health Age: Biological vs. birthday

One standout feature from Apple’s event was the Health app’s Longevity tab, which will include a feature called Health Age that uses health metrics such as your VO2 max (the maximum amount of oxygen your body consumes during exercise), resting heart rate, sleep and heart rate variability, along with lab data such as LDL cholesterol and A1c for your average blood sugar level, to provide your biological age, which represents how your body is aging on a cellular level when compared to your actual age. 

Apple’s own Heart and Movement Study, which it applies across all its health products, informs both Health Age and Readiness, which uses your activity data, daytime and overnight vitals and sleep data to tell you about your capacity for the day ahead. 

The five-year Heart and Movement Study was conducted in collaboration with the American Heart Association and Brigham and Women’s Hospital to explore the connection between heart health and physical activity. Apple used that data to create the normative ranges for the insights it provides in the app.

While Desai acknowledged the Health Age assessment is more of a “fun way to look at your health habits” and that no one can tell you your actual biological age, it’s another way to provide insight and suggest healthy habits users can integrate into their lives. 

I’m also hoping my Health Age is lower than my actual age. Apple

Apple’s secret sauce

Apple isn’t the first company to offer features such as a readiness score or biological age, but Desai said that it stands out from competitors because of its unique perspectives, experiences and the science behind its work. 

“When we first started our work in health, when we announced our irregular heart rhythm notifications and ECG, those were clinically validated scientific features,” she said. Desai likened those early days to building a muscle that lets the team create impactful products the medical community will appreciate, and users can easily understand.

That muscle Apple first built has been exercised with all the Health app’s new features, as Desai said that everything is rooted in science. On her team, for instance, physical therapists graded each movement in the app’s mobility assessments to ensure that when a movement is picked up and a result is given, it’s graded the way an actual physical therapist would grade it. 

Uniting science and expertise, Desai said that’s what Apple brings to the table, and its Health app experience. 

The new Health app’s ‘sleeper hit’

Much of the discourse following Apple’s event has been about the new readiness score and Health Age. I was curious what Desai felt was the “sleeper hit” feature that didn’t get as much attention. 

“It’s actually the assessments,” Desai said. “You’re going to be able to, on a regular basis, do a push-up test and a core test and see if you’re improving. Then we give you insights and things that you can do to improve, and then you can test again. It’s almost like having a physical therapist or a trainer.”

The VO2 max test, in particular, marks the first time Apple’s doing an on-demand, in-the-moment VO2 max test. 

You can then take all your assessment results, and the Health app will put them into a report you can share with your doctor. 

A person performing a movement assessment using their iPhone.Apple/Screenshot by CNET

Homing in on your body’s big players

Based on its new assessments, the Longevity tab’s visualization has seven tabs: heart health, sleep, mental wellbeing, movement health, metabolic health, hearing and nutrition. But how did Apple narrow it down to those seven?

“We picked areas where we felt like we had the appropriate data to comment on,” Desai explained. “For example, we do a cardiovascular risk score through some of the questions. It’s based on traditional risk scores and cardiovascular risk scores that are done.”

The team prioritized information they believe people will use and assessments they’ll complete, while ensuring the chosen health areas feel holistic and will help people concerned about long-term quality of life.

“There’s still more that we think we can do, but this is where we’re starting,” Desai stated. In other words, Longevity’s rainbow visual could gain more colors in the future. 

Keeping privacy at Apple’s core

When it comes to its Health app, Desai said privacy is where they start and end. 

“Candidly, we may not always be the first to market, but when we release something, we can stand behind it from a privacy standpoint,” Desai stated. “All the features you saw [announced] are no different. … It’s part of the conversation every day, and up till the day that the products are launched.”

Apple will hold off on releasing a product if it hasn’t met its privacy bar. The team behind the Health app also uses a checks-and-balances system, having other teams review their work to ensure they are nailing their privacy approach. 

“In this world where more things happen in the cloud, we want to make sure that’s all encrypted and private, which is why we have Private Cloud Compute,” said Desai. Private Cloud Compute is Apple’s cloud intelligence system designed for private AI processing.

The team’s approach is end-to-end because privacy matters for all your data, not just health data. 

Apple Intelligence has suggestions

The Health app’s new Insights tab uses Apple Intelligence to analyze your health metrics and provide a timely summary that updates throughout the day. 

“We also make suggestions,” said Desai. “For example, if you have an injury or you’re trying to work on your mobility, we’ll give you suggestions on the types of exercises you might be doing.”

It’s another example of how the app is evolving from a database to something that more closely resembles a personalized health advisor.

The daily insights are meant to be bite-size pieces of information that are one small thing you can do for your health each day. Some days these insights may be interesting; other days, you might be given information you already know.

Under Insights, the For You section will use your data to offer personalized recommendations and relevant articles.Apple

Health on a cellular level, explained

For $119, the new Health app will let you purchase a blood panel with over 50 biomarkers through Quest Diagnostics. You can also get your blood pressure, height, weight and waist and hip circumferences measured. All this helps provide a more complete picture of metabolic health.

The revamped app will include videos from doctors that help people better understand what they see in the app. 

“When you get your assessment results, you’ll actually see your own data in the videos where they’re explained by clinicians,” said Desai. “We have a physician, a physical therapist, a sleep expert, a mental health expert. The reason we did that is, for certain things, gamification works, but for certain things, you just want to know the information in an easy-to-understand way from an authoritative resource.”

While an expert explains the subject at hand, your health data, whether from your labs or your Apple Watch, will be overlaid on the video so you can see it as you learn more. 

Ultimately, Desai doesn’t see the future of the Health app as one size fits all. Depending on the feature, the team always chooses what makes health as accessible and understandable as possible. In a world with an abundance of health data, perhaps that’s what matters most: ensuring people understand the numbers they see on their devices, and knowing what to do with them once the screen goes black.

title: Apple Fitness+ team hit by layoffs, as ‘major changes’ reportedly loom
snippet: Apple is assessing the future of Apple Fitness+, according to a new Bloomberg report. The company has reportedly laid off a “handful of employees” working on the service, a move viewed as just the beginning of bigger changes still to come. more…
fullText:
Apple is assessing the future of Apple Fitness+, according to a new Bloomberg report. The company has reportedly laid off a “handful of employees” working on the service, a move viewed as just the beginning of bigger changes still to come.

In the latest edition of his Power On newsletter, Mark Gurman says the layoffs affect people working on the audio features for Fitness+. That includes features like the guided Time to Walk and Time to Run audio sessions. Gurman notes, however, that new releases aren’t going away “completely,” but rather they will “drop in frequency.”

Apple Fitness+, however, is not “on the chopping block,” at least as of right now:

I don’t believe, as of this second, that the service is on the chopping block, but given the considerable costs, ever-present demand for new content and subscriber churn rates, it’s an easy place for Apple to look to make cuts. And that is starting now.

These layoffs are likely just the first shoe to drop for the future of Fitness+, though:

Still, this is widely seen within the Fitness+ organization as the beginning of more drastic cost-cutting measures and other major changes to the service in the months and years ahead.

Last November, Gurman reported that the future of Apple Fitness+ was “under review.” Leadership of the service shifted to services boss Eddy Cue and health boss Sumbul Desai. Cue has reportedly pressed Apple to “move faster and be more competitive” in health and fitness.

Gurman speculates that Apple will eventually integrate Fitness+ into the revamped Health app. I think he’s spot on with this. What about you? Let us know down in the comments.

title: Report: Apple leads slowing true wireless stereo market as open-ear earbuds gain ground
snippet: Apple reportedly maintained its lead in the global true wireless stereo (TWS) market and saw modest year-over-year growth, even as overall shipments declined. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
Apple reportedly maintained its lead in the global true wireless stereo (TWS) market and saw modest year-over-year growth, even as overall shipments declined. Here are the details.

Open wireless stereo shipments counter true wireless stereo slowdown

According to a new report from Omdia (via MacMagazine), Apple shipped 16.8 million TWS devices during the second quarter of 2026, a 1.2% increase from the same period in 2025.

Despite the modest growth, Apple still outperformed the broader market, which declined 0.7% year over year.

Apple’s shipments amounted to 20.5% of the total TWS market for the period, nearly doubling Xiaomi’s 10.4% share in second place. Samsung came in third at 6.7%, followed by Huawei at 6.2%, and OPPO at 5.0%.

Other than Apple, OPPO was the only top-five vendor to see shipment growth. The figure, which includes devices from OnePlus, rose 14.9% year over year.

Interestingly, Omdia also reported worldwide shipments of open wireless stereo (OWS) devices, a subset of TWS devices.

Essentially, Omdia separates conventional TWS products, including in-ear and semi-in-ear earbuds, from OWS devices such as clip-on and ear-hook models that leave the ear canal open.

Omdia says the OWS market saw shipments grow 12% for the period, with Shokz taking the lead at 1.1 million units shipped, representing a 10.3% market share and 107.9% year-over-year growth.

During its “Surprise and Shine” event earlier this month, Apple’s VP of Hardware Engineering, Dave Pakula, referred to the new AirPods 5 as the company’s “beloved open-ear fit,” adding moments later that “AirPods 5 deliver the industry’s best ANC in an open-ear design.” Still, it appears Omdia did not consider the non-Pro AirPods part of the OWS market.

Back to Omdia’s worldwide OWS shipments ranking, Sanag followed Shokz with a 7.6% share and 2.4% year-over-year growth, while Huawei came in third with a 7.0% share despite shipments declining 4.1%. Baseus ranked fourth with 6.6% share and 29.9% growth, followed by Edifier at 5.4% share and 0.2% growth.

Commenting on the results, Omdia said:

Omdia expects OWS to remain one of the most promising growth areas within TWS over the coming years. Annual OWS shipments are forecast to increase from 43.9 million units in 2026 to 90.5 million units by 2030, representing nearly one in five TWS shipments.

title: Google Home app brings battery-efficient widget, reduces gray device tiles
snippet: Besides Home MCP, Google today is also rolling out Home app (especially for the homescreen widget) and Gemini for Home voice assistant updates. more…
fullText:
Besides Home MCP, Google today is also rolling out Home app (especially for the homescreen widget) and Gemini for Home voice assistant updates.

The Google Home widget has now been optimized to “pause background updates and polling whenever your phone’s screen is powered off, locked, or running a screensaver.” This helps save battery on your phone and connected cameras, while “ensuring your widgets refresh immediately the moment you unlock your phone.”

Meanwhile, Google has resolved an issue with device tiles for sensors, cameras, and smoke and carbon monoxide detectors. They could previously “appear grayed out after returning from device controller screens.” As such, you no longer have to reload the screen.

Other quality improvements include:

	

Smoother multi-account switching: If you have multiple accounts that you use with Google Home, switching between them is now more reliable with fewer “Home not found” errors and preference resets.

More reliable smart device setup: Addressed several setup and onboarding issues, including eliminating stalls during Wi-Fi pairing. This ensures a smoother, frustration-free onboarding journey when adding new smart devices to your home.

Smoother Google TV startup: Resolved a startup crash on Google TV devices, ensuring the Google Home experience launches reliably on your television.

More flexible in-app banners: Improved UI for triggering actions in announcement banners in the Google Home app.

Smoke alarm notifications: Rolling out improvements to smoke and carbon monoxide alarm notifications to show current device status in the Google Home app after an alarm has already been cleared.

On the camera front, there are three fixes:

Improved camera live stream tile reliability (Android): Resolved an issue where returning from the full-screen camera view back to the Favorites tab caused live stream tiles to temporarily turn black until manually scrolled. Live feeds now continue streaming seamlessly upon navigating back.

Smoother camera history scrolling across recording gaps (Android): Video timeline scrolling now smoothly scrolls past unrecorded or offline gaps without freezing.

Faster switching to live camera stream (iOS): Fixed an issue where tapping the “Live” button while watching recorded events failed to redirect smoothly into the live view, leaving playback paused.

Finally for September 16, 2026, Google has five Gemini for Home voice assistant updates:

Improved follow up question behavior: Minimized cases where Gemini asks unnecessary follow-up questions or ends conversations awkwardly.

Fixed TV streaming playback: Fixed an intermittent issue that prevented Gemini from launching TV streaming providers on smart displays.

Reduced Live Mode interruptions: Addressed an issue where some devices interrupted themselves during Live Mode.

Reduced Broadcast errors: Resolved an issue where there were error messages when attempting to broadcast. You can now more reliably broadcast across your whole Home.

Improved Playlist reliability: Fixed some issues where Gemini wasn’t able to identify and play personal playlists.

title: Apple Watch Series 12 might finally convince me to switch away from WHOOP
snippet: Earlier this year, I picked up a WHOOP for the very first time. As a longtime Apple Watch user I was looking forward to having a new way of tracking my health stats in a cleaner interface that the Apple Watch wasn’t offering. Now, with Apple Watch Series 12, I’m very convinced to switch back to the Apple Watch. Here’s why. more…
fullText:
Earlier this year, I picked up a WHOOP for the very first time. As a longtime Apple Watch user I was looking forward to having a new way of tracking my health stats in a cleaner interface that the Apple Watch wasn’t offering. Now, with Apple Watch Series 12, I’m very convinced to switch back to the Apple Watch. Here’s why.

First things first, it’s worth noting that the Apple Watch Series 12 isn’t the only factor. There’s also the new Apple Health app in iOS 27.

The new Apple Health app has a much better interface. It offers your stats in a much cleaner manner. It’s very easy to understand all the data, which for me was the main thing breaking the Apple Watch.

Apple Health isn’t the only reason why I didn’t use the Apple Watch, though. It was also the fact that the Apple Watch didn’t collect data as frequently as the WHOOP did. The Apple Watch Series 12 now collects your heart rate once every 5 seconds, compared to every 5 minutes on previous models. This is still less than the WHOOP’s every 1 second, but so long as you’re not an athlete, I think every 5 seconds is fine.

Series 12 also introduced the new Readiness app on the Apple Watch, which gives you a 1-to-10 health score based on your HRV and other factors. This is akin to the recovery score the WHOOP calculated, which is one of the things that I like tracking, because even though Apple Watch always offered a sleep score, it wasn’t always the most useful piece of data. If you slept for a long time, you’d generally get a high score, regardless of whether other sleep factors weren’t quite great.

Wrap up

Only time will tell whether or not Apple Watch Series 12 is actually a game changer for health. As someone who’s used the WHOOP for the past half a year or so, I’m definitely looking forward to potentially going all in on the Apple Watch again.

Even though I’ve been a WHOOP user, I never ditched my Apple Watch, purely because having a screen offers a lot of utility. I don’t want to always pull my phone out.

title: iPhone 18 Pro Max’s battery is so big Apple had to add this new feature to iOS 27
snippet: The iPhone 18 Pro Max offers a huge jump in battery life, partly because the battery itself is physically larger. In a new support document published today, Apple says the iPhone 18 Pro Max has such a big battery that it has additional shipping requirements. more…
fullText:
The iPhone 18 Pro Max offers a huge jump in battery life, partly because the battery itself is physically larger.

In a new support document published today, Apple says the iPhone 18 Pro Max has such a big battery that it has additional shipping requirements.

iPhone 18 Pro Max: New battery feature

Apple says the iPhone 18 Pro Max has a battery capacity over 20 watt-hours (Wh). As it turns out, most countries and regions have additional shipping requirements for products “with a single-cell battery over 20 Wh.”

To accommodate these requirements, Apple says the iPhone 18 Pro Max uses an “innovative battery-firmware solution.” That firmware will limit the battery capacity of the device to below 20 Wh until it’s activated by the user:

To address these requirements, iPhone 18 Pro Max uses an innovative battery-firmware solution that limits battery capacity to below 20 Wh from the time it’s manufactured through its transport from the factory. When you activate your iPhone, the limit is removed and the battery’s full charging capacity is available.

The shipping requirements, however, also apply to other scenarios like shipping the iPhone 18 Pro Max for repair, trading it in, returning it, selling it, or gifting it to someone else.

For this, Apple has added a new “Prepare to Ship” feature in the Settings app. This will discharge your device’s battery below 20 Wh and set a charge limit to keep it below that threshold.

Your iPhone 18 Pro Max might need to discharge for Prepare to Ship to complete. While your iPhone battery discharges, it might become warmer than usual. This is expected. Your iPhone will cool down again when it’s ready to ship.

You can use your device as usual while your iPhone 18 Pro Max discharges. This might take only a few minutes, but if you start with a full charge, it can take up to a couple of hours. When the Prepare to Ship process is complete, the Settings app will display “Ready to Ship” with a red badge. If you erase your iPhone, you won’t be able to use it while the battery discharges.

The new option is in the Settings app. Open Settings, tap General, tap Transfer or Reset iPhone, then tap Prepare to Ship.

You can learn more in the full Apple support document.

title: Apple Weather adds two convenient new features in iOS 27
snippet: Apple Weather adds two convenient features in iOS 27 that make it easier to track rain and wind forecasts. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
Apple Weather adds two convenient features in iOS 27 that make it easier to track rain and wind forecasts. Here are the details.

iOS 27‘s Weather app adds rain and wind forecast views to home page

iOS 27 is packed with new features for Apple Wallet, Calendar, Notes, Messages, and more.

While Apple Weather is lighter on changes, there are two convenient additions worth noting:

Rain forecast view

Wind forecast view

Essentially, Apple has taken a bunch of data that was previously buried behind different menus and hidden screens and made it conveniently front and center.

We’re all familiar with the default forecast view in the Weather app. It’s one of the first things you see every time you open the app.

In iOS 27, Apple has split the forecast view into three options: Conditions, Precipitation, and Wind.

Conditions is the same view that was there before. But now, you can tap the new rain and wind icons to switch to Precipitation and Wind views.

When you hit each icon, both the hourly and 10-day forecasts instantly change.

The Precipitation view offers the chance of rain for each hour coming up, plus chances of rain with helpful measurements and time-of-day estimates for the next 10 days. Similarly, the Wind view shows the speed of gusts per hour, and ranges of what to expect in the days ahead.

I’ve been loving these changes during my time using iOS 27. They make key information more accessible than before while letting you stay in the familiar environment of the home screen.
