snippet: This month’s stable release of Android 17 QPR1 comes with some unexpected status bar icon changes on Pixel. more…
fullText:
This month’s stable release of Android 17 QPR1 comes with some unexpected status bar icon changes on Pixel.

The silent or mute icon goes from a crossed-out speaker to a bell.

This might be an accidental regression as Google switched from the bell to the speaker in Android 14. Notably, this change was not present during the Android 17 QPR1 Beta cycle and only went live with the stable OTA this week. 

The speaker icon is still live in 17 QPR2 Beta 5. (Meanwhile, the switcher at the top of the volume slider still uses the bell.)

	

Another icon change further complicates whether this tweak was intentional. The VPN icon is now much thicker and filled in, with this update also only appearing with the stable release.

We’ll know this was a mistake if Google changes it back in future releases, though any fix may not arrive until the sizable QPR2 update in December. Android 17 QPR1 is not yet available for the Pixel 11 series.

title: Judge rejects OpenAI’s bid to see X’s confidential settlement with Apple in antitrust lawsuit
snippet: Judge Mark Pittman today rejected OpenAI’s request to obtain X and SpaceXAI’s confidential settlement agreement with Apple in their ongoing antitrust case. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
Judge Mark Pittman today rejected OpenAI’s request to obtain X and SpaceXAI’s confidential settlement agreement with Apple in their ongoing antitrust case. Here are the details.

Judge says terms aren’t relevant to the remaining case against OpenAI

A few days ago, X and SpaceXAI informed the federal court overseeing their antitrust lawsuit against Apple and OpenAI that, after reaching an agreement with Apple, they would move to dismiss their claims against the iPhone maker.

In the lawsuit, Elon Musk’s companies accused Apple and OpenAI of colluding to shut competing AI apps out of the market, including by preventing them from gaining visibility on the App Store, allegations both companies denied.

After X and SpaceXAI informed the court of the agreement, OpenAI filed an emergency motion asking the judge to compel them to produce its terms, arguing that they could contain information relevant to its defense as the lawsuit continues solely against OpenAI.

Judge Pittman then ordered X and SpaceXAI to submit the agreement privately to the court so he could assess whether it contained information relevant to the remaining case against OpenAI.

Today, he issued his decision, saying that after reviewing the agreement, he found that it does “not present information relevant to the issues” at hand.

From the decision:

The Court hesitates to compel the production of confidential settlement agreements entered by parties. […] Courts have, at times, permitted the production of confidential settlement agreements to the extent they contain information relevant to specific issues at summary judgment or trial. Having conducted an in camera review of the requested materials, however, the Court finds that they do not present information relevant to the issues to be decided at summary judgment or trial in this case.

In his decision, Judge Pittman also notes that OpenAI plans to file a motion for summary judgment (meaning it will ask the court to rule on the case or some of its claims without a trial), and that the court has granted the company additional time to prepare it.

title: MediaTek Dimensity 9600 Pro goes official with 2nm process and performance gains
snippet: MediaTek has unveiled its latest flagship chipset in the Dimensity 9600 Pro, a chip built on TSMC’s latest 2nm process. more…
fullText:
MediaTek has unveiled its latest flagship chipset in the Dimensity 9600 Pro, a chip built on TSMC’s latest 2nm process.

The Dimensity 9600 Pro has a 2+3+3 All Big Core CPU design using Arm’s new C2-Ultra cores at 4.55GHz, three C2-Pro cores at 4.35GHz, and three more C2-Pro cores at 3.1GHz. Altogether, MediaTek says that its latest design delivers 17% better single-core performance and 15% higher multi-core performance compared to last year’s chip. 

Leading where others follow, the MediaTek Dimensity 9600 is a first-wave 2nm smartphone chip design that’s built to simultaneously raise the bar on performance, capability, and power-efficiency…

At its heart is MediaTek’s 4th-generation All Big Core CPU: a revolutionary 2+3+3 design pairing two Arm C2-Ultra processors, three Arm C2-Pro processors with 1MB L2 cache and three Arm C2-Pro with 512KB L2 cache, which altogether contribute to a 21% larger L2 cache system.

…MediaTek leads the industry with first-wave support for both UFS 5.0, which delivers 2x faster read/writes than the previous generation, and LPDDR6, which boosts effective memory bandwidth by 33% at the same frequency.

This latest chip adopts LPDDR6 memory and UFS 5.0 storage. The G2-Ultra NX GPU brings a 27% boost to peak performance while hitting 24% lower power consumption. Ray-tracing is 18% faster and games support up to 185fps. 

On the AI side, Dimensity 9600 Pro’s second-gen Super Efficient NPU reduces power consumption by 40% while delivering better performance and higher token generation per watt. 

	

Rounding things out, the Imagiq 1290 ISP supports 4K240 native direct-output ultra-slow-motion video, 4K120 cinematic log, and AI-powered True Color Tone and 60fps motion capture features. 

One of the first devices powered by the Dimensity 9600 Pro will be Oppo’s Find X10 Pro Max, due to be announced next week. Meanwhile, MediaTek is also announcing the Dimensity 9600M as a lower-cost version of this chip with “flagship-level performance.” It lacks UFS 5.0 and uses Arm’s C1 cores instead of C2.

title: Android Auto update might fix cellular signal icon – is it back for you?
snippet: For months now, there have been reports of Android Auto’s status bar having a broken icon for cellular signal, but the latest updates seem to finally put an end to the debacle. more…
fullText:
For months now, there have been reports of Android Auto’s status bar having a broken icon for cellular signal, but the latest updates seem to finally put an end to the debacle.

The bottom/side bar on Android Auto shows your apps, the time, and your phone’s current battery and cellular signal status through icons. But, for around 4-5 months now, there have been reports of users seeing the cellular signal icon go missing at random, only to come back just as randomly for some. 

When it’s missing, it leaves a funny-looking gap in Android Auto.

Image via Reddit

With Android Auto 17.8, it seems Google may have finally addressed this problem more widely.

	

A number of users on Reddit all report that the latest update has suddenly fixed the cellular signal icon on Android Auto. That said, reports are limited to just a handful of users, one of which cleared their app cache following the update’s installation.

So, we’ll open this one to you. Has your cellular signal icon returned on Android Auto? Sound off in the comments and let us know.

title: Google rolling out Android 17 QPR1 for Pixel
snippet: Following an extended beta period, Android 17 QPR1 is rolling out to Google Pixel devices with the September 2026 Feature Drop and security patch. more…
fullText:
Following an extended beta period, Android 17 QPR1 is rolling out to Google Pixel devices with the September 2026 Feature Drop and security patch.

There are a number of interface changes in Android 17 QPR1, starting with more blur effects across the system UI. The volume panel is where you’ll most likely notice the Dynamic Color-themed translucency, with the full bottom sheet also updated. The Power menu has also been refreshed and is joined by a background blur. This matches the updates that the widgets picker received in the initial Android 17 June release.

The system media player has a new Material 3 carousel-based interface when there are multiple apps. Instead of dots at the bottom, you now see a preview of other open applications, with your current card shrinking to make room.

When opening Quick Settings, you’ll notice a new bouncy animation, while there’s a new icon in the bottom-right corner for making edits.

	

The Mobile Data Tile has been updated with a “Don’t ask me again” toggle. There’s also a new QS Tile for “Keyboard” that lets you access the system switcher. The Screen recording tool now defaults to the last-used application.

When long-pressing on homescreen apps, the menu has been split into app Shortcuts and system Actions (like Bubble and Widgets).

Meanwhile, holding down on an empty homescreen spot reveals an updated fast wallpaper switcher that has more pronounced corner rounding, while the gaps between menu items have been removed. Other changes include:

There’s a new M3 Expressive Settings app icon that was first introduced on the Pixel Watch.

New animation when launching the camera from lockscreen with power button double-tap.

Health Connect on phones can now track distance and calories burned in addition to step count.

Android 17 QPR1 is rolling out starting today for the Pixel 6, Pixel 6 Pro, Pixel 6a, Pixel 7, Pixel 7 Pro, Pixel 7a, Pixel Tablet, Pixel Fold, Pixel 8, Pixel 8 Pro, Pixel 8a, Pixel 9, Pixel 9 Pro, Pixel 9 Pro XL, Pixel 9 Pro Fold, Pixel 9a, Pixel 10, Pixel 10 Pro, Pixel 10 Pro XL, Pixel 10 Pro Fold, Pixel 10a, Pixel 11, Pixel 11 Pro, Pixel 11 Pro XL, and Pixel 11 Pro Fold.

Visit Settings > System > System update and click the “Check for update” button if the OTA hasn’t already appeared on your device. Android 17 QPR1 Beta 9 users will get a small update to this final release.

The Android Beta Program will remain open and continue testing QPRs and feature drops. 

To get the stable version, those running the Android 17 QPR1 Beta have to opt out first. Devices will not be wiped by the stable OTA once that becomes widely available.

title: Amazon fixes bug that caused problems with Fire TV app sideloading [U]
snippet: Fire TV hardware will be able to freely sideload apps again without issue after an upcoming Android software update for Amazon’s streaming hardware. more…
fullText:
Fire TV hardware will be able to freely sideload apps again without issue after an upcoming Android software update for Amazon’s streaming hardware.

Late last year, Amazon rolled out a series of software patches to its Fire TV hardware. On the surface, the Android update for the streaming devices contained the usual security patches and performance updates. It was later discovered that the update also seemed to disable sideloading on certain Fire TV devices, preventing third-party apps from being installed if they didn’t come from certified app stores.

Amazon recently commented on that aspect of its previous Android updates in a response to AFTV News. Amazon says sideload prevention was due to a bug in the update and wasn’t an intentional part of the patch.

If users attempted to install a third-party app, the Fire TV device would list an error and block the process in some instances. It didn’t appear to affect all Fire TV devices, though the issue was widespread enough to be considered intentional. According to Amazon, it wasn’t.

	

There was a bug in a recent Fire TV Settings update that caused the “Install unknown apps” list to appear incomplete or empty on some Fire TV devices. We have identified the cause and a fix will roll out in an upcoming Fire TV Settings update, installed automatically on affected devices over the coming week.

This comes as the company recently announced its latest Fire TV Stick, which runs on Vega OS – not Android. It also confirmed that all future Fire TV Stick devices would run Linux-based software in lieu of Google’s OS to achieve a better performance-to-power ratio.

In essence, existing Fire TV devices will seemingly be able to sideload apps again, but that likely won’t be the case for streaming hardware Amazon launches in the future. Amazon says the patch will roll out to affected devices “over the coming week.”

title: YouTube’s login-breaking bug is getting a fix on TVs and consoles
snippet: Users met with an error at login, preventing them from accessing their YouTube account on TVs, and some consoles will be happy to know Google is rolling out a fix. more…
fullText:
Users met with an error at login, preventing them from accessing their YouTube account on TVs, and some consoles will be happy to know Google is rolling out a fix.

An issue began popping up for some users in the last couple of days, preventing a successful login on the TV or console app. Even with the proper password, some users were reporting they were unable to log back in after being kicked out. The issue seemed to persist on Xbox, PlayStation consoles, smart TVs, and streaming hardware – what YouTube classifies as “licing room devices.”

According to YouTube, the login bug that logged users out and blocked them from re-entry has been fixed. YouTube says the issue has been investigated and is now “fully fixed” in a community post separate from existing threads.

It’s unclear when this issue truly began, but there have been several new threads posted on Reddit within the last 24 hours, suggesting the bug affected a wide number of users worldwide.

	

The community post didn’t suggest an app update was needed. It was likely a server-side bug blocking Google Accounts from access, and in some cases, guest accounts.

Inbox is written by Daniel Bader. Read previous issues here, and then catch up with Ben Schoon’s excellent Weekender column published every Sunday.

⭐️ Starred

We’ve known for years that Apple was building a foldable phone, which means that Samsung, the company that popularized the format, also knew. So in July, when the company unveiled the Galaxy Z Fold 8, a wide foldable with proportions similar to the rumored iPhone Duo, it was seen largely as a preemptive move to claim, once again, that Samsung was ahead of the curve.

	

And thankfully the phone was a success; it sold better than expected, and Samsung has been left scrambling for components from next year’s model to satisfy demand today.

But Samsung, as it is wont to do, couldn’t let the phone’s success just speak. It had to inject itself into the conversation around the iPhone Duo in a series of posts that can only be described as cringe. To me, it’s another case of this “I don’t think about you at all” meme.

Of course, this is just silly stuff, but it speaks to the perception that even when Samsung leads, it follows. The good news is that, as Samsung points out in this funny but awkward ad called “Switchers,” it’s now much easier to move from iPhone to Android since Apple and Google collaborated on a new framework.

Samsung appears to be taking the Duo’s release in stride, doubling down on its commitment to foldables by reportedly moving up the release of its second-generation TriFold.

Apple on wide Android foldables beating iPhone Duo; ‘They got the aspect ratio’

✉️ Inbox

Android rolling out passkey transfers between password managers. It’s no longer difficult to transfer credentials between password managers, but passkeys have always been another matter. This system-level change is more than welcome.

Samsung’s first Android XR glasses with a color display may launch in late 2027. We’re only a month or so away from Samsung’s first smart glasses released in collaboration with Google, Warby Parker, and Gentle Monster, so it’s no surprise that by the end of next year there will be an option with a display.

Google brings Gemini for desktop app to Windows. It feels like it’s been forever since Google announced a Windows version of its popular Gemini app, but it’s now available and appears fully featured.

Google details ADB Wi-Fi 2.0 for more reliable wireless Android debugging

YouTube details NFL Sunday Ticket pricing & availability for 2026 season, including a 50% discount. The absolute disaster that is watching NFL games in one place with one subscription doesn’t appear to be any better for the 26/27 season. 

NFL Sunday Ticket is $204/year for YouTube Premium subscribers, nearly 60% off

Google’s hyper-personalized ‘Dreambeans’ feed is now free to test. I still have no idea what this is; I just know that it has the worst possible name for an app.

The Galaxy Z Fold 8 needs battery banks that actually fit; iPhone Duo might help. One benefit of Apple launching a similarly sized foldable is that accessory makers may unintentionally make things better on the Android side.

Possible Google device at FCC could be Wear OS-powered fitness tracker. It would not surprise me if Google is working on more fitness trackers after the runaway success of the Fitbit Air. Hope this one lacks a screen, too.

Oppo confirms Find X10 series details ahead of September 22 launch. The next Find X flagships are coming soon, and they’re just as ambitious as previous generations.

Googlebook pre-orders start on September 21. I’m waiting with bated breath to see why anyone should care about these laptops, particularly in light of a new slate of very good, relatively inexpensive Windows-powered MacBook Neo competitors.

Samsung reportedly launching Galaxy Tab S12, maybe more devices on October 7

Samsung launches ‘Re-Newed’ Galaxy S26 series, $1,099 for Ultra

Today in Google app updates:

Google Wallet passes get fullscreen redesign on Android

Google Wallet for Android getting vertically stacked card list

Google rolls out Motion Assist bubbles to Pixel, Samsung

Google Maps rolling out Android Auto speed limits and speedometer that show even without navigation

Elsewhere:

Apple’s A20 Pro shatters Geekbench 7 single-core record — 2nm chip beats desktop Intel Core i9 and AMD Ryzen 9 by up to 32% | Tom’s Hardware

Inside ‘Project Lily’: The Humans Reading Your ChatGPT Chats | 404 Media

Upcoming Apple Products: What to Expect in Late 2026 and Early 2027 | Bloomberg

🤝 Cc: Nicholas Sutrich

Welcome to a new project I’m calling Cc:, where I ask interesting people in the community about what’s making them happy both inside and outside the world of tech. This week, I’m speaking with my friend and former colleague, Nicholas Sutrich.

Who are you?

Nicholas Sutrich

What do you do for work?

I’m the Senior Content Producer at Android Central. This is a fancy title that really means I test a lot of devices every week and write about them.

What do you do for fun?

I reviewed devices for 10 years on the side before going full-time, so I still like to think of my job as being a fun hobby I just so happen to get paid for. Other than work, I love video gaming with my wife and son, reading novels, gardening and chicken tending, CrossFit, and the occasional hike when I can squeeze it in.

What is your relationship like with technology these days?

I spend less time on my phone now than maybe ever. I’ve deleted all social media off my phone (otherwise, I find I work too much for my own good), and I don’t generally play games on my phone unless I’m doing it for a review. My goal is to get off my devices when work is over and spend more quality time with friends and family in person, instead. 

What are a few apps you can’t live without and why?

eMeals: A meal planning service I subscribe to. It’s $5 a month and has a boatload of recipes on there, plus new recipes each week and plans for specific dietary restrictions, stores, or budgets.

Zepp: This is the app for Amazfit smartwatches. I use it for food logging and for workout logging. The food logging portion is particularly fantastic because it’s LLM-driven, so you can tell it you had “2 eggs fried in coconut oil with 2 slices of avocado toast and a glass of orange juice for breakfast” and it’ll log all that crap instantly. No more scrolling through tedious lists.

Discord: Everyone probably uses this, but it’s my main chat app with friends. We bounced between apps for years until it came out and haven’t switched since. 

What is a gadget that you love right now?

Motorola Razr Fold. This phone is just such a joy to use. Excellent camera and displays, never have to worry about battery life. Software is snappy and has great features (double-chop for flashlight, woot!). Oh, and the sides are CURVED, not friggin’ flat. I hate stupid phones with flat sides, especially foldables.

What’s a recent TV show you loved?

Gotta be Pursuit of Jade on Netflix. It’s a time period drama/romance/kung-fu show set in ancient China. We randomly tried it after The Algorithm™️ recommended it to us and haven’t stopped since. We only watch like 20-30 mins of TV a day tops, so it’s taken a while to get through all 40 episodes, especially since they’re usually 45 minutes or so apiece.

What’s a recent book you loved?

Jurassic Park by Michael Crichton. I somehow never read these books (although I love the OG movie). It was fun reading the original content and seeing the author’s direction for the story versus the films. Also fascinating to see what parts of the book the films stripped out and randomly slapped into other movies.

What’s a recent movie you loved?

Project Hail Mary. I read this book twice (one of which was out loud to my family) and was so happy that they were making a movie. It’s such an excellent mix of science reality and science fiction in a unique end-of-times scenario. If aliens exist, I hope they’re like Rocky.

What’s a recent game you loved?

Orbitals for the Nintendo Switch 2. I’ve played many co-op games in my time, but few are as well produced and executed as Orbitals. The visuals are beyond stunning and make you feel like you’re playing a Studio Ghibli movie. It’s basically impossible to describe the gameplay other than a wild mix of adventure, puzzle, and platforming.

What’s something offline you do every day that brings you joy?

Family reading time. We’ve done this since our son was little and it never ceases to be wonderful. At the end of most days (I wish we did it every day), we’ll curl up in bed or on the couch and read together. Sometimes, it’s reading manga; other times, it’s an audiobook or reading aloud to each other. We’ve gone through a lot of books this way, and it’s a great way to spend quality time together, drink some tea, have snacks, and start conversations.

Thank you, Nick, for being awesome as always. See you on the putting green.

Over the weekend, American AI titans, including Anthropic’s Dario Amodei, OpenAI’s Sam Altman, xAI’s Elon Musk, and Google DeepMind’s Demis Hassabis, came out in support of “pacing the frontier,” a term popularized by a letter released in July by nearly 1,400 employees of large American AI companies.

In fact, Amodei wrote his own 3,000+ word paean called “We Must Pace the Frontier,” in which he posits that the industry needs to slow down its frenetic work on improving AI model capabilities in order to prioritize alignment and safety.

“Given the accelerating rate of AI capability development, it’s my worry that in 6–12 months such a swarm could be capable of taking over the entire internet with a persistent botnet (potentially causing hundreds of billions of dollars in damage), and that the scale of damage would continue to increase from there if AI becomes more powerful without the necessary guardrails.”

This self-policed slowdown comes as the US government continues to distance itself from regulation, despite entreaties from both sides of the aisle, as well as countries around the world. In a Truth Social post, President Trump said that “the only control or ‘guardrails’ that AI needs is a STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT, and the U.S.A. has that, in spades! There is a SICK conspiracy going on against AI and Data Centers, and the only one that is happy about it is China. WHOEVER WINS AI, WINS! We are leading China, and all others, and will continue to do so.”

title: September 2026 Pixel Drop: VIPs widget redesign, more Pixel Watch gestures
snippet: Google today is rolling out the September 2026 Pixel Drop. This is a smaller update, with Android 17 QPR1 bringing the bulk of new features and changes. That said, recent weeks have seen updates for Pixel Journal, Now Playing, Recorder, Screenshots, and Weather. more…
fullText:
Google today is rolling out the September 2026 Pixel Drop. This is a smaller update, with Android 17 QPR1 bringing the bulk of new features and changes. That said, recent weeks have seen updates for Pixel Journal, Now Playing, Recorder, Screenshots, and Weather.

Phones

Google has redesigned the Pixel VIPs widget to let you quickly call and text contacts with a single tap from your homescreen instead of having to first open the bottom sheet.

A new floating navigation overlay lets you swipe the bottom of your screen to switch between your favorite people. Finally, Pixel VIPs will show glanceable notification badges on the widget. 

This redesign is rolling out for the Pixel 6+ in all regions and languages with version 2.0 of the Pixel VIPs app/service and Google Contacts 4.77+.

	

After introducing on the Pixel 11 series, Pause Point is now coming to the Pixel 6 and newer. This Digital Wellbeing feature “adds a pause before you open a distracting app of your choice.”

Updated: Scam Detection warnings now appear in the Gboard suggestions strip “wherever you chat.” The “Likely scam” warning will appear ”when you start typing a response to a suspicious message.” Available on the Pixel 6+ in the US, processing happens on your device.

Additionally, the existing Scam Detection in notifications is expanding to nine new countries (Australia, Canada, France, Germany, India, Japan, Mexico, Singapore, and the United Kingdom), as well as six new languages (Arabic, French, German, Portuguese, Japanese, and Spanish).

To mark the release of Harry Potter: The Full-Cast Audio Editions, there are three new Pixel Themes. This covers wallpapers, icons, and sounds, with eligible Pixel users also getting a two-month Audible free trial.

Pixel Watch

Owners of the Pixel Watch 3 and 4 can now scroll through their notification tray using the one-handed pinch gesture. This has been quite convenient on the PW5.

Meanwhile, the Pixel Watch 4 receives an updated raise-to-talk model that improves accuracy and performance when activating Gemini.

fullText:
9to5Mac is brought to you by CleanMyMac by MacPaw. With the release of macOS 27 Golden Gate, use CleanMyMac first to free up space, optimize your system, and ensure your new Mac runs at 100% on day one. Learn more.

macOS 27 Golden Gate doesn’t give the Photos app a dramatic redesign. Instead, Photos gains a surprisingly broad set of various improvements this year. These range from Apple Intelligence-powered editing, new ways to organize and sort your collection, better sharing tools, and much more.

More powerful Apple Intelligence editing

The flashiest updates to the Photos app in macOS 27 Golden Gate live in a new Tools pane. They require Apple Intelligence on a compatible Mac.

Clean Up gets a significant quality boost. Apple says it can now handle larger objects and more complex scenes with more realistic results.

Separately, a fast mode is intended for small blemishes, while high quality mode tackles more intricate edits not possible before.

The new Extend tool uses generative models to expand an image beyond its original edges.

That can help when straightening a horizon, changing an aspect ratio, or simply creating more space around a subject. Extend is also available from the Crop tool.

Then there’s Spatial Reframing.

First, Photos builds a 3D view of a scene using on-device spatial models. This lets you rotate around a subject, pan, or zoom to change the apparent camera position.

When the new perspective exposes gaps, image models generate the missing areas.

In macOS 27, iCloud Shared Albums finally support full-resolution sharing and all common photo and video formats.

They’re also becoming much friendlier to people outside the Apple ecosystem. Friends using Android or Windows can join a Shared Album and contribute their own photos through iCloud.com.

Apple is also addressing some everyday friction. You can save every photo from a Shared Album to your personal library with a single click.

For albums that do not need to live forever, there is a new option to have them expire after 30 days.

Slideshows, ratings, and a new collection

Next, Photos is bringing back more control over slideshows. You can turn any selection of photos and videos into a slideshow, then customize its slide duration, transition style, and music.

After that, the finished slideshow can be saved as a video file in your photo library. That makes it much easier to replay or share the presentation without making it again each time.

Additionally, a new Captured by Me collection gathers photos you took with the Camera app, including shots captured on previous devices. The same criteria can also be used as a filter elsewhere in your library.

And photographers who want another way to organize their work, Photos adds one-to-five-star ratings. Ratings can then be used to filter the main library and collections. Just be sure to enable star ratings in Photos app settings as it’s off by default.

Faster uploads and better search

Lastly, two less visible changes could make Photos feel better in daily use.

macOS 27 lets you prioritize iCloud Photos syncing so new photos and videos begin uploading sooner.

This sounds especially useful when you’ve just imported a large batch and want it available on your other devices without waiting for lower-priority work.

Apple has also rebuilt the search foundation used by Spotlight, Photos, and Mail. Apple says the new system creates a more comprehensive index of your content and keeps it updated throughout the day, so that can only be positive.

macOS 27 Golden Gate improves how you share, organize, find, sync, present, and edit your photos. Together, these changes make for a more meaningful year for the app for regular Photos app users.

title: Out of Pocket: Detailing our everyday carry
snippet: I love building a “kit,” a “pack,” a bag with enough stuff in it to make sure I am ready for every eventuality. I’m not talking about a survival kit per se, just some things that mean I am basically ready for any modern situation. more…
fullText:
I love building a “kit,” a “pack,” a bag with enough stuff in it to make sure I am ready for every eventuality. I’m not talking about a survival kit per se, just some things that mean I am basically ready for any modern situation.

EDC or Every Day Carry is basically part of my personality at this stage. It started with smartphones, moved on to earbuds, and steadily, like many of you, I accrued an assortment of gadgets, products, and things I found myself dragging with me everywhere.

I am constantly on the lookout for the next thing to enhance my EDC. I’m not alone in this; Andrew is in the same boat. We’re product people first and foremost, but practicality has to be a component before it becomes a bigger part of daily lives.

We figured that we’d share some of that intimate knowledge, driven by building packs for trade shows, travel, and just, well, hanging around.

	

So, this is Out of Pocket, our new series diving into what makes our EDC tick. Expect more deep dives into the kinds of things that are adjacent to your smartphone, the things that you carry every day, or brand new products that might pique your interest. After all, we all have our own specific EDC essentials. Here are a few of ours to hopefully get your own creative juices flowing…

My current kit (Damien)

The Sidebag – TomToc T33 (3.5L)

My search for the perfect sidebag has been, I’ll be honest, arduous. Day-to-day, I’m not much of a backpack guy, so a sling or a sidebag is the perfect accessory for all the little things I feel like I need. I already own a Bellroy Venture Ready sling, and while it’s awesome. It is just a little bit too small for a real EDC kit.

TomToc’s T33 sidebag is exponentially better with more pockets, exceptional internal organization, and interior sections. You could fit a small-ish water bottle or drink in the middle section, but netted segments mean I can throw in paracetamol or lip balm for easy access. There’s enough room for a really small tablet or notebook and documents in the back portion.

There’s a key carabiner so I can throw in my house keys and keychain right at the front. It’s stretchy enough to open a door and have the key snap back into the front pocket.

One of my must-haves on a sling is a body-facing “secret” pocket. When I’m traveling, my passport goes here so it’s accessible, but also harder for someone to try and slip their hand in – not that this has been a problem.

One of the most important things for me is that it’s waterproof. While it’s hot right now in England, we’re due a downpour. I like that all my stuff inside is safe and dry. The zippers are smooth, with waterproof seams, and there are lots of carabiner anchor points too, so you can attach a hat or a water bottle. It hits all the right notes, and I’ve abused it thoroughly, and it just wipes clean.

It’s super cheap for what it offers at under $45. My only gripe is that the color options aren’t all that extensive, but you could level that criticism at basically any sidebag. This is one that won’t break the bank.

Get the TomToc T33 sling

The Juice  – Anker Nano 5,000mAh power pack

Power banks are just so ubiquitous now that you can basically boil it down to what you want or need. Because I use the Pixel 11 Pro, I always want a Magsafe-compatible power bank around to slap to the back of the phone.

I had been using the Genki Energy Pack for almost a year now, and there were a number of reasons for that. Firstly, it looks awesome with the black and orange color scheme. Secondly, it’s Qi2 certified, so it does all the necessary handshake stuff required to get faster and more efficient charging speeds.

However, it’s blocky and bulky, so I switched it out recently for something a little lighter. I’m rocking the Anker Nano power bank now because it isn’t as bulky and has enough juice to give me a full charge on basically any phone I’m carrying.

There’s a tiny strip of LEDs that shows remaining battery level; it’s Qi2 certified, but that is limited to 15W. I use the solitary USB-C charging port if I need 20W and above, but most of the time it’s absolutely fine when you’re out and about. For what it’s worth, I carry a super short USB-C cable that’s like 10cm for that specific reason too.

I do think it’s a little pricey, but you can get it in different colours and mine has taken a beating over the year or slightly longer I’ve been using it. It’s just something that can slip on to the back of your phone without being huge or messing around with cables – which is something I appreciate.

Get the Anker Nano power bank

On-the-go entertainment – Boox Go 6 e-reader

I reviewed the Boox Go 6 e-reader almost two years ago, and since then, it has become a staple in my EDC setup. It’s just so small and inconspicuous that it basically lives in my sidebag.

As an e-reader, it’s nothing special. I’d even say it’s a little underpowered for what it offers, but the size and shape are what keep me coming back basically every single day. I basically leave it running the Kindle app or download some epub files, and it handles those absolutely fine. It is technically an Android tablet, so you can share files using Quick Share. I find this is great if you find something you want to read because you can just fire things over without messing with cables. Heck, I have hundreds of EPUBs that just work now, which is lovely. Even PDFs work just fine.

It’s under 300g with a magnetic flip case attached, so it’s not heavy by any stretch of the imagination. I have my eye on a few of the even smaller Magsafe e-readers, but at 6-inches this is like a pamphlet or an especially large coupon. Perfect for reading novels, documents, or even a downloaded webpage – not that I would recommend that!

A newer version has just been released that enables note-taking and various other improvements. I’m hoping to test drive that soon, but I have genuinely loved the compact design of the Go 6 and think I’d struggle to go back to a full-sized Kindle for that reason alone. It has come down in price to around $160, which isn’t cheap, but still not bad if you want something super small. That said, something even smaller might be better for just throwing into an even smaller sling bag…

Get the Boox Go 6 e-reader

Always available audio – USB-C earbuds

I simply hate not having some earbuds with me when I’m out of the house. I simply must be distracted with podcasts, YouTube Music, or if I want to take a call, I cannot live without a pair in my bag.

I usually have about 20 pairs of Bluetooth earbuds lying around my desk, but when the battery dies, they’re useless. I was so annoyed at a pair of buds dying mid-flight while traveling last year that I bought a random pair of USB-C earbuds from an airport vending machine to keep the music flowing. I think they’re from Xiaomi as there’s a little “Mi” logo embossed on the inline remote. I only paid like $16, but Belkin makes a pair that are $15 and reputable enough that I might pick up a pair as a spare.

Honestly, they sound fine. The threshold is that a pair of earbuds just needs to sound better than traffic or that dull airplane drone. These earbuds live in my bag as a last resort audio option, heck, they’re great to just share with someone if they’ve forgotten their own earbuds. They take up basically negligible space, too. When I’m done with them, I quickly wipe them with an alcohol pad, and they’re sterilized. Trust me, it’s worth having at least one backup option because the one time you need them, it’s a lifesaver. If you lose them, it’s not a big deal. Win-win in my book.

Get some cheap USB-C earbuds

Retro on the go – Gamesir Pocket Taco controller

If I’m taking a backpack, I usually try to make room for my Steam Deck or Switch 2, but if I’m going out for a few hours, I’ll usually stick to something much smaller. I love Gamesir’s range of controllers, but the Pocket Taco is one that, as a millennial gamer and Gameboy obsessive, I’m sticking with for now.

It clips onto your phone – don’t worry, it has rubber pads to stop scratches – and gives you real buttons to play games in portrait orientation like Nintendo intended back in the late 1980s. It really does feel like a DMG Game Boy in the best ways. Thankfully, there are more buttons that you can map so that you can play other emulators, not just Gameboy.

If you’re not a gamer, mobile or otherwise, this might not be for you, and that’s absolutely fine. For nerds of a certain “vintage,” you’ll probably love this as much as I do.

Get the Pocket Taco game controller

The extras – ‘stuff’ and ‘things’

We’re all humans, so we can’t just have cables and batteries in our bags. I carry a few other key things that are useful. Most of these are just cheap things that I’ve found are worth having.

After a trip to a city with questionable-quality streetlights, I picked up a little keychain torch that just attaches to my keys. Olight makes a ton of EDC lighting products, but I love the iMini 2 at just $20 because it can just go on my keys with the carabiner clip.

I just charge it every couple of months using the integrated USB-A plug at the back, and it lasts a lotng time despite the fact that it’s absolutely tiny. Detach to power on, then it magnetically snaps back into place, and the light turns off. Super useful if you don’t want to drain your smartphone’s battery, and it’s bright enough to light a small room. Sometimes I just use it to fine stuff I’ve dropped down the side of my car seats.

Get the Olight iMini 2 keychain flashlight

I have spilled tea and coffee on my clothes so many times that I started carrying around a Tide stain pen a while back, and it has saved many a shirt. It’s not going to get out huge stains, but it’s still nice to stop something from ruining your outfit. They’re around $15 for a 5-pack. I can’t recommend them highly enough because they’ve stopped so many of my shirts and t-shirts from getting completely ruined over the past few years.

On a similar note, I try to carry a microfiber cleaning cloth, alcohol cleaning pads, and napkins or tissues. Throw in some hand gel, lotion, a little sunscreen, and I’m covered for basically any eventuality.

My current kit (Andrew)

The backpack – Peak Design Travel Backpack 20L

Whether I step outside with a sling or my backpack is entirely down to whether I decide to tote my laptop along. I use a MacBook Air 13-inch, which has the smallest footprint one can reasonably expect a bag to fit. But even so, there is a true limit to the number of slings that can carry a small laptop. So if that’s coming with me, I’m taking the Peak Design Travel Backpack 20L.

The 20L variant has easily become my favorite backpack to lug around if I’m going with a heavier loadout. It weighs very little, and it’s completely unassuming. If there needs to be more on my back, it can expand slightly beyond that small capacity. But otherwise, I’m able to carry my laptop and a few essentials without worry.

The main compartment is great for just throwing random items in. When I’m using this bag, stuff doesn’t need to be organized as it would in a dedicated camera bag. I’m generally going to bring my tech pouch along, too. But that’s almost overkill because the top pocket has all of the same inner pockets for those little things I want to tag along.

It has all of the little creature comforts you’d want. Magnetic strap keepers, a pass-through for luggage handles, and an internal water bottle holder, so a giant container of liquid isn’t sloshing around way off balance. Overall, it’s simple but incredibly effective at what it does.

Get the Peak Design Travel 20L

The sidebag – Bellroy Lite Sling Mini

As for the sling, my rule states that I’ll swap to this if my laptop isn’t coming along. The Sling Lite Mini has the feel of an outdoor bag without so much of the look, so it flies under the radar more than a technical pack might. The outer material is strong and lightweight, but it doesn’t repel liquid as well as I’d hope it would. The internal pocket structure is simple, but efficient. The main pocket is plenty large enough for random items, and it’s complemented by a zipper pocket for thinner items. One of the gussets that let it expand is lined with a pocket I use to slip my Nomad titanium pen and handy USB ChargeKey. On the other side, I clip my knife and flashlight.

The best part about it being geared towards outdoor use is that it’s expandable. The gusseted construction keeps it compact, no matter how much you stuff in it. So even if it’s full, the shoulder strap pulls it tight so the overall profile is kept slim.

It’s tough and just easy to grab and go. I love this bag.

Neither is traditionally “cheap,” and Damien offers a great alternative with his TomToc sidebag. But at $79 for the sling and double that for the Travel Backpack, it’s a “buy it for life” sort of purchase.

Get the Bellroy Sling Lite Mini

The power – Baseus Qi2 25W

I generally don’t have the fear of running out of power with whatever phone I’m using. I wouldn’t say I’m an ultra-power user, but there are times when I just start to run out of steam on my Galaxy Fold 8 Ultra or Pixel 11. You can carry a slim charging brick, which I do anyway, or you can take a magnetic power bank.

I always carry the Baseus 10,000mAh Qi2.2 25W power bank with me. Because the Pixel has magnets on the back without the help of a case, I can always slap it on. If needed, I can plug the bank into something else via USB-C. Speeds aren’t really an issue, either, because it runs at 25W – right where the Pixel 10 Pro XL is rated, even if it doesn’t always charge that fast.

It’s kind of big, and it’s kind of bulky, but if I’m bringing a bag, I have little reason not to throw this in. Statik’s MagStack cable is a 100W magnetic cable that essentially coils itself back up every single time. It solves the issue of cables that are all over the place and are resistant to any coercion to get them back into shape.

I’ve been using the MagStack cable for the better part of a year, and it just refuses to lose it’s uniform appeal. I bring it with me whenever I can because it’s just easy to pack away, given you have the pocket space. Plus, I know it’s a high-speed cable, as opposed to all of my identical USB-C cables with varying levels of power delivery.

Get the Statik MagStack Pro cable

The wallet – Peak Design Mobile Slim

Yeah, maybe I am a Peak Design nerd. I can’t really help it. The design speaks to me on the photography side, as well as on the engineering side. I’ve been using the mobile slim wallet for what has to be three or four years. It’s almost time to replace it, because that once “Sun” yellow color has now darkened to a dijon.

It’s a standard slim pull-tab wallet. I hold a few cards in there, including a Google Find My Device tracker, unlike my European counterpart, who seems adamant that carrying a physical ID is no longer a normal part of society. Until Google Wallet can add my license without any potential governmental hiccups, I’m carrying a MagSafe wallet with me.

I don’t know what it is about flashlights, but they come in clutch way more than you’d think. The ArcPro Ultra is technically a “flat” light, but it’s still sort of beefy. Still, I’ve used it too many times to start leaving it behind. The battery essentially never dies, and I can beam up to 1,700 lumens with a simple double-tap. Plus, the slider to switch between UV, spotlight, and floodlight acts as a fantastic fidget toy.

title: The Quantified Scientist tests the Apple Watch Series 12’s new heart rate sensor
snippet: In a new video, The Quantified Scientist’s Rob ter Horst compares the new Apple Watch Series 12’s heart rate sensor against a Polar H10 ECG chest strap. Here’s what he found. more…
fullText:
In a new video, The Quantified Scientist’s Rob ter Horst compares the new Apple Watch Series 12’s heart rate sensor against a Polar H10 ECG chest strap. Here’s what he found.

Revamped heart sensor delivers

For the Apple Watch Series 12, Apple completely revamped the device’s heart sensor, which now measures heart rate every five seconds even when the user isn’t active.

In our review of Apple Watch Series 12, which you can read here, we found that the added data can provide more detailed insights into how everyday activities and moments throughout the day affect heart rate, such as hauling groceries, doing yard work, drinking an afternoon cup of coffee, or dealing with a stressful moment at work.

That said, Rob ter Horst from The Quantified Scientist YouTube channel published an in-depth look (via MacMagazine) at the Apple Watch Series 12’s new heart rate sensor during indoor cycling, running, and weightlifting, and compared its readings with those from a Polar H10 ECG chest strap.

All in all, the Apple Watch Series 12’s new heart sensor performed very well, particularly during indoor cycling, where its readings were nearly identical to the Polar H10 data.

During a running session, the Series 12 also performed well, with a 0.98 correlation with the chest strap (versus a near-perfect correlation of 1.0 during indoor cycling), though ter Horst noted some minor deviations at higher heart rates.

During weightlifting, which ter Horst notes is traditionally one of the hardest activities for wrist-based heart rate sensors, the Series 12 posted the lowest correlation of the three exercises tested, at 0.97. Even so, ter Horst said the result was “quite good” compared with the competition, placing the Series 12 above 85% of devices he has tested for weightlifting.

Compared with his longer-term testing of the Apple Watch Series 11, ter Horst said the new Apple Watch Series 12 delivered broadly similar heart rate accuracy overall, with the older model actually performing slightly better during running in his tests. It could be the case, ter Horst notes, that Apple is still tweaking its algorithms for the new sensor.

Finally, ter Horst also tested the Apple Watch Series 12’s step counter. He manually counted roughly 5,000 steps and found the Series 12 was generally spot-on or only slightly overcounted.

title: AirPods Pro 3 keep getting better, here’s what’s new in iOS 27
snippet: AirPods just got a variety of new features in iOS 27, several of which are exclusive to AirPods Pro 3. Here’s everything new. more…
fullText:
AirPods just got a variety of new features in iOS 27, several of which are exclusive to AirPods Pro 3. Here’s everything new.

Custom EQ

Custom EQ is a feature that some AirPods users thought Apple would never ship, but iOS 27 adds it.

With Custom EQ, Apple now lets you set your own sound profile for AirPods. Per Apple:

AirPods are designed and engineered by Apple to faithfully represent music, TV shows and movies, and calls. If you prefer a different sound profile, you can customize how AirPods represent any audio played.

You can change the EQ by going to your AirPods’ settings ⇾ Audio & Routing ⇾ Equalizer ⇾ Custom. From here, you can adjust the sound profile for low, mid, and high frequencies.

Custom EQ is available on AirPods Pro 3, AirPods Pro 2, AirPods Max 2, AirPods 5, and AirPods 4.

GymKit can sync AirPods Pro 3’s heart rate data

Apple GymKit has been available for years, but only for Apple Watch. It lets you pair and sync workout data with compatible cardio equipment, like treadmills, ellipticals, indoor bikes, and more.

In iOS 27, GymKit expands to support iPhone using AirPods Pro 3’s heart rate sensor. My colleague Zac gave it a try:

The setup is simple. I tapped my iPhone to the treadmill, picked Indoor Walk (Indoor Run is also offered), and started the workout from the treadmill. With GymKit, workout data is stored privately on iPhone and removed from the equipment.

Once the workout started, the treadmill received heart-rate data from AirPods Pro 3. Meanwhile, the Fitness app on iPhone received the treadmill’s distance, pace, incline, and calorie data. Treadmills know details that an iPhone and AirPods can’t know on their own, especially incline and precise belt distance.

For more details on iOS 27’s GymKit feature for AirPods Pro 3, check out Zac’s full hands-on below.

Read more: iOS 27 basically turns your iPhone and AirPods into an Apple Watch at the gym

Siri AI

For most AirPods users, the single biggest upgrade in iOS 27 will be Siri AI.

Siri AI is available on compatible iPhone hardware in iOS 27, and Apple made sure to expand full support for the AI assistant to AirPods too.

AirPods are essentially becoming an AI wearable thanks to the new Siri. It will let users do a lot more than the current Siri. Here are some key features via Apple’s website:

World Knowledge: “Ask about virtually any topic that’s on your mind, from important facts to recipes and restaurant recommendations. Siri AI can reference information online to give you detailed, up-to-date insights.”

Conversational: “Siri AI is your conversational AI assistant with entirely new capabilities…Ask open-ended questions, brainstorm ideas for work or creative projects on the go, and engage in natural, back-and-forth conversations.”

Personal Context: “Siri AI can find relevant answers to what you’re looking for just by asking. Search for a photo from years ago, easily locate an email buried in your inbox, or pull up a note you saved on your iPhone.”

Read more: AirPods keep getting better, and iOS 27’s biggest upgrade is Siri

Precision Finding via Apple Watch

Earlier this year when AirTag 2 launched, Apple brought Precision Finding support to Apple Watch for the first time. Until now though, it’s been limited to AirTag 2.

But with iOS 27 and watchOS 27, Apple expands Precision Finding on the Watch to AirPods Pro 3.

AirPods Pro 3’s case includes the latest second-generation Ultra Wideband (UWB) chip, letting you find it with greater precision and step-by-step guidance right from your wrist.

With every batch of new AirPods features that debuts, the AirPods settings screen in the Settings app gets more cluttered.

But in iOS 27, Apple has a welcome fix: it’s redesigned and reorganized all AirPods settings.

Now, you’ll find AirPods settings organized into more categories and submenus, accompanied by colorful icons. It makes finding the right setting way easier and more intuitive than before.

title: Judge scrutinizes Musk’s move to drop Apple from antitrust lawsuit involving OpenAI
snippet: Federal judge Mark Pittman wants details on any agreement that may have led Elon Musk’s companies to drop their antitrust claims against Apple. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
Federal judge Mark Pittman wants details on any agreement that may have led Elon Musk’s companies to drop their antitrust claims against Apple. Here are the details.

Judge wants to see any Apple agreement

Earlier this week, X and SpaceXAI submitted a motion to voluntarily dismiss with prejudice their claims against Apple in the case they brought against Apple and OpenAI last year.

According to the original filing, Apple and OpenAI were colluding to keep competing AI apps from gaining visibility on the App Store, as a result of their agreement to integrate ChatGPT into Siri and Apple Intelligence. Apple and OpenAI rejected the claims.

In its filing earlier this week, X and SpaceXAI said only that they had “resolved their claims in this Action against” Apple, stressing that they did not seek to dismiss their claims against OpenAI.

Now, as first reported by POLITICO, Judge Mark Pittman, who has been overseeing the case, has ordered X and SpaceXAI to provide the court with “any agreement or combination of agreements with Apple that relate to the resolution of Plaintiffs’ claims against Apple in this litigation.”

The order came in response to an emergency motion filed by OpenAI seeking to compel X and SpaceXAI to produce their agreement resolving the dispute with Apple. Pittman also ordered the companies to respond to OpenAI’s motion by noon on September 17.

title: GM just found the ‘sweet spot’ for supporting Android Auto & CarPlay [Gallery]
snippet: GM has been stubbornly standing by its decision to axe Android Auto and Apple CarPlay from many of its newer vehicles in recent years, despite loud and constant negative feedback from consumers. In its latest software update for two new trucks, GM has found the “sweet spot” for implementing Android Auto and CarPlay, but it’s unclear if that compromise will extend to other vehicles. more…
fullText:
GM has been stubbornly standing by its decision to axe Android Auto and Apple CarPlay from many of its newer vehicles in recent years, despite loud and constant negative feedback from consumers. In its latest software update for two new trucks, GM has found the “sweet spot” for implementing Android Auto and CarPlay, but it’s unclear if that compromise will extend to other vehicles. 

A new software experience – based on Android Automotive / Google built-in – debuting in the 2027 Chevrolet Silverado and 2027 GMC Sierra will see GM’s software not only get a nice new coat of paint, but also some welcome functionality. As detailed by CNBC, the update will “proactively surface relevant controls” such as call controls and even a garage door opener. Both vehicles have plenty of physical controls, too.

The biggest news here, though, is GM finding a new way to implement Android Auto and CarPlay integration.

GM announced in 2023 that it would remove phone projection systems from its vehicles while embracing Android Automotive and native functionality in its infotainment system, a decision that has not been positively embraced by customers. While GM has not backed down from this change on its electric vehicles, many of its vehicles still support both platforms. 

	

The change here is that the Silverado and Sierra will support Android Auto and CarPlay, but in a new windowed mode. The projection appears on a part of the display, with aspects of the native infotainment coming through around the sides so you can still easily control parts of the car that projection systems cannot without actually closing anything. 

Speaking to The Verge, GM group product manager for Google built-in, projection, and profiles Colin McCormick explained that this is the “sweet spot.”

I think we’re landing in a spot where… we don’t have a customer that has to decide, “Oh, I’m going to use projection, or, oh, I want to use the native system…” That’s our sweet spot.

That said, there’s no word here on whether or not GM will actually bring Android Auto and CarPlay back to more of its vehicles. Gas-powered vehicles remain with support for phone projection, but that’s still missing in its EVs, including the latest Chevy Bolt that launched earlier this year.

title: Meet the next wave of VCs judging Startup Battlefield 200 at TechCrunch Disrupt 2026

For founders, Startup Battlefield 200 is one of the biggest moments of their careers. For everyone else in the TechCrunch Disrupt 2026 audience, it’s one of the best ways to learn how great companies are actually evaluated by VCs.

This startup pitch competition is as intense as you’d expect. That’s when the judges start asking the questions every investor, customer, and future employee will eventually want answered. Can this team execute? Is the market big enough? Why now? That’s why we’re continuing to build one of the strongest judging panels in Startup Battlefield’s history. Today we’re excited to introduce another group of five top-tier investors who’ll help identify the companies with the potential to become tomorrow’s breakout success stories.

The next five VCs deciding which Startup Battlefield contenders advance

Without further ado, meet the next batch of investors who will judge which early-stage founder walks away with the $100,000 prize. Get to know these judges, along with the first 10 already announced on the Disrupt agenda.

Image Credits:TechCrunch

Vaibhav ‘Dr.V’ Agrawal, Co-Founder and General Partner, ODDBIRD VC

Dr.V is the co-founder and general partner of ODDBIRD VC, a pre-seed fund he founded in 2024 to back AI companies reindustrializing the West — with a focus on health and bio, critical supply chains, and real-world automation. A trained physician with an MBBS degree, Agrawal also holds an MBA from Stanford and previously served as a General Partner at Lightspeed Venture Partners India, where he backed early-stage startups beginning in 2016. His current portfolio includes Anterior, a healthcare AI company that has raised $64 million from NEA and Sequoia.

Anu Bharadwaj, Partner, ICONIQ Growth

Anu Bharadwaj is a partner at ICONIQ Growth, where she focuses on enterprise software and AI companies. Before joining ICONIQ, Bharadwaj served as President and COO of Atlassian for nearly 12 years, where she led the product, engineering, and enterprise business across Jira, Confluence, and the Atlassian Cloud platform as the company scaled to billions in annual revenue. She previously held leadership roles at Microsoft and holds a B.Eng. in Computer Science from R.V. College of Engineering.

Sho Sho Leigha Ho, Partner, General Catalyst

Sho Sho Leigha Ho is a partner on General Catalyst‘s seed team, where she invests in early-stage founders. She serves as a board observer at Together AI. She joined General Catalyst in 2024 as its youngest partner. Her public investments include Graylark, Autoscience, Standard Kernel, and The Interaction Company of California (Poke), which Cognition acquired in July 2026. She holds an A.B. from Harvard and is based in San Francisco.

Miloni Madan Presler, Partner, IVP

Miloni Madan Presler is a partner at IVP (Institutional Venture Partners), where she partners with first-time founders building inflection-stage technology companies in enterprise software, healthcare, and security, from Series B through pre-IPO. She brings a disciplined growth equity and private equity perspective to company building, shaped by earlier roles at Summit Partners and Warburg Pincus. Presler holds a degree in Economics and Finance from Johns Hopkins University and speaks four languages.

Aidan Madigan-Curtis, Partner, Eclipse Ventures

Aidan Madigan-Curtis is a partner at Eclipse Ventures, where she invests in AI, IoT, computer vision, and software solutions for manufacturing, logistics, supply chain, and climate transition. Named one of Business Insider’s 22 Investors to Know in Robotics and Physical AI, she leads Eclipse’s Carbon Optimization framework to track real emissions reductions across the firm’s portfolio. title: The long dream of the Googlebook

fullText:
In late 2010, an up-and-coming Google executive named Sundar Pichai took the stage in front of a bunch of reporters and explained that Google had a big new idea about laptops. In the future, he said, the only thing you’d need on your computer was a web browser — that was where all your apps, data, and connections would live going forward. Your computer didn’t need much storage, Pichai explained, or any fancy hardware, because the cloud would do the work. The software designed for these new laptops, Chrome OS, was an enormous bet that the web would eventually overtake everything.

Chrome OS (which eventually became ChromeOS) has been, in many ways, a huge hit. But the computer currently on Rick Osterloh’s desk isn’t a Chromebook. Osterloh is Google’s head of hardware and devices, and the sleek, slim device he’s tapping on as he joins our Google Meet is a 13-inch Dell clamshell with decidedly un-Chromebook specs: 16 gigs of RAM, a cutting-edge Qualcomm processor, a light and thin and MacBook-ish metallic look. It’s called the XPS Googlebook, and it’s one of five new devices running Googlebook OS, Google’s latest big idea about computers.

At first blush, Googlebooks feel like classic Google in a bad way: yet another operating system, yet another brand, yet another thing destined for the Google graveyard. But Osterloh sees it differently. He greenlit the whole project in part because he saw it as “the ultimate focusing move” for Google. For a long time, he says, Google has built, maintained, and shipped two operating systems. ChromeOS stayed on laptops, while Android conquered phones and tablets and TVs and cars and everything else. Slowly but surely, Google has built Android into a familiar interface and a large app ecosystem across all those devices. Except for laptops.

It’s your computer. It’s your phone. It’s your phone-puter!

Meanwhile, Google became convinced that the advent of AI might change the way we use computers forever — but might not need to change the computers themselves. Osterloh says he has tables full of wheel-reinventing prototypes, and of course the company is betting big on things like smart glasses, but high-end PCs, which have the power needed to run AI models for coding, dictation, and more, have been a surprise winner of the AI revolution so far. (Just ask Apple, which has seen AI enthusiasts buy high-end Macs in huge volume.) “I think laptops are one of those resonant form factors,” Osterloh says. “It’s an established category that’s incredibly useful for productivity and apps, and it’s going to be really hard to replace that.”

Those two ideas together — Android’s dominance and the rise of AI — tell the whole story of Googlebook. There are a lot of bets inside of the Googlebook project, both about what we do on computers and how we’ll do it going forward, but maybe the most surprising is Google’s commitment to building kickass laptops. A generation ago, then-CEO Eric Schmidt argued that the future was “disposable” hardware, that devices wouldn’t matter as the internet took over. Googlebooks represent Google’s growing belief that devices matter more than ever. And that a good laptop is worth paying for.

“The key thing that had changed was just the rapid pace of evolution that Android itself has gone under.”

The Googlebook project started in earnest a couple of years ago, but some of the ideas have been floating around much longer. Rumors and reports of a ChromeOS-Android merger have been around for more than a decade, and Google has tried various ways to bring the two operating systems into harmony. The company spent years programming ChromeOS to be able to run Android apps (and even Windows apps), but never nailed the integration. For years, a project called Fuchsia looked like the combination users had been waiting for, but that petered out into a smart home-specific project.

In early 2024, though, a couple of Googlers asked a new question: What if, instead of trying to bring Android apps to ChromeOS, we brought the best of ChromeOS to Android? They weren’t the first people to ask that question, but they were the first to time it right. “The key thing that had changed,” says Prajakta Gudadhe, Google’s VP of engineering for laptops and tablets, “was just the rapid pace of evolution that Android itself has gone under.”

For so many years, Android was a phone operating system that was sometimes hamfistedly shoved into other devices. But Gudadhe felt like Android had finally matured into something truly cross-platform. Developers had begun to embrace multiple screen sizes and orientations, and the Android team at Google had changed the way they built the operating system. “Android at that time was serving multiple form factors, from phones to wearables to TVs to autos,” Gudadhe says, “and because of that they just had to invest in a much more modular stack that could support this diversity.”

What that meant in practice was that it might finally be possible to build an Android laptop that could natively run the universe of Android apps, without looking and working like a grossly oversized Android phone. By combining base Android technology with some of the best features of ChromeOS — excellent multitasking and multi-window support, fast boot times, easy software updates — Google could have the best of both worlds.

The idea became a memo proposing a new laptop OS, which was excitedly received by Google leadership, and Project Aluminium was born. (To be clear: It is A-lu-min-i-um, not aluminum, and there was a swear jar in the office for people who dared to pronounce it the American way.)

In addition to the technical underpinnings, the Aluminium pitch included a couple of big ideas about the future of laptops. The first was that more and more users were starting their computing journey with Android devices, and thus were expecting all their other computers to both interact with and even look like their Android phones. They wanted widgets, homescreens, notification shades, and customization options. They also wanted all their apps on their laptop, and their data in perfect sync all the time. That became one of the core tenets of the operating system — perfect integration with Android devices. (iPhone owners were, and are, mostly out of luck on this front.)

The team was also convinced that Gemini and other AI tools were part of the future of computing, and that they should be built into the operating system and not just a separate app. The advent of vibe coding meant people might want to build their own software, in a terminal or with the help of on-device agents, and would surely want easier ways to get it running on their devices. But even little things about computer use felt ripe for AI change. “The mouse pointer? That thing seems pretty stupid,” says Alexander Kuscher, Google’s senior director of product management for laptops and tablets, just naming one example. Your cursor represents your attention, and moves around with your brain and your eyes, so why can’t your computer just see and respond to it? “I’m copying and pasting stuff all over the place, and typing to chatbots that don’t give me the ability to just express my needs with the mouse pointer.” That thinking became one of the most novel features of Googlebook OS, Magic Pointer, which lets you invoke your AI bot just by wiggling your cursor over an image or a bit of text. The idea, Kuscher said, was to “not change the ergonomics [of a laptop], but to make sure we take care of people coming from the ecosystem, living in an AI world.”

Running, and making, Android apps is core to Googlebook.

As the Aluminium team started working on an AI-centric, Android-powered laptop, they began discovering problems — and other teams at Google trying to solve them. “One is Android Automotive, which cares a lot about multi-user,” Kuscher says. “They need fast user switching because different people get in the car. We were like, oh, me too!” They found folks on the Android Wear team working on improving the Bluetooth stack for better accessory connectivity, and people on the XR team thinking about multi-window support for Android.

This is the focusing that gets Osterloh excited. The well-earned stereotype about Google is that nobody ever talks to anybody else, and so the company ships a thousand slightly different messaging apps, reminders systems, and AI subscriptions. In that vein, the Aluminium team could have come up with new ideas about everything and baked them all into ChromeOS; what they did instead was integrate so many disparate ideas about Android into a single platform.

Even the ultimate name of the devices and the software, Googlebook and Googlebook OS, hint at the extent to which Google hopes Aluminium brings everything Google-y together in one place. “We realized pretty quickly that this is about the whole Google experience,” Kuscher says. “If you have a phone that runs Google, and a car, and a laptop, that’s what this is about.”

(The naming here is a delightful bit of Google chaos, by the way. Googlebooks run Googlebook OS, which is mostly Android, but with some ChromeOS trappings thrown in. Get it? Me neither. They’re Android laptops.)

It became very clear to the Googlebook team that this operating system was going to ask a lot of the hardware it ran on. All the system-level AI would need enough processing power and memory to feel seamless, of course, but it went further than that. “We didn’t want to have Magic Pointer, and then it’s really hard on your trackpad to actually use it,” says Kuscher. “That’s just incongruent.” Likewise, what good is letting you build software with a prompt if the keyboard is awful to type on or the battery dies before it’s done? If the screen is too small, or too low-res, nobody will want to use it instead of their phone. For a Googlebook to be even a little bit worthwhile, the hardware would need to be great.

From the beginning, Osterloh says, Google wanted to build an ecosystem of Googlebooks. The company began reaching out to PC makers, chip companies, and even phone manufacturers, all with roughly the same pitch: You’ve already been making either great laptops, great Android devices, or both, and now we’re putting the whole puzzle together. For a PC industry always looking for Windows competition and increasingly interested in building ecosystems of products to compete with Apple, the pitch worked: Google is starting with five devices from five partners — Acer, Asus, Dell, HP, and Lenovo — and Osterloh says there are many other partners waiting in the wings. Potentially including Google’s own Pixel team. The first five devices, he said, are merely the ones that are ready now. And he says partners are clamoring to be next.

“I still fundamentally believe it will always be your central computer.”

The harder group to convince of this whole thing? Users. For all their success in education and elsewhere, Chromebooks never really caught on as personal computers. That’s largely Google’s fault, and largely for two reasons: because Google never successfully convinced people that all they needed was a web browser, and because Google and its partners spent so many years making and marketing crappy computers. Early Chromebook commercials were, in fact, explicitly anti-hardware: They showed people lighting their laptops on fire and throwing them into rivers, because who cared about the device when everything was in the cloud? As a result, even when Google and its partners have made high-end Chromebooks, like the terrific Pixelbook, they failed to convince anyone that they were worth the money.

The first lineup of Googlebooks will cost between $899 and $1,299, which puts them squarely in competition with devices like the MacBook Air. Osterloh says he thinks Googlebooks will eventually reach other form factors and lower prices, but seems unfazed by the task of convincing people to spend top dollar on a Google laptop. For one thing, he thinks the increasing popularity of AI has made people more willing to buy high-end computers in general, and has maybe even increased the importance of laptops and desktops. “I still fundamentally believe it will always be your central computer,” he says. “The thing that connects you to networks, that has the primary brain, the important screen for entertainment and productivity.” But more than that, he agrees that this kind of hardware, and this kind of price tag, are simply what it requires to do Googlebooks well. And Google definitely won’t get a third chance to convince you it’s right about laptops.

Googlebooks have some fun features like a glowing bar, but mostly they’re laptops.

When Google first announced the Googlebook concept in May, it was heavily focused on AI and Gemini. But the work that led to Googlebooks goes back much further than the company’s current obsession with LLMs, and is about more than Google’s chatbot. In some ways, Osterloh says, the whole history of Android has led up to the launch of Googlebooks. Their first job, as he sees it, is to “run the applications you know how to use and sync really well with all your Android usage and applications and devices that you’ve connected to it. And it just happens to be an awesome laptop.”

Sixteen years ago, Google shipped a laptop for the internet age. Now it’s trying to build one for the mobile era that has already come, and the AI-centric one that’s still forming. Getting it right will require marshaling nearly everything Google does well — and the best devices it has ever made. It will also require proving to users that they need a computer that’s more like their phone, and more connected to their AI ecosystem. None of that is a given; it might be an even bigger leap than trying to move your laptop to the web. But if Google’s bet pays off, our cursors might never wiggle the same way again.

title: WhatsApp starts rolling out new in-chat search button on iOS
snippet: Following a few weeks of beta testing, WhatsApp is now rolling out its new in-chat search button to iPhone users. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
Following a few weeks of beta testing, WhatsApp is now rolling out its new in-chat search button to iPhone users. Here are the details.

Early last month, WhatsApp started testing a new search button in the bottom-right corner of the in-chat interface, making it easier to start a search.

Up until now, in-chat search required users to tap on the contact or group name at the top of the conversation, select the search option from the chat info screen, and then enter their query after being taken back to the main chat.

An in-chat search button, by contrast, streamlines the process by letting users start searching without leaving the conversation.

Now, WABetaInfo reports that WhatsApp is officially rolling out the in-chat search button, though it appears in a different location than it did during beta testing.

Inage: WABetaInfo

Here’s WABetaInfo:

The new search button appears at the top of the screen when users scroll up through the conversation. When users return to the bottom of the chat, the button disappears again. It shows up contextually, only when it is useful. Users who see the button can tap it to activate search mode directly within the conversation. As soon as users enable search mode, they can type a keyword and find matching messages without leaving the chat. The search mode works just like the existing one, so users who are already familiar with it will not have to learn anything new.

WABetaInfo notes that the new shortcut is available across individual chats, group chats, and channels. In all three cases, the button appears near the top of the screen when users scroll up through the conversation or channel, and disappears again when they return to the bottom.

As with most WhatsApp feature rollouts, the new search button may take some time to reach everyone.
