fullText:
If you’re anything like me, you’ve been all-in on smart lights for years. I almost never use light switches anymore and the luxury I’ve grown used to is immediately made apparent when I spend a night away from home. That said, smart lighting has continued to evolve far beyond the basic bulbs I’ve grown used to, and this was plain as day when I got my hands on the new Linkind Smart Light Stick.

First and foremost, these bulbs pack Matter compatibility for simple controls, but the perks really come to life when you tap into the AiDot app. This is where you can take advantage of addressable zones within the bulb, which sort of blew my mind. I also love the clean cylindrical look of these bulbs, which I will showcase down below.

The first thing that stood out to me when unboxing it was the hardware design. Rather than sticking to the familiar pear shape of standard household bulbs, Linkind opted for a clean, frosted cylinder. For this reason, I really think it will look great in frosted and transparent fixtures alike.

Matter-compatible bulbs with rich app customization

The setup process was refreshingly straightforward. As shown in the screenshots, grabbing the AiDot app and running through the pairing sequence took about a minute or so, and I was relieved straight away when I saw that the app actually had solid ratings. While Matter certification allows users to skip third-party apps entirely, skipping AiDot would cause you to miss out on a lot of the features that an app like AiDot can offer.

	

As you can see below, the number of available scenes is sort of obscene. It was a little overwhelming to see the number of options, but it’s easy to create favorites, which I’ll certainly be doing so it is easy to switch for whatever holiday season we are in the middle of.

To put these bulbs through their paces, I installed them across three different fixtures. First up was the pergola and hot tub area. Transparent wall mounted lanterns along the white lattice frame gave the Light Sticks plenty of room to show off. I then added them to one of the lamp posts in my yard, followed by the lamp that resides in my home office.

Hero feature is the customizable flame effect

Easily the coolest trick up the Light Stick’s sleeve is its built-in flame simulation. Rather than settling for a basic pixelated flicker, the frosted cylindrical design diffuses light to deliver a much more authentic look than I tend to see with other bulbs, especially when dropped into an open fixture like my office lamp or outdoor lanterns.

Setup is straight forward, allowing me to quickly customize the look I was after. I did my best to capture it in action in the video below. In my opinion, the video doesn’t quite do it justice, as I think it looks much better in person.

Seasonal curb appeal with festive scenes

Until now, I’ve been going with warm white lighting 100% of the time. With Linkind Smart Light Stick Pro, I don’t have a reason to forego shaking up the look of my space when the seasons change or a holiday arrives.

While there are plenty of pre-made dynamic scenes to pick from, the DIY tab in the AiDot app is where the hardware really shines. As mentioned earlier, there are individually addressable zones, offering up 50 individual areas you can customize. I was able to use the app to create a neat color effect in under a minute, and you can see the UI below.

The settings above lead to another neat animation that I tried to capture on video. Like before, while it looks great on video, it’s even better in person. I took the lamp shade off and you can see that the bulb looks great even when fully on display, which is something I cannot say for a lot of the other smart bulbs out there.

And if you want clearer examples of what the bulbs actually look like in person, check out the official footage in the video below. It highlights a wider variety of dynamic presets, from festive holiday scenes to subtle ambient glows. It really drives home just how versatile these are compared to standard, single-color smart bulbs.

Pricing and availability

If you want to step up your outdoor or indoor lighting like I have, head over to Linkind’s website to find these bulbs (and all of the others they sell). You can pick up the bulbs directly on Amazon, where they are currently selling for $39.99.

title: Pixel VIPs 2.0 redesign starts rolling out with fullscreen look
snippet: Following last week’s Feature Drop, Pixel VIPs 2.0 is beginning to roll out, and it brings more changes than just the widget redesign. more…
fullText:
Following last week’s Feature Drop, Pixel VIPs 2.0 is beginning to roll out, and it brings more changes than just the widget redesign.

With version 2.0, tapping on a contact in the widget no longer slides up a bottom sheet over your homescreen. Instead, it now opens a fullscreen layout, which was previously accessible by swiping up. The previous design was better for one-handed use as the call and message shortcuts were closer to the bottom of the screen.

Other changes to this page include a pencil icon in the top-right corner that lets you quickly edit in Google Contacts, while the call, message, video, and contact buttons now use outline-style icons.

Old vs. new

	

Google has moved the “Local updates” card to the top spot over “Last connection,” while “Notes” is now the last section as Pixel VIPs has removed the media and place recommendations.

Meanwhile, the big update today is a new pill-shaped switcher that shows all your VIPs. This allows for quick switching without having to go back to the homescreen.

The actual widget redesign is not yet live after updating to Pixel VIPs 2.0. However, there is a preview of the new layout with “space for quick actions” that lets you call and message directly from the widget.

Pixel VIPs 2.0 is widely rolled out via the Play Store.

title: New Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4 fitness feature is surprisingly motivating
snippet: Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4 include a new fitness-tracking feature: live step tracking on the watch face. Alongside live heart rate data, it’s a surprisingly welcome and motivating change to the new hardware that I’m loving so far. more…
fullText:
Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4 include a new fitness-tracking feature: live step tracking on the watch face. Alongside live heart rate data, it’s a surprisingly welcome and motivating change to the new hardware that I’m loving so far.

Conceptually, step tracking data on the watch face is a rather unremarkable feature. Third-party apps like Pedometer++ have long been able to display your step count on your watch face. But Apple has waited until Series 12 and Ultra 4 to build in support for the Apple Watch.

Step tracking data has always been collected by Apple Watch. Even your iPhone can measure step tracking throughout the day, dating back to the iPhone 5s (before the Apple Watch existed). 

Before Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4, however, Apple tucked step tracking data away inside apps like Fitness and Health. Now, it’s a built-in complication option from the Fitness app, just like activity rings. 

My guess is that Apple didn’t surface this data before for a two reasons. First, Apple’s new hardware is more capable and more efficient. That must be the reason why live step data is hardware-specific.

Second, I think Apple has liked the idea of presenting the Apple Watch as more comprehensive than just step tracking. The heart rate monitor and other sensors tell a much more complete story than just steps walked per day.

Whatever the thinking may have been before, we now have built-in live step tracking on the Apple Watch face. And the result? For me at least, it’s a surprisingly motivating number to view so far.

While I most appreciate live heart rate data for real-time insight, I’m finding that little step tracking number to be most beneficial when I start my day. It’s basically a race to get out of the hundreds and into the thousands. Otherwise that triple-digit number is just staring me down all day. 

My current strategy is to knock out a 16-minute rolling hills workout on my GymKit-equipped BowFlex T6 treadmill early in the day. This adjusts incline up and down, allowing me to focus on speed and a fixed session time. The sooner I knock out the mile run, the more time for a cooldown walk afterwards.

It’s also just really satisfying to watch the number increase as you walk, even if you’re not logging a workout. It’s a small thing, but it’s a welcome new way to gamify increasing your activity, especially if you’re anchored to a desk for much of the day.

title: Apple Intelligence has 20+ brand new features in iOS 27, here’s the full list
snippet: iOS 27 is here, and many of its new features are powered by the next generation of Apple Intelligence. Here are 20+ new Apple Intelligence features in iOS 27. more…
fullText:
iOS 27 is here, and many of its new features are powered by the next generation of Apple Intelligence. Here are 20+ new Apple Intelligence features in iOS 27.

Siri AI

Siri gets its long-awaited AI overhaul in iOS 27. Apple rebuilt the assistant from the ground up for the LLM era, and it’s a major upgrade. Here’s an overview of the new features per Apple:

Broad world knowledge: Get answers to almost any question with broad world knowledge

Personal context understanding: Find what you need across Messages, Mail, Calendar, Notes, Reminders, and more with personal context understanding

Onscreen awareness: Ask about and act on what’s on your screen

App actions: Siri can get things done across your apps to send messages, create events, and more

Siri app: Pick up where you left off with the Siri app, which keeps your conversation history synced with iCloud across your Apple devices

Write with Siri: Describe what you need, and Siri can generate a draft from scratch, edit what you’ve written, or give you feedback—virtually anywhere you type

Visual Intelligence: Integrated with Siri and upgraded with new features

Expressive voices: Customize pace and expressiveness on compatible hardware

Apps with new and improved AI features

Apple Intelligence has been baked into more system apps in iOS 27, bringing all-new capabilities to the apps you use every day. Here’s what’s new per Apple:

Photos: Spatial Reframing; Extend; Improved Clean Up

Messages: Personalized Smart Reply

Calendar: Describe a calendar event in natural language

Reminders: Describe a reminder in natural language

Mail: Suggestions; Personalized Smart Reply

Safari: Notify Me; Describe an Extension; Organize tabs by topics

Shortcuts: Describe a shortcut in natural language

Image Playground: Redesigned app with new, realistic image generation; wallpaper creation

Files: Intelligent file and folder name suggestions

Home: Combining related activity notifications; HomeKit Secure Video AI Search and Captions

Journal: Customized writing prompts in Journal entries

Systemwide Apple Intelligence features

Finally, iOS 27 introduces a handful of new AI features that apply systemwide. They include:

title: Googlebook OS hands-on: It’s Android, stupid
snippet: An overwhelming sense of familiarity struck me the first time I used a Googlebook. That was immediately followed by a realization that this is just Android, and I think that feeling of similarity will go a long way in justifying and ultimately selling Googlebooks. more…
fullText:
An overwhelming sense of familiarity struck me the first time I used a Googlebook. That was immediately followed by a realization that this is just Android, and I think that feeling of similarity will go a long way in justifying and ultimately selling Googlebooks.

Going into this event, I was not particularly asking for a desktop operating system that felt like my Pixel phone. In fact, having used Chromebooks for many years (my first unit was the 2013 Acer C720), I thought Googlebook OS would not feel too different from ChromeOS. The desktop and app dock look the same, but the changes made by building on top of Android make all the difference.

That shared design and user experience allowed me to immediately start using Googlebook OS like a near-expert. Quick Settings and Notifications were obviously in the top-right corner, matching Android’s conventions. It’s a small change compared to ChromeOS, but it felt natural the first time I used it. I knew immediately to move the cursor to that top corner instead of the usual bottom corner on Chromebooks.

I also knew I could add and edit widgets, a long-requested feature ChromeOS lacks, by long-pressing on the desktop, while seeing the same ones from my phone homescreen evoked an almost nostalgia-like feeling.

	

The Settings app is identical to that on Pixel phones, while I was very happy to find Pixel Weather (and its widgets) along with the excellent Recorder pre-installed. Meanwhile, the app drawer is basically the Pixel Launcher. Compared to ChromeOS, you can put apps, widgets, and files/folders on the desktop for an infinite boost to productivity.

The best of the web 

Given how much Googlebook OS felt like using my Pixel phone, it was surprising to see that launching Gmail and Google Calendar opened the web versions rather than the Android apps. Talking with Google, I later learned that these were Trusted Web Activities (TWAs) instead of PWAs. Distributed from the Play Store, their main advantage is how this web wrapper-esque format allows for homescreen widgets.  

Zooming out, what shocked me was how much Googlebook OS leverages web apps, a move that strongly affirms the ChromeOS lineage. Going in, I assumed there would be a resurgence in desktop-class Android apps. 

However, I am told this was an intentional choice. Google’s viewpoint is ultimately to let app developers decide what the best strategy is for their application, and I think that’s fair. Google offered me the example of how it approached the Gmail and Workspace teams about whether they wanted to offer Googlebook adopters the web version or the Android app. They chose the former and ideally did not want to offer the Android app as an available Play Store download.

However, I do think this is partially a missed opportunity. Giving third-party developers a choice does reduce the barrier to entry for a new OS, but I strongly think Google internally should have enforced a strict first-party mandate to create desktop-class applications. 

Meanwhile, as I complained about in my Pixel Tablet review three years ago, it’s unbelievable that Google Messages is still using the same web-based version rather than anything more native. 

The Chrome browser on Googlebooks feels great and offers a full-featured experience from extensions to the new vertical tab list.

For all Android, always

That said, other experiences are clearly Android-powered. This includes the Google app and Gemini. When you invoke the Magic Pointer overlay, prompt responses appear in the Android Gemini app.

More broadly, Google sees this Android-based OS as an opportunity to leverage the existing Gemini and AI work done for phones as a starting point for the desktop. This is compared to having to rebuild everything from scratch for ChromeOS.

The on-device AI model is Gemini Nano, and that’s used to power AI descriptions of your screenshots that unlock search, as well as Magic Pointer, Rambler, and Create My Widget via a hybrid intelligence architecture.

I have to use the much-derided Magic Pointer a bit more to determine whether it’s some groundbreaking UX paradigm, but I do credit it for being very easy to enable. You will not forget that this feature exists on Googlebooks, and I think that could be valuable.

Rambler is the other major Gemini Intelligence feature, and you launch it from a Quick Insert key that’s in place of Caps Lock. Pressing the new Quick Insert key launches a rather convenient floating window that provides quick access to emoji, recent screenshots, and the Gboard clipboard, with Rambler in the bottom-right corner. This is a rather smart carryover from ChromeOS, now accessible with a single key press rather than a three-key combo.

Create My Widget is the other major tentpole. This is the introduction of generative UI to Android, and I think the ramifications for the future are tremendous. Right now, you get to make widgets that pull from live data sources, like Search. Googlebooks will definitely have to guide people on how to use this capability, but I think this could be a powerful selling point.

Google is adopting the successful Android OEM model for Googlebooks. However, they’ve fortunately drawn a line on how updates will work. Google is responsible for rolling out Googlebook OS updates, not OEMs, carrying over one of the strongest elements of ChromeOS. Partners will be able to specify preloaded apps, but they can’t do any heavy customization like altering what the status bar icons look like. The experience of using a Googlebook will be universal across partners. 

Google will be releasing major Googlebook OS updates on a quarterly basis to match the Android Quarterly Platform Release (QPR) model, but security updates can come at any time in between. 

Closing

Google spent a long time developing Googlebooks, and it shows. The specific example that really surprised me is that Google built an Antigravity app with native UI for Android. Going in, I thought they would just offer the Linux version, but this Antigravity for Android is distributed via the Play Store and interacts with the Linux terminal environment on Googlebook OS.

Frankly, Google fumbled its initial unveiling of Googlebooks in May. It was officially intended only as a preview, but the decision to highlight only a handful of features, including Magic Pointer, ended up being a great disservice. Googlebook OS is so much more than that, and the company should have led with the Android nature right off the bat.

Again, we actually have to see if it works in our daily workflows, but my initial impression is that Android gives Googlebooks a very solid foundation.

title: Here’s everything new for Messages in iOS 27
snippet: iOS 27 adds new features across many system apps, like Wallet, Calendar, Music, and Maps. Here’s what’s new for the Messages app in iOS 27. more…
fullText:
iOS 27 adds new features across many system apps, like Wallet, Calendar, Music, and Maps. Here’s what’s new for the Messages app in iOS 27.

’Drawing’ iMessage app

The Messages app gets a new ‘Drawing’ iMessage app in iOS 27 for sending sketches and handwritten notes.

In any other year, the new iMessage app might be a curious addition. But ahead of the iPhone Duo, it’s very obvious why the ‘Drawing’ app exists.

Apple’s latest iMessage app contains the same basic set of Markup tools you’ll find across the Notes app, Preview, and more, letting you send a quick doodle to your friends.

Any iPhone can use the new app, but it will no doubt prove especially useful on the iPhone Duo with an Apple Pencil.

RCS messaging upgrades

When messaging with your green bubble friends via RCS, iOS 27 adds some welcome upgrades.

In-line replies are now available, so you can reply to an RCS message just like an iMessage and see the same basic UI.

Tapback reactions are now properly supported in iOS 27 too. That means Android users won’t see tapbacks appear as annoying “Ryan loved an image” messages. Instead, they’ll just see the heart, thumbs up, or other reaction.

The RCS 2.7 standard, which both of these changes belong to, also includes the ability to edit and unsend messages. So we may get those RCS upgrades in iOS 27 or a subsequent update too.

One-tap suggestions

Apple Intelligence enables new ‘one-tap suggestions’ in the Messages app that can help you get things done or find relevant information to share.

From Apple’s press release:

Messages offers one-tap suggestions based on the context of users’ conversations, making it easier than ever to get things done, such as creating a reminder or a note. For example, if someone asks for photos, Messages can also help users find the right ones, recognizing keywords, locations, and people in their library to find the best options.

As seen in the image above, these suggestions will sometimes appear right below a message they’re relevant to, and sometimes they’ll appear in the top keyboard row.

Availability note: Suggestions were available in the iOS 27 beta all summer, but got pulled from the shipping version. Apple says they’ll return in a future update, hopefully very soon.

Miscellaneous new features and changes

Here are four more miscellaneous iOS 27 changes in Messages:

A new setting lets you optionally disable the audio button that’s normally on the right side of the active message field. Go to Settings ⇾ Apps ⇾ Messages ⇾ Show in Text Field to choose between ‘Record Audio,’ ‘Start Dictation,’ and ‘None.’

Consolidated notifications for multiple tapbacks will help keep your alerts from getting out of control.

Smart Reply suggestions that appear in the top keyboard row are now informed by a user’s personalized writing style, so they’ll be more useful in iOS 27.

For child accounts, Messages will automatically detect and block gore or violent content when it’s found in shared images or videos.

Performance improvements and refinements

The idea of bug fixes in a major new OS version may not sound the most exciting. But Apple has done a lot of work to make the Messages app perform better than ever, and the promised refinements sound significant.

Here’s what Apple says is newly improved in iOS 27:

Failed messages automatically retry sending

Faster message loading

Faster syncing across devices

Thumbnails display for offloaded media

Find offloaded media in Messages

Continuous sending of photos, videos, and texts in Messages

Search for conversations by phone number or contact’s nickname

title: Roku adding new apps & subscription bundles, homescreen redesign expanding
snippet: Roku is rolling out a collection of updates, including a wider release of its homescreen redesign, new “Labs” features, and the ability to bundle streaming service subscriptions to save money. more…
fullText:
Roku is rolling out a collection of updates, including a wider release of its homescreen redesign, new “Labs” features, and the ability to bundle streaming service subscriptions to save money.

Available “soon,” Roku Labs is a new way for viewers to test experimental apps on their TV. This includes a new “Roku City Dash” game that was first announced earlier this year, as well as first-party Roku apps for Stocks, Weather, and a customizable “Backdrops Studio” with custom screensaver artwork.

Beyond Labs, Roku is also more widely rolling out its redesigned homescreen. Available first in the US back in May, the updated look is now heading to Brazil and Mexico with some regional tweaks. Roku OS is also getting improved search with smarter, more personalized content recommendations. You can also use voice commands for more than just content, with new capabilities such as showing weather previews.

Roku is also making LT OS, the operating system for its remote, open-source.

	

Perhaps the biggest new addition, though, is being able to purchase streaming service subscription bundles from Roku. These bundles include “over 30 combinations” using services such as AMC+, Fox One, Starz, and more. Roku says you can save up to 30%.

Your favorite subscriptions are now available in convenient bundles with Premium Subscriptions on Roku in the U.S. and Mexico. With over 30 combinations in the U.S. from services like AMC+, FOX One, Hallmark+, Howdy®, and STARZ, each bundle offers savings of up to 30% compared to a la carte subscriptions. Like all Premium Subscriptions, bundles are discoverable across the Roku platform, including within the Subscriptions Destination, Streaming Store, Premium Subscriptions Home, and more. Users also have the flexibility to easily change their subscriptions anytime, right on their Roku device or online.

Subscription bundles are available in the US and Mexico.

title: Apple is taking a little bit of a gamble with iPhone Duo software: Will it pay off?
snippet: With the new iPhone Duo, Apple is taking a little bit of a software gamble. All apps, in order to take advantage of the larger inner display of iPhone Duo, will need to be recompiled for iOS 27.0 at a minimum. To use the Duo’s unique new tab bar and other UI components, you’ll need iOS 27.1. Of course, this means a lot of developers will have to rebuild to support the Duo. On the flip side, it also means Apple is taking a risk of many apps on iPhone Duo being stuck in black bars. more…
fullText:
With the new iPhone Duo, Apple is taking a little bit of a software gamble. All apps, in order to take advantage of the larger inner display of iPhone Duo, will need to be recompiled for iOS 27.0 at a minimum. To use the Duo’s unique new tab bar and other UI components, you’ll need iOS 27.1.

Of course, this means a lot of developers will have to rebuild to support the Duo. On the flip side, it also means Apple is taking a risk of many apps on iPhone Duo being stuck in black bars.

One obvious solution would’ve been for Apple to allow iPad binaries that support resizing to run on iPhone Duo. The compromise here is that it’d likely feel a little more janky. Many developers would also likely take longer to support the iPhone Duo interface elements if they had a compatibility layer.

I get why Apple didn’t do that, because the interface they designed for iPhone Duo is genuinely intuitive, and it makes it feel like a lot of care went into the product. If Apple supported resizable iPad apps, it’d feel a lot more like any other Android foldable.

That said, you have to wonder how long some developers will take to at least compile for iOS 27. Compiling for iOS 27 doesn’t just mean you have to support the Duo, but it also means you’ll no longer have the compatibility option to opt-out of supporting Liquid Glass. For developers who haven’t prepared, the latter likely means many will drag their feet on iPhone Duo updates.

Seeing as you can split screen apps on the Duo, apps not fully expanding on the inside display might not be the biggest deal. That is, if Apple supports split screen with non-native apps.

However, for mobile gaming, a use case I’m sure will be very popular on the inside screen on the iPhone Duo, not having a proper full screen experience would be a major deterrent for many users.

I do hope Apple’s efforts to encourage developers to support the Duo’s interface work out, though I do genuinely worry. Obviously, we’ll see how things pan out with enough time.

Worst case scenario, Apple could simply add an iPad app compatibility mode to iPhone Duo in iOS 28, as a means of improving the experience for users while also getting all of the initial wave of support.

I am genuinely excited for iPhone Duo, though Apple’s gamble on getting third party developers to support Liquid Glass and the Duo at the same time might cause a rough experience for the first few months.

title: The Best Way to Discard Frying Oil? Don’t
snippet: An expert explains how to prepare used oil for a future cooking again.
fullText:
There’s no denying the appeal of deep-fried foods, from donuts to drumsticks, plus numerous bite-sized appetizers and every kind of potato. But when it comes to whether to bother deep-frying at home, it isn’t necessarily a matter of difficulty. With the right vessel and thermometer, frying can be a quick, easy way to make memorable dishes — the real issue is: what to do with all that leftover oil?

Shallow frying can also get the job done in many cases, but it can also create a conundrum. Putting that oil down the sink? Potentially drain-clogging, environmentally dubious, and frankly, wasteful. I grew up in a household where leftover grease and oil went into a glass mayonnaise jar kept under the sink, to be discarded once it was full. Sure, this saves the sink, but it doesn’t address the other two issues. It’s a quick kitchen hack that makes it easier to put it out with food waste, but there’s also another solution.

Leftover frying oil is begging to be reused.Pamela Vachon/CNET

Don’t get rid of it. “Oil used for frying is not one and done,” says Melanie Underwood, cookbook author, culinary instructor, and founder of Nourish and Gather, “unless the oil has been overheated, or if you’re frying things that are particularly strong in flavor. With something like seafood, you want to be careful, but it’s perfectly reusable as long as it wasn’t smoking.”

With that, Underwood shares her best practices and advice for reusing oil multiple times before it’s done.

Manage the oil before and during the frying process

A proper frying temperature is between 350 and 400 F.Pamela Vachon/CNET

To ensure oil is good for multiple uses, first make sure you’re using the right oil — something neutral in flavor with a high smoke point. “Any vegetable oil, such as canola oil, peanut oil or sunflower oil, is best for frying,” says Underwood. While olive oil can be tricky to fry with because it has a lower smoke point, “I definitely have used olive oil,” she says, “and I have never had any problem with it whatsoever.”

Resist the impulse to eyeball your oil for temperature clues, or test bits and pieces to make sure you’re in the right zone, unless you fry so regularly that it’s second nature. Otherwise, that’s a recipe for pieces with burnt exteriors and undercooked interiors, and/or smoking out your upstairs neighbors. (Speaking from experience, sadly.) Using a thermometer, “the correct range for frying is usually between 350 to 400,” says Underwood, which prevents smoking.

Just a bit of residue, which you can easily skim off.Pamela Vachon/CNET

During the frying process, it’s a great idea if you can skim out any crumbs or whatever has come off in the oil,” she says, “because when you have little burned pieces, that will degrade the oil faster.”

After frying: cool, strain, and store

Cool, strain and store.Pamela Vachon/CNET

Once you’re done frying, managing the oil for future use is simple. “First, you let it cool,” says Underwood. Don’t try to speed up the process by refrigerating it; just let it sit until it cools to room temperature.

Straining it is also straightforward and can be done with whatever you already have on hand. “I use a fine mesh strainer,” Underwood says. “People also use cheesecloth or a coffee filter. You just want to strain it and get out all those teeny particles.” Some micro particles may still be visible in the oil after straining, but they will settle once the oil is stored, and it is easy to prevent them from transferring into a pot the next time you want to use it.

Finally, Underwood suggests transferring the oil to a clean and dry container. “It’s very important that it doesn’t have any residual water in it,” she says, “and then just put a lid on it, tightly sealed, and keep it away from heat and light.” If you don’t plan to use it immediately, you can store it in the refrigerator, but any place with a consistent temperature and away from light works.

Considerations for reusing oil

Microparticles may still remain, but will settle during storage.Pamela Vachon/CNET

There’s nothing special that needs doing in order to use preused oil the next time, but bear one thing in mind: “Just be aware that it would now carry allergens from anything that you previously cooked in it,” says Underwood, which is essential to know if you’re cooking for other people.

Since that can be hard to track over multiple uses, “Always label and date it,” she suggests. “I just put a piece of tape on it with the date and the number of uses. And I also actually put what was fried in it,” she says, which can help keep track of potential allergens.

Store in a clear, dry jar with a tight-fitting lid.Pamela Vachon/CNET

It also helps keep potentially odd flavors out of whatever you cook next, as certain items like seafood or onion rings can impart flavor into the oil. “I don’t typically like to fry a savory thing and then fry a sweet thing,” says Underwood. “Like I wouldn’t make schnitzel and then use that oil for a donut.” 

If you’re unsure whether an oil is still good to use, let your nose guide you to suss out if something is funky. If you’re not confident in your sniffing ability, Underwood advises smelling unused oil of the same type first, then smelling the used oil for comparison. You can use frying oil at least two or three times, maybe more if it was only used for light-flavored things that didn’t impart many particles and was never overheated.

Read more: An Expert Explains When to Use Certain Cooking Oils

Benefits of reusing oil

The biggest benefit of reusing frying oil is the savings in every possible regard — you save money, and it’s a much more environmentally friendly practice across the board. “When you’re reusing any product, then you’re lowering the demand for things like production, packaging and transport,” Underwood says. “I don’t think that we think about that big picture very much, but if we were all reusing it, it would reduce those demands on the environment.”

Each time you reuse oil, it also diminishes in volume a bit. In my experience, at least with shallow frying, you can use the same batch of oil until, after a few uses, nothing remains to discard — the ultimate win.

				

					

						

													

					

					

						

Pamela Vachon
						

						

							Contributor						
					

											

								

											Pamela is a freelance food and travel writer based in Astoria, Queens. While she writes about most things edible and potable (and accessories dedicated to those topics,) her real areas of expertise are cheese, chocolate, cooking and wine. She's a culinary school grad, certified sommelier, former bartender and fine dining captain with 10 years in the industry. When not sitting at the keys, she leads in-home cheese classes, wine tastings and cocktail demonstrations.

title: iOS 27.2 gives Apple TV a new profiles feature on iPhone
snippet: iOS 27.2 beta 1 arrived today, and with it a key new feature for the Apple TV app on iPhone: user profiles. more…
fullText:
iOS 27.2 beta 1 arrived today, and with it a key new feature for the Apple TV app on iPhone: user profiles.

iOS 27.2 brings Apple TV profiles to iPhone, a great feature for parents

User profiles are a common feature in the streaming era, but Apple TV has been slow to adopt them.

You’ve been able to set up and switch between different profiles in tvOS for a few years now. But it was only last December with tvOS 26.2 that two key upgrades shipped:

the ability to create profiles for users without an Apple Account, like a young child

kid profiles being limited to age-appropriate content

Those were great changes that were long overdue. But they only worked on TV-based devices, not more personal products like the iPhone.

iOS 27.2 changes that though, bringing support for Apple TV user profiles to the iPhone.

When you launch the Apple TV app in iOS 27.2 beta 1, you’ll see a screen with existing profiles tied to your account. There’s also the option to add a profile.

And before you ask: there is also a button that reads, ‘Don’t Show This Again.’ So if you never want to use profiles on your iPhone, there’s an easy fix.

Like in tvOS, if you select a child’s profile on your iPhone, their TV app will be limited to only TV shows and movies that match the permitted content rating you’ve specified.

For users who ever hand a child their iPhone or iPad to watch TV, the addition of profiles not only ensures that your ‘Continue Watching’ won’t be cluttered by children’s content, it also provides a safer environment for them to only watch appropriate options.

Are you glad to see Apple TV add user profiles in iOS 27.2? Let us know in the comments.

title: Here’s why Apple scrapped its shorter Apple Pencil designed for iPhone Duo: report
snippet: Leading into the iPhone Duo launch, we heard from Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman that Apple was considering a new Apple Pencil for iPhone Duo, though it was unlikely that the company would go forward with it. Of course, the iPhone Duo keynote came, and Apple did announce support for the USB-C Apple Pencil. Here’s how that happened. more…
fullText:
Leading into the iPhone Duo launch, we heard from Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman that Apple was considering a new Apple Pencil for iPhone Duo, though it was unlikely that the company would go forward with it. Of course, the iPhone Duo keynote came, and Apple did announce support for the USB-C Apple Pencil. Here’s how that happened.

Apple Pencil support was reportedly always on the roadmap for iPhone Duo, and the company had designed the product to be compatible. That said, the company had initially planned to build a new Apple Pencil for the Duo. It would’ve been smaller and attached to the hinge side of the iPhone Duo.

According to Bloomberg, that pencil ran into “technical problems” prior to mass production, so the company scrapped it and went with the traditional USB-C Apple Pencil.

After the keynote, you might’ve noticed on Apple’s website that Apple Pencil support won’t be available on iPhone Duo at launch. That delay is a result of the fact that the product wasn’t initially designed with the USB-C Apple Pencil in mind, and Apple still needs to test it thoroughly:

But getting the iPad Pencils to work on the iPhone Duo isn’t as simple as hitting a button to enable support. Apple has to roll out new software to make them compatible and run loads of internal tests. That process is now underway within Apple, with the company — as it said during the Duo unveiling — believing that support will be ready by the end of the year. I would take that literally: It will be fairly late in 2026.

It’s not quite clear if the technical problems with the new Apple Pencil design are with the Apple Pencil, or if it’s with the iPhone Duo being able to magnetically charge it. If it’s the former, it’s certainly possible that Apple will still debut the accessory at a later date.

title: Anthropic merging Claude Cowork with chat
snippet: Anthropic announced today that Claude Cowork is being merged with chat. This means Claude will drop from three to two modes: Claude Chat and Claude Code. more…
fullText:
Anthropic announced today that Claude Cowork is being merged with chat. This means Claude will drop from three to two modes: Claude Chat and Claude Code.

The company says the change will roll out over the next few weeks for Pro and Max subscribers. 

Here’s the announcement from Anthropic:

Starting today, Claude Cowork and chat are merging into one Claude. Bring a quick question, or hand over a report due at noon, and Claude takes it from there, even after you’ve closed your laptop. It’s rolling out on Pro and Max plans over the next few weeks, with more plans to follow.

Additionally, Claude’s main view is adding or integrating these features as well:

Claude Docs and Claude Slides are new today, and Claude Design now works inside your conversations too. 

As for why the change is happening, here’s what the company says:

We built Cowork as a separate place for bigger work, and Design for visual work. People used both, and told us the frustrating part was deciding where a task belonged. What they’d started in one also didn’t carry into the other. So we stopped making you choose. Claude can now figure out what a task needs, so what Cowork and Design can do is available from any conversation, with the context, skills, and connectors you already have.

As mentioned, the change isn’t happening overnight. Instead, here’s what to expect:

This is rolling out to Pro and Max plans first, in the Claude app on web, desktop, and mobile over the coming weeks to existing and new users on these plans. There’s nothing to turn on. Team and Free plans will follow soon, and Enterprise admins will hear from us at least 30 days before anything changes for their organizations.

title: Apple Watch Series 12 has subtle design change that Apple didn’t mention
snippet: Apple Watch Series 12 arrives this Friday (pre-order here), but some upgraders might be surprised by a subtle design change that Apple didn’t mention in its announcement: larger bezels around the display. more…
fullText:
Apple Watch Series 12 arrives this Friday (pre-order here), but some upgraders might be surprised by a subtle design change that Apple didn’t mention in its announcement: larger bezels around the display.

Apple Watch Series 12 has slightly larger case size for increased bezels around display

If you track the history of Apple product design, one clear trend is that the company likes to reduce bezels around the display as much as possible.

Over time, the iPhone, iPad, Mac, and Apple Watch have all progressively shrunk the bezels for a design that puts all focus on the display.

But with Apple Watch Series 12, the reverse is happening as bezels increase slightly.

Per Apple’s website, here’s the breakdown of case sizes for Series 12 compared to the last two models:

Series 12

Series 11

Series 10

42mm

42mm by 37mm

42mm by 36mm

42mm by 36mm

46mm

46mm by 40mm

46mm by 39mm

46mm by 39mm

As you can see, while Apple Watch Series 12 has the same case height as its predecessors, the width is slightly larger. Per this comparison page though, all three models have the same display sizes. 

42mm: 374 by 446 pixels with 970 sq mm display area

46mm: 416 by 496 pixels with 1196 sq mm display area

What this means is that compared to previous models, Apple Watch Series 12’s display is slightly undersized for its larger case size. As a result, it has more noticeable bezels around the display.

Series 12 packs a ton of internal upgrades, like the new Health Sensing System and S11 chip. So it’s unsurprising that the case size would need to change some.

But if you’re upgrading from a recent Apple Watch model, just know that the design might look like a small step backwards rather than following the standard trend of shrinking bezels.

What do you think of Apple’s decision to increase bezel size on Apple Watch Series 12? Let us know in the comments.

title: I Toured the Company Mapping Space Debris. Then I Polled Worried and Hopeful Scientists
snippet: From portable radars in shipping containers to orbital cameras, I asked scientists how the space-junk tracking industry plans to avoid catastrophic crashes.
fullText:
Walking inside LeoLabs’ new space radar nestled in the Maui hills felt like entering a computer. Wires dangled overhead, servers whined, and the temperature climbed in the metal box as the air conditioning leaked out when we entered. 

“You don’t want to be in there when the whole thing’s running,” said Matthew Adelman, LeoLabs’ senior manager of radar systems. “Not just for the safety, but also for the noise.”

LeoLabs’ Scout-S radar is designed to be transported and setup within hours anywhere in the world. Allyza Umali/CNET

Called Scout-S, this radar designed to track space objects is the size of a 20-foot shipping container and can be transported anywhere in the world. You can hook it up to an electrical grid and fiber internet, but its real calling card is portability. You could drop the Scout-S off-grid and have it running in a couple of hours. All you need is a generator and a Starlink dish to feed the radar’s data back to a computer.

I couldn’t help but appreciate the irony at the mention of the Starlink dish: The satellite internet service revolutionized the space industry, but it also jump-started a race to space that created the need for transportable radars like the Scout-S. 

The Soviet Union launched the world’s first satellite in 1957; it would take another 53 years for the population to pass 1,000. When Starlink launched its first satellite in 2019, there were still only around 2,000 orbiting Earth. Today, we’re at 16,810, and nearly 2 out of every 3 belong to Starlink. 

Each one of them is zooming above us at 17,000 mph. A collision between two of them could range from extremely troubling to catastrophic. Worst-case scenario, satellites colliding with each other or a piece of space debris could set off a feedback loop known as Kessler syndrome, in which one collision creates thousands of new pieces of debris that cause yet more collisions. It could ultimately make low Earth orbit, or LEO, the sweet spot where Starlink beams down fast, low-latency internet from 342 miles over our heads, so filled with space junk that it’s no longer usable. 

“We worry a lot about it because we have seen that in the last few years, the number of spacecraft has increased exponentially, and we are not stopping it,” said Lorenzo Olivieri, a professor at the University of Padova. I spoke with him this week at the Advanced Maui Optical and Space Surveillance Technologies Conference, where he was presenting a paper on space debris populations from break-up events.

“The worrisome idea of the Kessler syndrome could be a real close future,” Olivieri said. 

Exactly how worried you should be about a Kessler syndrome-like scenario depends on who you ask. When I polled scientists at AMOS, their answers ran the gamut. Some said it’s only a matter of time if we stay on our current trajectory, while others waved it off as the domain of science fiction. (See the 2013 movie Gravity for a particularly vivid dramatization.)

But you don’t have to be a Kessler syndrome pessimist to take crowded orbits seriously. Whether you’re a satellite operator looking to avoid collisions or the US military deploying space weapons, everyone at AMOS wants to know what’s going on in the skies. The industry, referred to as space situational awareness, is estimated to reach $1.9 billion this year. 

Aside from dodging millions of pieces of satellite-killing debris, operators also have to communicate with each other about where and when they’ll be moving. It’s an enormous challenge: How do you get adversarial nations and competing companies to agree on appropriate behavior in space? 

“Driving on the highway would be terrifying if everyone had their eyes closed,” Gabriel Swiney, the director of policy at the US Department of Commerce’s Office of Space Commerce, told me. “The problem is communication and knowledge.”

The issues circulating the AMOS conference were as terrifying as space lasers and as mundane as standardizing space data for easier sharing. 

I was almost ready to write off these topics as niche industry concerns when I pulled my phone out to get directions back to my hotel. A GPS satellite zooming 12,550 miles over my head instantly showed me where I was and needed to go. 

Key takeaways 

Orbital congestion: Nearly 17,000 active satellites raise serious concerns about potential orbital collisions and Kessler syndrome.

Tracking technology: Ground-based portable radars and in-orbit cameras monitor space debris, though tracking objects under 10 centimeters remains difficult.

Communication barriers: The main obstacle to space safety is the lack of open data sharing among competing entities and adversarial nations.

Traffic cameras for the skies

One engineer at AMOS described space awareness to me as having three stages: collection, processing and analysis. Many of the companies hawking their wares at the conference dabbled in multiple phases, but for the most part, they specialized in one of these buckets.

LeoLabs, the company that developed the transportable Scout-S radar, is primarily in the collection business. It has a dozen radar sites around the world, some of which can detect debris as small as 10 centimeters – a dangerous blind spot for most trackers.

“Think about the busy part of Seattle,” says Darren McKnight, senior technical fellow at LeoLabs. “If you have two traffic cameras, you don’t really know what route to take. You want traffic cameras at all the major intersections.”

It’s not always tiny pieces of debris — sometimes companies are even trying to find their own satellites up there. SpaceX, the company that operates Starlink, landed its reusable Falcon 9 rocket for the first time in 2015, kicking off a wave of “rideshare” launches. 

Some of these had as many as 140 payloads, making it a challenge for satellite operators to even determine which ones were theirs. 

“Once the first rideshare launch became a thing, that just exploded the number of things in orbit pretty quickly,” said Belinda Marchand, chief scientist at Slingshot Aerospace. “It was no longer just one launch vehicle and one object. It was one launch vehicle and a hundred.”

LeoLabs’ traffic cameras are all based on the ground, but other companies use cameras in orbit to give them a more detailed account of what’s happening in space.

“We use cameras that are in space to take pictures of other satellites in space,” said Hilary Cohen, director of operations at HEO USA. “There are trackers that track the dots and you know exactly where those satellites are. But this lets us go a layer deeper.”

This photo from an HEO space camera shows a solar panel in an abnormal configuration.HEO USA

Google Maps for satellites

But even if companies and countries do a good job of gathering information about their orbital goods, sharing it with other operators is an entirely different challenge. The key piece of information that everyone needs is called “ephemeris,” which lists the position and velocity of an object in orbit.

“Ephemeris basically is like my Google Maps,” McKnight said. “You’re sending it to everybody on the road with you and saying, ‘Here’s where I’m going to be.’”

The way scientists talked about ephemeris at AMOS sounded like castaways on deserted islands pleading for water. As good as the radars and space cameras have gotten, they don’t tell you when and where a satellite is planning on moving.

“Our community has an ephemeris sharing problem,” Jonathan Herman, senior director of Starlink Constellation Engineering, said at his keynote address. “The No. 1 risk in LEO is not debris. It is instead that operators don’t know where other satellites are going.”

A visualization from COMSPOC, a company that tracks objects in space, shows a Chinese satellite crossing orbits.COMSPOC

Herman noted that Starlink satellites perform around 1,000 collision-avoidance maneuvers per day, all of which consume valuable fuel and decrease the lifespan of the satellites. That number of maneuvers was described to me as “horrendously high” in a previous interview. 

It’s a double-edged sword: Starlink does an exceptional job at avoiding objects in space, but the fact that they have to move so much makes it harder for other operators to know where its satellites are going to be. 

Still, almost everyone I talked to at AMOS spoke about Starlink as a responsible steward of space. If you wanted an example of reckless behavior in orbit, there were much easier targets. 

The geopolitical barrier

Not all of the technical problems involving satellite maneuvering are particularly complex. Herman, the Starlink director, said they could be solved in a few hours by getting everyone in a room together. The bigger hurdle is communication. 

“We may understand at an operator-to-operator level what the best practices are, and the Chinese operators may understand that, too,” Audrey Schaffer, senior VP of global policy and government strategy, said on a panel. “But the challenge that we have is that the Chinese government is uncomfortable with their operators going directly to other operators.”

Commercial and defense domains in space are deeply interwoven. (I heard some version of the sentence, “Space is a warfighting domain,” at least a dozen times at AMOS.) If there’s a space company that doesn’t rely on military money at all, I didn’t find it here. 

“Within the last 18 months, we’ve seen a lot more open discussion of the importance of defense funding,” said Ian Christensen, senior director of private sector programs at the Secure World Foundation. “There’s been a real pivot towards defense funding as the most stable and largest source of funding.”

That tension between military and civilian operations was woven through many of the conversations I had at AMOS. This development hasn’t come out of nowhere – Elon Musk said over a year ago that Ukraine’s “entire front line would collapse if I turned it off” — but you could feel AMOS’ attendees on both the military and commercial sides grappling with the balance in real-time. 

“Russia’s actions consider every vendor here a legitimate target based on their cooperation with the US government and governments of NATO,” Col. Jonathan Whitaker, chief of staff of NATO’s Combined Forces Space Component Command, said at a panel. “When you take that perspective, there’s really no safe harbor for a commercial company.”

The bottom line

I walked away from AMOS feeling simultaneously comforted and pessimistic. As one person put it to me, there are around 40,000 tracked objects, but the island of Maui alone has about 184,000 registered vehicles. 

The reality is more complicated — there are an estimated 1.2 million objects in orbit the size of a softball or smaller that aren’t tracked – but it’s a fair point. As Elon Musk is fond of saying, “Space is really big.”

“What I worry about is not so much the number of objects, which do make easier headlines,” said Swiney, the director at the Office of Space Commerce. “The much harder problem to solve is, how do you get someone on the phone if you’re not allowed to talk to them, or if you don’t even know what their phone number is in the first place?

“The technical problems are relatively easy to solve if we can get past the policy.”

title: Gemini app for macOS adding send and read iMessage integration
snippet: Google’s latest update to the Gemini app for macOS readies local iMessage integration. This follows the app coming to Windows last week. more…
fullText:
Google’s latest update to the Gemini app for macOS readies local iMessage integration. This follows the app coming to Windows last week.

Gemini’s latest Connected App on the Mac is @messages to “Read, search, and send messages in Apple Messages.” Specifically, the integration can:

Send messages to contacts or phone numbers

Read recent conversations, unread messages, and search message history

This will aid context by being able to look up information from conversations. Example prompts include:

Send a message to John: “Running 5 minutes late!”

Show my recent messages from Sarah

Search Messages for dinner reservations

 In terms of limitations, Gemini cannot:

	

Manage group participant membership or change group chat photos

Schedule messages for future delivery or edit sent messages

Send file, photo, or media attachments (plain text messages only)

Send tapback reactions (love, like, dislike, laugh, emphasize, question)

Generate photos or images within automated task workflows

This integration appears in Settings > Connected Apps at the very bottom after updating to version 1.116.5.889 of Gemini for macOS. However, as of this afternoon, a server-side component appears to be missing, with @messages not yet recognized in the prompt box.

Recent updates to Gemini for macOS introduced a File Providers extension that shows “Add to Gemini” when you right-click on a file in Finder. This immediately adds the photo or document to the prompt box. It can be enabled in Settings > Extensions. Google also added Images, Videos, and Daily Brief to the side panel.

title: Apple VP of hardware talks iPhone Duo durability, crease, hinge, and more
snippet: Apple’s new Vice President of Hardware Engineering, Tom Marieb, sat down with TechRadar for an interview all about iPhone Duo. Here’s what he said about iPhone Duo’s durability, the hinge, display crease, and more. more…
fullText:
Apple’s new Vice President of Hardware Engineering, Tom Marieb, sat down with TechRadar for an interview all about iPhone Duo. Here’s what he said about iPhone Duo’s durability, the hinge, display crease, and more.

Apple put ‘blood, sweat, and tears’ into making iPhone Duo’s hinge durable and versatile, per interview

iPhone Duo will launch next month, bringing an all-new software experience to iPhone (see examples here) but also several hardware innovations.

Anyone interested in iPhone Duo may have questions about three key hardware features especially:

durability

the display crease (or lack thereof)

and the hinge

Today Axel Metz at TechRadar published quotes from an interview with Tom Marieb, the Apple’s new Vice President of Hardware Engineering. That’s the same role current CEO John Ternus once held.

The full interview is well worth a read, but here were some highlights.

When asked about the crease in iPhone Duo’s folding display, Marieb pointed to nano-texture as a great solution that he said would continue to minimize a visible crease even after extended use.

“Hold us accountable to that, please. The choice of a matte finish — apart from it being beautiful — is part of that equation. When you look at glossy displays, their specularity makes it very easy to pick up topology differences. That’s part of the reason we picked the matte finish — it’s not only beautiful in terms of preventing glare, but it’s also more forgiving of [hinge] changes over time.”

On the subject of iPhone Duo’s hinge, he said:

“We really worked on the torque profile very heavily, and that means changing a lot of the mechanical properties of the hinge to have it feel solid, like a high-end automobile’s car door, when you shut it. That was design intent, so people would have a feeling like, ‘Oh, it’s okay. This is well crafted, and it’s safe for me to use and not worry about it.’

And then, as you said, we have a lot of use cases where the Duo is [in a half-folded state]. And so we also had to think, ‘Can people interact with this [device] and not have it feel floppy?’ So getting those torque profiles right at both those ends, as well as in the middle — not having it feel like you’re pulling something open, and not feeling as if it’s floppy — we spent a lot of time optimizing that. So thank you for noticing, because a lot of blood, sweat, and tears went into that.”

Marieb also praised Ceramic Shield 2 as an incredible technology that makes third-party screen protectors unnecessary. He said, “Personally, when I see someone put a screen protector on their iPhone, it makes my skin crawl, because we work so hard to make beautiful front screens.”

You can read the full interview here on TechRadar.

title: Google rolls out Motion Assist bubbles to Pixel, Samsung
snippet: After announcing earlier this month, Google has rolled out Motion Assist to Pixel and Samsung phones running Android 17. more…
fullText:
After announcing earlier this month, Google has rolled out Motion Assist to Pixel and Samsung phones running Android 17.

The aim is to reduce motion sickness when you’re in a car, bus, or other moving vehicle with an onscreen bubbles overlay that adjusts to the device’s motion.

To enable, search for “motion assist” in the Settings app or open the Quick Settings editor and scroll down to “From system apps” (on Pixel). The long route is Settings app > Google > All services tab > Personal & device safety > Motion assist. Part of Google Play services, it appears alongside Advanced Protection and Theft protection.

This menu lets you have Motion Assist automatically “Start in a moving vehicle,” but Google also recommends adding a Quick Settings Tile to manually enable and disable “from any screen.” Once active, there’s also a silent system notification that lets you disable with a tap. On most phones, you get two columns of shapes on the left and right edges.

	

The Customize menu lets you adjust:

Color: Based on system (Dynamic Color), Red, Yellow, Green, Blue

Shape: Circle, Square, Pentagon, Diamond

Opacity: Slider

Randomization: “Color and shape change every few seconds”

As of today, Motion Assist has widely rolled out on all our Google Pixel and Samsung Galaxy (Fold 8 series) devices running Android 17. Be sure to restart your phone if it’s not yet live. We’re seeing the bubbles with version 26.33.32 of Google Play services.

title: Delayed Apple TV series ‘The Savant’ may finally air next year
snippet: If you cast your mind back to almost a year ago from today, Apple TV was about to launch a new series called The Savant starring Jessica Chastain … until it was pulled from the schedule at the last moment, in the wake of the assassination of political activist Charlie Kirk. Apple never gave an exact reason for cancelling the release, but promised it would release the series at a later date … more…
fullText:
If you cast your mind back to almost a year ago from today, Apple TV was about to launch a new series called The Savant starring Jessica Chastain … until it was pulled from the schedule at the last moment, in the wake of the assassination of political activist Charlie Kirk. 

Apple never gave an exact reason for cancelling the release, but promised it would release the series at a later date …

At the time, star Jessica Chastain made a statement to say that she was ‘not aligned’ with Apple’s decision to postpone the show’s premiere.

Nevertheless, here we are a year later, and The Savant has still not come out. In fact, if you look up the series in the Apple TV app, the page still reads “coming at a later date” and has an awkwardly outdated ‘2025’ year label. 

However, Variety reports today that the streamer has finally put the series back on its slate, with a release date scheduled for spring 2027.

The spring launch would aim to put the series in prime contention for the next Emmy awards season, which means Apple would want to get all episodes aired sometime before the cutoff date of May 31, 2027.

Of course, Apple could decide to once again delay the release when we get closer to springtime. Whatever Chastain’s thoughts are on how The Savant has been handled, the actress has continued to work with Apple on other upcoming projects, including starring in ‘The Dealer’ with Adam Driver, and alongside Ben Stiller in ‘The Off Weeks’.

title: Breville’s Wild New Toaster Swaps the Timer for Optic Sensors to Tell When Toast Is Done
snippet: The Eye Q may be too pricey for most households, but it’ll dazzle toast lovers with a padded budget.
fullText:
It may not seem like much, but a slice of toast is often the subtle touch a meal needs — one reason toasters remain a mainstay in many kitchens, even in the age of air fryers and toaster ovens. While it’s certainly a more convenient option than making toast in a pan, it’s not always easy to lock in your preferred doneness. Toasters typically monitor doneness in two ways: time and temperature.

That said, most people use one method, but few toasters use a third: visual doneness. Enter the recently launched Breville Eye Q 850 Auto Toaster. It uses a pulsing internal sensor to watch the color of the bread as it toasts, only finishing when it hits the perfect result, at least in theory. I put the theory to the test over the last month with a sample from Breville to see if this $300 high-tech toaster lives up to its promise. While I generally think it does, I noticed a few things that are worth considering. Let’s dig in.

	

			

	

			

									

						Breville Eye Q 850					

							

		

What makes the Breville Eye Q Auto Toaster different?

An optic sensor seems like a good way to ensure your toast always reaches the right doneness without tweaking settings between batches.John Carlsen/CNET

At first glance, the Breville Eye Q Auto Toaster looks like any other high-end toaster — my test sample featured a matte black brushed stainless steel case and a ceramic top portion. But the real magic happens when you start the toast cycle. The Eye Q lowers the bread, and a green light inside the toaster begins to flash. This Eye Q Optic Sensor reminds me of something you’d see on fitness trackers, but instead of tracking a pulse, it monitors the bread’s visual doneness.

The sensor is only in the left-side slot, so you can toast a single slice, which I think is very helpful. Importantly, the toaster won’t run without something inside, which is a great safety feature. Like most premium toasters, this Breville unit uses a motorized lift to lower and raise your bread. It won’t pop up with a spring-loaded mechanism as on a typical toaster. It will, however, play a little chime at the beginning and end of each toasting cycle — the volume is adjustable, so you can turn it off or up depending on your needs.

I found the controls fairly intuitive once I figured out how to activate each mode, like timer mode.John Carlsen/CNET

Five buttons on the unit start/stop the toasting process, adjust the doneness, toggle bagel and English muffin modes, and trigger a feature called A Bit More. Most notably, the start button selects the operation: One press toasts normal bread, a long press does the same for sourdough, and two presses switch on the timer mode for things like Pop-Tarts.

I’m a huge fan of the power cord storage slot on the bottom of the unit, which holds the cord when you need to put the toaster away. This saves you from having to wrangle the cord another way. The crumb tray is completely removable, making the Breville Eye Q Auto Toaster fairly easy to clean out. However, the tray isn’t dishwasher safe, so you’ll need to wipe off the old crumbs with a cloth instead. I doubt there’s much else to say about the tech in this toaster without digging into its performance, so let’s jump into my tests.

My time with the Breville Eye Q

Hitting the A Bit More button is an excellent way to finish toasting if it’s not quite perfect. It’s also a good option for folks who want to reheat forgotten toast that sat in the toaster too long, though you should expect it to get even more done.John Carlsen/CNET

Unlike an air fryer, a toaster isn’t a particularly versatile kitchen appliance. It makes toast, more toast, and the occasional Pop-Tart or frozen waffle. So this simplifies my testing, allowing me to focus on a few different types of bread — white, brown and sourdough — in addition to Pop-Tarts and frozen French toast (something I’ve long used my toaster to reheat).

I had a few problems with most of what I toasted. Aside from the darkest setting being a bit much for my usual preference, both white bread and sourdough turned out well across all of the doneness settings. I really liked the results for the sourdough using the corresponding setting, which was nice and crisp, despite not showing as much visual browning. I’m confident that the Eye Q Auto Toaster is perfectly suited for light-colored breads. 

I can’t say that the surface of the toast always browns evenly—one side generally sees less toasting than the other, but I’m happy with the results.John Carlsen/CNET

However, dark brown bread threw a curveball. The lowest setting was way too crispy, and I had to cancel the toasting on the second-lowest after smoke appeared. I’d previously tested some of the same dark bread in the toaster without issues, so it’s possible my continuous toasting session somehow threw off the accuracy for darker bread. I can’t say whether this would be a long-term issue, but it’s something to watch out for.

Beyond my tests with sliced bread, Pop-Tarts showed that the Timer Mode requires a little more attention and experimentation to get the results you want. At one point, I accidentally used the Auto Mode on Pop-Tarts, and they came out overdone, but not burned, so it’s probably best to stick to the timer or a low setting for toaster pastries. Reheating frozen French Toast went fairly smoothly, but I set the timer too short and had to retoast until the center was nice and hot. I imagine the experience would be similar for frozen waffles.

Should you buy the Breville Eye Q Auto Toaster?

If the choice came down to getting a toaster or an air fryer for $300, I’d choose the air fryer.John Carlsen/CNET

I’ll say it outright: the Breville Eye Q Auto Toaster is a fantastic toaster, but the $300 price tag is out of reach for budget-conscious households. If you want a more affordable standalone toaster, I recommend something like the $40 Cuisinart CPT-122, which has been a reliable workhorse in my home for years.

Similarly, you might check out the Breville BTA720XL, a solid mid-range model for around $110, even though it’s Breville’s most affordable option. That said, if you use a toaster daily and can afford something in the premium category, it’s worth considering, especially compared with the disappointing $450 Revolution Cooking R180 Connect Plus Smart Toaster.

title: iFixit tears down iPhone 18 Pro, explores variable aperture, finds concerning repair issue
snippet: iFixit has published its traditional teardown of the iPhone 18 Pro, which shows the variable aperture mechanism up close and explores a potential issue involving display repairs. Watch it below. more…
fullText:
iFixit has published its traditional teardown of the iPhone 18 Pro, which shows the variable aperture mechanism up close and explores a potential issue involving display repairs. Watch it below.

iFixit worries about possible display frame issue

iFixit’s teardown of the iPhone 18 Pro is now live, exploring not just the variable aperture, this year’s biggest camera upgrade, but also the device’s larger vapor chamber, the new under-display Face ID camera, and more.

When it comes to the variable aperture mechanism, iFixit notes that its six tiny blades are controlled by electromagnets, much like the optical image stabilization system, though the two mechanisms operate independently.

During the teardown, one of the tiny aperture blades flew out as iFixit dismantled the lens stack, underscoring how impractical a component-level repair would be. The group says that if the aperture gets stuck, it would likely require replacing the entire main camera assembly.

Another highlight of the new iPhone 18 Pro is its under-display Face ID infrared camera. For this year’s Pro devices, Apple moved the infrared camera beneath the display, while keeping the selfie camera and IR dot projector within the smaller Dynamic Island.

Under a microscope, iFixit found that Apple hides the relocated infrared camera by removing every other row of pixels above the sensor. iFixit notes that the effect fades toward the edges, and that there is an IR-pass filter beneath the OLED layer to block visible light.

Interestingly, the filter doesn’t extend all the way to the edge of the opening, creating what iFixit describes as an “eclipse effect” under certain microscope settings.

As for the iPhone 18 Pro’s bigger vapor chamber, the teardown offers a closer look at Apple’s redesigned cooling architecture.

As the company explained during its “Surprise and Shine” event, the A20 Pro uses a new package that places the silicon die side-by-side with the memory, removing the latter from the SoC’s thermal path and allowing the chip to connect directly to the vapor chamber. Apple also said the new vapor chamber has three times the surface area of the one in the iPhone 17 Pro.

iFixit’s teardown lets us see that setup up close, including the thermal material that presses the A20 Pro directly against the vapor chamber and the chamber itself extending across much of the phone’s body.

Now for the concerning part: iFixit says the plastic frame around the display was damaged on three of the four iPhones its team opened.

While the group notes that other iPhone 18 Pro teardowns haven’t encountered the same issue, and that Apple has been using this same plastic frame since the iPhone 15 Pro, it says it’s too early to tell whether this was an anomaly or a broader repairability concern.

iFixit also suggests that the device’s improved thermal system may be drawing heat away from the display as the heating pad tries to soften the adhesive.

Be that as it may, in practice, as iFixIt explains in the video, a cracked frame means the display may no longer sit perfectly flush after reassembly, and could compromise the phone’s water resistance.

Add to that the fact that some components remain difficult to reach, particularly the USB-C port, which iFixit says requires removing much of the phone’s internals to replace, and DIY repairs of the iPhone 18 Pro may prove challenging depending on which component needs replacing.

All in all, iFixit says the iPhone 18 Pro carries over many of the same repairability strengths and weaknesses as last year’s model, including the glue-free battery tray and modular camera assemblies, but also the need to enter through the display for most major repairs.

For now, the group has given both the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max a provisional repairability score of 7 out of 10 as it waits for parts, conducts more tests, and watches whether the display frame issue proves widespread.

title: Photographer Austin Mann reviews the iPhone 18 Pro camera
snippet: iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max bring several changes to the Main camera and iOS Camera app, and photographer Austin Mann has just published a great review of everything new. more…
fullText:
iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max bring several changes to the Main camera and iOS Camera app, and photographer Austin Mann has just published a great review of everything new.

Austin Mann publishes in-depth review of iPhone 18 Pro camera upgrades

Credit: Austin Mann using iPhone 18 Pro

Every year, photographer Austin Mann puts out an in-depth review of the iPhone’s new camera features—complete with plenty of photos, of course.

Mann’s review of the iPhone 18 Pro camera upgrades was published today. I highly recommend checking it out for an overview of the new features and sampling of photos they enable.

On the new variable aperture feature, Mann says:

I recommend leaving your aperture in Auto. The camera is very, very good at picking the best aperture for the scene, and it’s usually better at it than me. Inside at dinner? f/1.48, auto-selected. Outside with plenty of light and depth? It picks a higher f-stop to keep everything in focus.

He shares beautiful examples of iPhone 18 Pro’s new wider aperture capturing the Colorado sky at night.

Credit: Austin Mann using iPhone 18 Pro

Regarding the new Pro controls that are exclusive to iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max, Mann was especially excited to find Manual Focus:

One of the most-asked-for features by photographers has been the ability to separate exposure and focus, and now we can! All you do is set your focus manually (with focus peaking that works quite well!) and then tap where you want to expose.

In covering Photographic Styles 3, other reviewers like Tyler Stalman have highlighted the ability to create a film-like look with your photos. Mann echoes this and provides the following tips for the best film effect:

“Shoot dark, like -1.0, and shoot wide open at f/1.48. Use manual focus, which will make the image slightly softer (which is OK!).”

“Shoot HEIF so you can apply Photographic Styles.”

“Then in post, on the D-Pad, put the dot in the very lower right. This reduces the tone-mapping (aka the HDR look) and crunches your shadows and blows your highlights.”

“You can dial back the Film effect to reduce halation, which sometimes goes a bit overboard.”

You can watch Austin Mann’s video review below.

Also covered in Mann’s full review are features like Focus Tracking, Apple Reference Image, 4K time-lapse, and more.

title: Apple TV just dropped trailers for two upcoming premieres
snippet: Apple TV just kicked off a new season of Slow Horses, and plenty more premieres are coming soon, including a new movie and returning show that just got new trailers. more…
fullText:
Apple TV just kicked off a new season of Slow Horses, and plenty more premieres are coming soon, including a new movie and returning show that just got new trailers.

#1: Knife Edge: Chasing Michelin Stars (season 2)

Knife Edge: Chasing Michelin Stars is a culinary docuseries that first debuted last fall and has a new season coming very soon.

If you’re into The Bear, but want a real-world, nonfiction version of the show, Knife Edge might be the perfect fit. Its first season scored a BAFTA nomination for excellence in “Factual Entertainment.”

Knife Edge: Chasing Michelin Stars returns next Friday, September 25 for season 2.

Here’s Apple’s summary of the show, followed by its trailer:

Across season two, “Knife Edge: Chasing Michelin Stars” follows 16 restaurants at pivotal moments in their journeys: A chef and his family risk everything to put a tiny island on Michelin’s map. Two generations of a legendary culinary family pursue recognition on their own terms. Two chefs voluntarily give up their Star when they open a new restaurant and have just 52 days to win it back. One sandwich shop transforms into a fine dining restaurant each night, while a young couple seeks to put Filipino cuisine at the center of one of America’s most competitive dining scenes. Their circumstances could hardly be more different, yet each faces the same uncertainty: When Michelin makes its decision, will everything they have strived for be enough?

#2: Tenzing

Apple Original Films has a pair of movies coming this fall that have big award ambitions. The first of those titles is Tenzing.

The film hails from award-winning director Jennifer Peedom and stars Genden Phuntsok, Tom Hiddleston, Willem Dafoe, Caitríona Balfe, Thinley Lhamo, and Tenzin Dalha.

Tenzing hits select theaters on Friday, October 9 before streaming October 16 on Apple TV.

Here’s the plot summary, followed by the trailer:

Based on true events, “Tenzing” chronicles the little-known story of Tenzing Norgay (Phuntsok), a gifted Himalayan climber who, alongside New Zealand mountaineer Edmund Hillary (Hiddleston), became the first to summit Mount Everest. Encouraged by his wife, Dawa (Lhamo), Tenzing finds an ally in expedition secretary Jill Henderson (Balfe). Together, they persuade Colonel John Hunt (Dafoe) that Tenzing belongs on the British climbing team, rather than merely serving it. Where Western climbers see “Everest” as something to be conquered, Tenzing reveres “Chomolungma” as the sacred mother goddess. What follows is an ascent defined as much by the tensions between backgrounds, classes and competing ambitions as by the perils of the mountain itself. But high above the world, empire, rank and aspiration fall away, leaving two outsiders bound by mutual respect and trust — and for Tenzing, the fulfillment of both a lifelong dream and a spiritual calling.
